citations.quote: A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field) constructed in this
library (The real numbers) and carrying its order (Order on the reals).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
Which metric axiom list this library uses, the live naming fork between semimetric and pseudometric, and why extended metrics are not treated here records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
(Maximum and minimum of a set, Every nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The rationals embed densely in the reals), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
Order on the natural numbers, which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$, proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an at most countable dense set $C\subseteq X$. Since $\mu(X)=1$ and $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ by [F7], $X$ is nonempty, so $C$ is nonempty. Let $\mathbb Q_{>0}$ be the positive rationals. By [F3], $C\times\mathbb Q_{>0}$ is a nonempty at most countable set, so [F4] gives a surjection $e:\mathbb N\to C\times\mathbb Q_{>0}$. The composite of $e$ with $(c,q)\mapsto B(c,q)$ is a surjection onto $\mathcal B_0:=\{B(c,q):c\in C,\ q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\}$, so $\mathcal B_0$ is at most countable. Each of its members is open by [F2]. It is a base: if $x\in U$ with $U$ open, choose $r>0$ so $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, choose $c\in C$ with $\|x-c\|_X<r/3$, and choose rational $q$ with $\|x-c\|_X<q<r-\|x-c\|_X$ using density in [F3]. Then $x\in B(c,q)$, and for every $z\in B(c,q)$ the triangle inequality gives $\|z-x\|_X<q+\|x-c\|_X<r$, so $x\in B(c,q)\subseteq U$.

Let $\mathcal N:=\{B\in\mathcal B_0:\mu(B)=0\}$ and $N:= igcup\mathcal N$. By [F3], $\mathcal N$ is at most countable; by [F5] $N$ is Borel, and by [F6] its measure is zero (with the empty-family case giving $N=\varnothing$). If $x\in N$, a zero-measure open basis ball contains $x$, so $x
otin\operatorname{supp}\mu$. If $x
otin N$, every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains some $B\in\mathcal B_0$ with $x\in B\subseteq U$ by step 1.1; since $B
otin\mathcal N$, $\mu(B)>0$, and [F6] gives $\mu(U)\ge\mu(B)>0$. Thus $X\setminus N=\operatorname{supp}\mu$, which is Borel and has measure one.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked current Proof 1.1–2.1 and all direct supplier statements. The nonempty dense set and positive-rational radius product admit one enumeration without AC; its image is the ball base (least-index fibers give countability). current_manifest_record.title: Hellinger stability of function-space posteriors under data perturbations
current_manifest_record.statement:
Let $X,Y$ be separable real Banach spaces, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Assume there is a bounded Borel subset $E\subseteq D$ with $\mu_0(E)>0$. Give $D$ the relative norm topology and trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $R>0$ and let $\Phi:D\times Y\to\mathbb R$ be jointly continuous and measurable from $(D\times Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal B(Y))$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of the extended real line after including its finite real values there. Suppose $M_1,M_2:[0,\infty)^2\to[0,\infty)$ are Borel and nondecreasing in each argument, and for all $u\in D$ and $y,y'\in B_Y(0,R):=\{v\in Y:\|v\|_Y\le R\}$,
$$\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(R,\|u\|_X),\qquad |\Phi(u;y)-\Phi(u;y')|\le M_2(R,\|u\|_X)\|y-y'\|_Y.$$
Assume
$$J_R:=\int_D e^{M_1(R,\|u\|_X)}\bigl(1+M_2(R,\|u\|_X)^2\bigr)\,\mu_0(du)<\infty.$$
For each fixed datum $y\in B_Y(0,R)$, define the evidence and posterior by
$$Z(y):=\int_D e^{-\Phi(u;y)}\,\mu_0(du),\qquad \Pi^y(du):=Z(y)^{-1}e^{-\Phi(u;y)}\,\mu_0(du).$$
Then there is $z_R>0$ such that $z_R\le Z(y)\le J_R$ for every $y\in B_Y(0,R)$, and, with the library root-L2 Hellinger distance $h$,
$$h(\Pi^y,\Pi^{y'})\le C_R\|y-y'\|_Y,\qquad C_R:=\frac{\sqrt{J_R}}{2\sqrt{z_R}}+\frac{J_R}{2z_R},$$
for all $y,y'\in B_Y(0,R)$. This is a pointwise fixed-data statement; no observation law or conditional-law version is asserted. In a separate branch, if AC is assumed for the library density/total-variation comparison convention, then
$$\|\Pi^y-\Pi^{y'}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(\Pi^y,\Pi^{y'})\le C_R\|y-y'\|_Y,$$
where $\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal B(D)}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Fix two objects $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, distinct from one another and neither of
them a real number (The real numbers), and set

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}.$$

This is a **new object**, introduced here explicitly with its own order and its
own partial arithmetic. It is not an enlargement of the field $\mathbb{R}$, and
no operation of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) is redefined by
anything below.

**The order.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ declare

$$a \le b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a = -\infty \ \text{ or } \ b = +\infty \ \text{ or } \ \big(a, b \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } a \le b \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\big),$$

with $\mathbb{R}$ ordered as in Order on the reals, and write $a < b$ for
"$a \le b$ and $a \ne b$" as usual (Partial order and partially ordered set).

**$(\overline{\mathbb{R}}, \le)$ is a totally ordered set, and the inclusion of
$\mathbb{R}$ preserves and reflects the order.** All four checks are immediate
from the displayed clauses.

- *Reflexive.* For $a = \pm\infty$ one of the first two clauses applies; for
  $a \in \mathbb{R}$ the third does, since $a \le a$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Antisymmetric.* Suppose $a \le b$ and $b \le a$. If $a = -\infty$ then
  $b \le a$ forces $b = -\infty$, since the clause $a = +\infty$ fails and $b, a$
  are not both real. Symmetrically $b = -\infty$ forces $a = -\infty$, and
  $a = +\infty$ or $b = +\infty$ forces the other to be $+\infty$. In the one
  remaining situation $a$ and $b$ are both real and antisymmetry is that of
  $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Transitive.* Let $a \le b \le c$. If $a = -\infty$ or $c = +\infty$ the
  conclusion is one of the first two clauses. Otherwise $a \ne -\infty$ forces,
  in $a \le b$, either $b = +\infty$ or $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$; and $c \ne +\infty$
  forces, in $b \le c$, either $b = -\infty$ or $b, c \in \mathbb{R}$. The value
  $b = +\infty$ is incompatible with the second alternative pair, so $b$ is real,
  hence so are $a$ and $c$, and transitivity is that of $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Total.* If $a = -\infty$ or $b = +\infty$ then $a \le b$; if $b = -\infty$ or
  $a = +\infty$ then $b \le a$; otherwise both are real and the order of
  $\mathbb{R}$ is total.
- *Preserved and reflected.* For $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ the first two clauses fail,
  so $a \le b$ in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ says exactly $a \le b$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

In particular $-\infty$ is the least and $+\infty$ the greatest element of
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, and $-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

**Reflection.** Extend negation by

$$-(+\infty) := -\infty, \qquad -(-\infty) := +\infty,$$

keeping the field negative on $\mathbb{R}$. The resulting map
$\nu : \overline{\mathbb{R}} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$, $\nu(a) = -a$, satisfies
$\nu(\nu(a)) = a$ and

$$a \le b \iff -b \le -a \qquad (a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}).$$

For $a$ and $b$ real this is the elementwise order reversal in $\mathbb{R}$:
translation invariance (Order is preserved by adding a constant and by adding inequalities) applied with the constant $-a-b$
turns $a < b$ into $-b < -a$ and, applied with the constant $a+b$, turns it back,
while $a = b$ holds exactly when $-a = -b$. In every other case both sides are
decided by the first two clauses of the order: $a = -\infty$ makes both sides
true, as does $b = +\infty$, and if $a \ne -\infty$, $b \ne +\infty$ and $a, b$
are not both real then one of $a = +\infty$, $b = -\infty$ holds and both sides
are false.

**Partial addition.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ the sum $a + b$ is
defined by

- $a + b$ = the field sum, when $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$;
- $a + b := +\infty$ when $a = +\infty$ and $b \ne -\infty$, or $b = +\infty$ and $a \ne -\infty$;
- $a + b := -\infty$ when $a = -\infty$ and $b \ne +\infty$, or $b = -\infty$ and $a \ne +\infty$;

and **the two sums $(+\infty) + (-\infty)$ and $(-\infty) + (+\infty)$ are left
undefined**. Addition is commutative where defined, and

$$-(a + b) = (-a) + (-b),$$

each side being defined exactly when the other is: the excluded pairs
$\{+\infty, -\infty\}$ are exchanged by $\nu$, and the three clauses above are
exchanged accordingly.

**Partial multiplication.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ the product $ab$
is defined by

- $ab$ = the field product, when $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$;
- $ab := +\infty$ when one of $a, b$ is $\pm\infty$, the other is $\ne 0$, and both are $> 0$ or both are $< 0$;
- $ab := -\infty$ when one of $a, b$ is $\pm\infty$, the other is $\ne 0$, and one is $> 0$ and the other $< 0$;

and **every product with one factor $0$ and the other $\pm\infty$ is left
undefined**. The comparisons $> 0$ and $< 0$ here are taken in the order above,
under which $+\infty > 0 > -\infty$.

**Nothing else is defined.** There is no subtraction, no division, no
exponentiation and no absolute value on $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ in this library;
where such an expression is wanted it is written out in the two defined
operations, and where a case falls in the undefined list the statement carries an
explicit hypothesis saying so.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad \int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$. Define
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu:=\{x\in X: \mu(U)>0\text{ for every norm-open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}.$$
Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu$ is Borel and $\mu(\operatorname{supp}\mu)=1$.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, both dominated by a specified common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. For supplied finite-valued nonnegative measurable density representatives $p=dP/d\mu$ and $q=dQ/d\mu$ in the convention of [[def-likelihood-density]], the **root-L2 Hellinger distance** is

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int \bigl(\sqrt p-\sqrt q\bigr)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The square roots are measurable: for every real $r$, $\{\sqrt p>r\}$ is the whole space if $r<0$ and equals $\{p>r^2\}$ if $r\ge0$, and the same holds for $q$ ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]). The arithmetic and lattice rules make the nonnegative integrand measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). It is integrable because $(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\le p+q$ and the integral is additive on nonnegative functions ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]), so its integral is at most $P(\mathsf X)+Q(\mathsf X)=2$.

The generic density-selection convention [[def-likelihood-density]] assumes the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. When $p$ and $q$ are explicitly given, this displayed integral requires no further choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the imported density-representative convention. Let $P,Q$ be probability laws on a measurable space, both dominated by one specified common sigma-finite positive measure. Then the root-L2 Hellinger distance from [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]] is independent of the choice of common dominating measure. With the library convention $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]],

$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(P,Q),\qquad h(P,Q)^2\le 2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$x, y, z \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,z) - d(y,z)| \le d(x,y),$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-abs-value]]).
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$
A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras).

A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

current_manifest_record.title: Exact posterior second moment and contraction bound for a Gaussian sequence inverse problem
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

derivations.claim: For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$.

For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$: independence of the prior element from the noise element and independence within each coordinate family factor the probabilities of finite coordinate rectangles into the product of the pair marginals, and [F5] extends this factorization from the generating rectangles to the corresponding product-Borel events. Each $Y_j$ is a measurable function of its pair $(\theta_j,\xi_j)$, so $(\theta_J,Y_J)$ is independent of $Y_{J^c}$. For the finite block, put $D_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_j^2)_{j\in J}$ and $D_s=\operatorname{diag}(s_j)_{j\in J}$. [F2] gives posterior covariance $$D_\tau-D_\tau D_s^T(D_sD_\tau D_s^T+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}D_sD_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(v_j)_{j\in J},$$ and posterior mean with coordinates $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$. Since each $v_j>0$, the Gaussian coordinates have zero cross-covariance, and repeated application of [F10] shows they are independent. Thus the finite-block conditional law is the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1. Independence of the complement makes this also the conditional law given the full data: the conditional identity first holds on data rectangles by finite-block conditioning and independence, and [F5] extends it to all product-Borel data events. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space.

Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. The norm-Borel sigma-algebra of $\ell^2$ equals the trace of the product Borel sigma-algebra: finite-support rational sequences are countable and dense (truncate a square-summable sequence and approximate the retained coordinates), and for $a\in\ell^2$ and $r>0$, $B_{\ell^2}(a,r)=\ell^2\cap\bigcup_{\substack{q\in\mathbb Q\\0<q<r^2}}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}:\sum_{j=1}^N(x_j-a_j)^2\le q\}$. Thus every norm ball, and hence every norm-open set, is trace product-Borel; conversely the coordinate maps on normed $\ell^2$ are continuous. Therefore the restriction of $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ is measurable on its norm-Borel sets. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation.

For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed.

Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity.

For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate.

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume AC. Observe $Y=\theta+Z$ with fixed truth $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and proper prior $\theta\sim N(0,1)$. Let $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^y\phi(x)\,dx$, let $z>0$ be the unique number satisfying $\Phi(z)=0.975$, and put $r=z/\sqrt2$. The posterior is $N(Y/2,1/2)$, so the central interval $I(Y)=[Y/2-r,Y/2+r]$ has posterior mass exactly $0.95$ for every $Y$. At the fixed truth $\theta_*=2r+1$, its frequentist coverage is $P\{1\le Z\le4r+1\}<0.95$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length,
Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], the standard normal probability law of [F2] is supplied. Its density φ is positive and symmetric and integrates to one, so Φ is continuous and strictly increasing, with Φ(0)=1/2 and Φ(y)→1 as y→∞. Choose B>0 with Φ(B)>0.975. By [F3] on [0,B], there is a unique z>0 with Φ(z)=0.975.

The prior density times likelihood is proportional to $\exp\{-\tfrac12[\theta^2+(Y-\theta)^2]\}=\exp\{-(\theta-Y/2)^2\}$ times a factor independent of $\theta$. Normalization gives posterior law $N(Y/2,1/2)$.
Under the fixed truth $\theta_*=2r+1$, write $Y=\theta_*+Z$. The event $\theta_*\in I(Y)$ is equivalent to $|Z-\theta_*|\le2r$, hence to $1\le Z\le4r+1$.

The interval membership graph is $\{(Y,\theta):|\theta-Y/2|\le r\}$, the inverse image of the closed interval $[-r,r]$ under a continuous map. It is closed, hence Borel, so the sampling membership event is measurable.
Under that posterior, $(\theta-Y/2)/\sqrt{1/2}$ is standard normal. The interval radius $r=z/\sqrt2$ therefore gives posterior mass $\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=0.975-0.025=0.95$ for every observed $Y$.
Since the standard normal density is positive and symmetric, $P(1\le Z\le4r+1)<P(Z\ge0)=1/2<0.95$. Thus the interval has posterior mass $0.95$ but frequentist coverage below $0.95$ at $\theta_*$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

current_manifest_record.title: Infinite-dimensional Gaussian random-walk reverse flow is singular
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix $\beta\in(0,1]$. Let
$H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its complete coordinate basis positively indexed as $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $e_j$ has its nonzero coordinate at $j-1$. Write $u_j=\langle u,e_j\rangle$ for coefficients in this basis throughout. Take
mutually independent standard normal variables $(X_j,Y_j)_{j\ge1}$ and set
$$U=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2}X_je_j,\qquad \xi=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2}Y_je_j.$$
These series converge almost surely in $H$ and define independent centered
Borel Gaussian random elements with the same law $\mu_0$. Define the Gaussian
random-walk proposal $V=U+\beta\xi$, its probability kernel
$$Q_\beta(u,B)=\mu_0(\{z\in H:u+\beta z\in B\}),$$
its forward flow $\eta(du,dv)=\mu_0(du)Q_\beta(u,dv)$, and its transpose
$\eta^\top(C)=\eta(\{(u,v):(v,u)\in C\})$. Then $\eta$ and $\eta^\top$ are
mutually singular: a Borel set $A_\beta\subseteq H\times H$ satisfies
$$\eta(A_\beta)=1,\qquad \eta^\top(A_\beta)=0.$$
For the same reference law and scale, the pCN proposal flow is symmetric.
