citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ of $\Omega$, and unisolvent reference finite elements assembled on that mesh. Thus the mesh is a finite face-to-face cover by nondegenerate affine simplices with disjoint interiors, and each local finite-element degree-of-freedom map is bijective on its polynomial space. Fix coefficient spaces $\Theta_h=\mathbb R^m$, $V_h=\mathbb R^n$, and $Y_h=\mathbb R^s$ with their standard Euclidean inner products, where $m,n,s\ge1$. Let $Q_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $O_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be open with $Q_h\subseteq O_h$.

A **finite-element PDE model** in this contract consists of a continuously differentiable residual map $R_h:O_h\times V_h\to V_h$ and a continuously differentiable observation map $G_h:O_h\times V_h\to Y_h$. It must supply a continuously differentiable state branch $S_h:O_h\to V_h$ satisfying $R_h(q,S_h(q))=0$ for every $q\in O_h$. For every $q\in Q_h$, this branch must be the specified unique admissible state and the matrix $D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))$ must be invertible. The discrete forward map is $F_h(q):=G_h(q,S_h(q))$. The unisolvent finite-element degrees of freedom identify $V_h$ with its coefficient space; all matrix transposes below are in the fixed Euclidean coefficient inner products.

For data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, reference parameter $q_0\in\Theta_h$, and $\alpha>0$, the discrete nonlinear Tikhonov objective is
$$
\Phi_h(q):=\frac12\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2\qquad(q\in Q_h).
$$
Define the finite-dimensional objective before eliminating the state by
$$
J_h(q,u):=\frac12\|G_h(q,u)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2.
$$
The symbols $\nabla_uJ_h$ and $\nabla_qJ_h$ denote the Euclidean gradient vectors representing the two partial derivative functionals. At an admissible $q$, the **exact discrete adjoint** $p_h(q)\in V_h$ is the unique solution of
$$
\bigl(D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q)=\nabla_uJ_h(q,S_h(q)).
$$
The associated discrete-adjoint gradient vector is
$$
g_h(q):=\nabla_qJ_h(q,S_h(q))-\bigl(D_qR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q).
$$
The next lemma proves that this vector is the gradient of $\Phi_h$; the definition itself asserts no minimizer exists and no gradient iteration converges.

An **admissibility predicate** is a specified finite-time test $\operatorname{adm}_h(q)$ that decides whether $q\in Q_h$ and checks the model's stated coefficient, boundary, mesh, and time-step hypotheses before a PDE solve. For an explicit time discretization, a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition (CFL condition) is a method-specific bound relating the time step to the mesh and the discrete evolution operator; no universal CFL threshold is part of this definition. A true predicate result certifies that the declared model hypotheses hold for that input, not merely that a heuristic check passed.

The model must also supply an exact finite-dimensional projection routine which returns $P_{Q_h}(z)$ for a queried $z\in\Theta_h$ in finite time or reports failure only when its declared finite call budget is exhausted. The unique nearest point exists because $Q_h$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, but an operational routine for computing it is an additional part of this contract.

A solver routine with declared nonnegative state and adjoint tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and a finite solve budget must return either `failure` or approximate state and adjoint vectors $\widetilde u,\widetilde p$ together with certified finite bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p,\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$. The residual bounds have the exact-system meaning $\|R_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_u$ and $\|(D_uR_h(q,u))^T\widetilde p-\nabla_uJ_h(q,u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_p$, where $u=S_h(q)$; both must satisfy $\rho_u\le\tau_u$ and $\rho_p\le\tau_p$. In particular, an adjoint residual evaluated at $\widetilde u$ alone does not certify $\rho_p$ unless the model also bounds the resulting state and derivative-data defects. With $u=S_h(q)$ and $p=p_h(q)$, the model must certify
$$
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{V_h}\le\eta_u,\qquad \|p-\widetilde p\|_{V_h}\le\eta_p,\qquad \|p\|_{V_h}\le P,
$$
$$
\|\nabla_qJ_h(q,u)-\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{\Theta_h}\le L_{J,u}\eta_u,
$$
$$
\|(D_qR_h(q,u))^T-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le L_{R,u}\eta_u,\qquad \|(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le M_q,
$$
and $\|G_h(q,u)-G_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{Y_h}\le L_{G,u}\eta_u$. It then returns
$$
\widetilde g:=\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\widetilde p,\qquad \widetilde F:=G_h(q,\widetilde u),
$$
All constants and state/adjoint error bounds must be justified for the chosen model with every derivative-data, geometry, quadrature, and algebraic-solve defect retained. Certified residual bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p$ do not by themselves imply $\eta_u,\eta_p$; a separate model-valid stability estimate is required. The proposition below derives the resulting $\varepsilon_g$ and $\varepsilon_F$ bounds. An objective-evaluation routine must return in its finite budget either `failure` or an interval $[\ell_h(q),u_h(q)]$ containing the exact value $\Phi_h(q)$; `failure` is permitted only when a required state/adjoint solve fails its contract or the evaluation-call budget is exhausted. Exact evaluation is the degenerate-interval case. Projection and objective-evaluation calls consume the algorithm's finite evaluation budget. Each routine must return within its declared budget or report failure.

If a continuous model $F$ is also supplied, an optional mesh certificate $\varepsilon_{\rm mesh}$ must separately bound the claimed continuous-to-discrete error, such as $\|F_h(q)-F(q)\|$ or $\|\nabla\Phi_h(q)-\nabla\Phi(q)\|$. The state and adjoint algebraic residual certificates do not imply this mesh certificate.

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $V=\mathbb R^n$ have its standard Euclidean inner product. Let $R:O\times V\to V$ and $G:O\times V\to Y$ be continuously differentiable, where $Y$ is a finite-dimensional real Euclidean space. Suppose $S:O\to V$ is continuously differentiable, $R(q,S(q))=0$ for every $q\in O$, and the matrix $D_uR(q,S(q))$ is invertible at a fixed $q\in O$. Let $y\in Y$, $q_0\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\alpha>0$. Define
$$
J(q,u):=\frac12\|G(q,u)-y\|_Y^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_2^2,\qquad \Phi(q):=J(q,S(q)).
$$
Let $p\in V$ be the unique solution of
$$
\bigl(D_uR(q,S(q))\bigr)^T p=\nabla_uJ(q,S(q)),
$$
where $\nabla_qJ$ and $\nabla_uJ$ are the Euclidean representatives of the two partial derivative functionals. Then for every $h\in\mathbb R^m$,
$$
D\Phi(q)[h]=\left\langle \nabla_qJ(q,S(q))-\bigl(D_qR(q,S(q))\bigr)^T p,\ h\right\rangle_{\mathbb R^m}.
$$
Consequently $\nabla\Phi(q)=\nabla_qJ(q,S(q))-(D_qR(q,S(q)))^Tp$. This is the exact derivative of the specified finite-dimensional model; it asserts no convergence of an iteration that changes $q$.

Assume a finite-element PDE model satisfying the admissibility and certificate contract, with nonempty closed convex coefficient set $Q_h$, discrete Tikhonov objective $\Phi_h$ using reference coefficient $q_0$, a state/adjoint solve routine, an exact projection routine, an objective interval routine, and finite solve and evaluation budgets. Let the input be an initial coefficient $q_{\rm init}\in Q_h$, data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, noise bound $\delta\ge0$, penalty $\alpha>0$, state and adjoint residual tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p\ge0$, discrepancy factor $\kappa\ge1$, stationarity tolerance $\tau_g\ge0$, scaling parameter $L>0$, and positive integer budgets $N_{\rm iter}$, $N_{\rm solve}$, $N_{\rm eval}$, and $N_{\rm backtrack}$. The global budget $N_{\rm solve}$ counts state and adjoint solves; $N_{\rm eval}$ counts exact projections and objective-interval evaluations. The scaling parameter $L$ is only a positive step-size scale; it is not assumed to be a Lipschitz constant. The algorithm returns a coefficient, one status from `converged`, `discrepancy-stopped`, `linear-solve-failed`, `inadmissible`, or `budget-exhausted`, and any diagnostics certified at that coefficient.

1. If $q_{\rm init}\notin Q_h$ or the model's exact admissibility predicate is false at $q_{\rm init}$, return status `inadmissible` without solving a PDE. Otherwise set $q:=q_{\rm init}$.

2. For $k=0,\ldots,N_{\rm iter}$, first check the finite-time admissibility predicate, which includes membership in $Q_h$. If it is false, return `inadmissible`. If no global solve or evaluation budget remains, return `budget-exhausted`.

3. Call the state/adjoint solver at $q$ with tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and the remaining solve budget. If it returns `failure`, if either certified residual bound exceeds its declared tolerance, or if any required state/adjoint error estimate or derivative bound is missing or invalid, return `linear-solve-failed`. Otherwise receive $\widetilde g_h$, $\widetilde F_h$, $\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$ and set $\varepsilon_g=(L_{J,u}+L_{R,u}P)\eta_u+M_q\eta_p$ and $\varepsilon_F=L_{G,u}\eta_u$.

4. Use the exact projection routine to compute $P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)$. If the routine fails or the evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`. Set $\widetilde\rho:=L\|q-P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)\|_2$. If $\widetilde\rho+\varepsilon_g\le\tau_g$, return `converged` with stationarity upper bound $\widetilde\rho+\varepsilon_g$. This status means only that the exact projected-gradient residual of the discrete objective is within tolerance; it is not a claim that an iterate sequence converges or that $q$ is a global minimizer.

5. Compute $d^+:=\|\widetilde F_h-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}+\varepsilon_F$. If $d^+\le\kappa\delta$, return `discrepancy-stopped` with data-residual upper bound $d^+$. This status certifies only the discrete model's data discrepancy.

6. If $k=N_{\rm iter}$, return `budget-exhausted` at the current coefficient with its current diagnostics. Otherwise, evaluate the current objective using its certified interval $[\ell_h(q),u_h(q)]$. If the evaluation fails because a required state or adjoint solve fails its contract, return `linear-solve-failed`; if the global solve or evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`.

7. For $j=0,\ldots,N_{\rm backtrack}-1$, set $t_j=2^{-j}/L$ and use the exact projection routine to compute $q_j=P_{Q_h}(q-t_j\widetilde g_h)$. If projection fails or the evaluation budget is exhausted, return `budget-exhausted`. Reject this trial and continue to the next $j$ if $q_j=q$ or its admissibility predicate is false. Otherwise evaluate a certified interval $[\ell_h(q_j),u_h(q_j)]$. If evaluation fails because a required linear solve fails its contract, return `linear-solve-failed`; if it only exhausts the finite evaluation budget, return `budget-exhausted`. Accept the first trial with $u_h(q_j)\le\ell_h(q)$, set $q:=q_j$, and continue to the next outer iteration.

8. If no trial is accepted within the backtracking budget, return `budget-exhausted` at the current coefficient.

The global solve budget counts all primal and adjoint solves used both at iterates and in objective trials. The evaluation budget counts every projection and objective-interval call. Any continuous-to-discrete mesh bound is reported separately by the model contract and is never inferred from the algebraic state or adjoint residuals.

Let $Q_h\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a nonempty closed convex set and let $q\in Q_h$. Write $u=S_h(q)$, $p=p_h(q)$, and $g_h(q)=\nabla\Phi_h(q)$ for the exact finite-element state, exact discrete adjoint, and exact discrete-objective gradient. Suppose a solver supplies $\widetilde u,\widetilde p$, a forward output $\widetilde F_h=G_h(q,\widetilde u)$, and a computed gradient $\widetilde g_h=\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\widetilde p$. It also supplies finite nonnegative bounds $\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$ satisfying
$$
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{V_h}\le\eta_u,\quad \|p-\widetilde p\|_{V_h}\le\eta_p,\quad \|p\|_{V_h}\le P,
$$
$$
\|\nabla_qJ_h(q,u)-\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)\|\le L_{J,u}\eta_u,
$$
$$
\|(D_qR_h(q,u))^T-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le L_{R,u}\eta_u,\quad \|(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le M_q,
$$
and $\|G_h(q,u)-G_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{Y_h}\le L_{G,u}\eta_u$. Define
$$
\varepsilon_g:=(L_{J,u}+L_{R,u}P)\eta_u+M_q\eta_p,\qquad \varepsilon_F:=L_{G,u}\eta_u.
$$
Then $\|\widetilde g_h-g_h(q)\|\le\varepsilon_g$ and $\|\widetilde F_h-F_h(q)\|_{Y_h}\le\varepsilon_F$. For $L>0$, define
$$
G_L(q):=L\bigl(q-P_{Q_h}(q-g_h(q)/L)\bigr),\qquad \widetilde G_L(q):=L\bigl(q-P_{Q_h}(q-\widetilde g_h/L)\bigr).
$$
Then $$\|G_L(q)\|_2\le\|\widetilde G_L(q)\|_2+\varepsilon_g,\qquad \|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}\le\|\widetilde F_h-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}+\varepsilon_F.$$
Thus the finite-element algorithm may certify discrete projected stationarity and discrete discrepancy from these bounds. The state and adjoint residuals must first be converted to valid $\eta_u,\eta_p$ bounds under the chosen model's hypotheses; raw residuals alone do not imply the asserted gradient or mesh error.

For any finite-element PDE model satisfying its solver and admissibility contract, the finite-budget Tikhonov algorithm returns after finitely many operations one of `converged`, `discrepancy-stopped`, `linear-solve-failed`, `inadmissible`, or `budget-exhausted`. A `converged` return satisfies the exact discrete projected-gradient bound $\|G_L(q)\|_2\le\tau_g$; a `discrepancy-stopped` return satisfies $\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}\le\kappa\delta$. Every accepted safeguarded step has nonincreasing exact discrete objective $\Phi_h$. `inadmissible` and `linear-solve-failed` are returned only on the corresponding failed predicate or solver-certificate checks. `budget-exhausted` asserts no optimizer or continuous-model accuracy.

derivations.claim: At $q=0$, the unique state is $u=0$ because $R(0,u)=u=0$. Its state residual is $|R(0,0)|=0$, so the state solve is exact. Also $D_uR=1$ and $D_qR=-1$.

Here $J(q,u)=\frac12(u-1)^2+\frac12q^2$, so $\nabla_uJ(0,0)=-1$ and $\nabla_qJ(0,0)=0$. The exact adjoint equation is $p=-1$. By [F1], the exact reduced gradient is $0-(-1)(-1)=-1$. The same value follows by differentiating $\Phi(q)=\tfrac12(q-1)^2+\tfrac12q^2$.

If an unchecked iterative adjoint returns $\widetilde p=1$, its computed reduced gradient is $\widetilde g=\nabla_qJ(0,0)-(D_qR)^T\widetilde p=0-(-1)(1)=1$, the opposite sign. Its exact adjoint-equation residual is $|(D_uR)^T\widetilde p-\nabla_uJ(0,0)|=|1-(-1)|=2$.

With declared adjoint residual tolerance $\tau_p=1$, the residual in step 2.2 exceeds tolerance. By [F2] and [F4], the algorithm rejects this vector as a solver result with status `linear-solve-failed`; it cannot receive `converged`. Step 2.2 nevertheless exhibits opposite gradient signs when the unchecked vector is substituted. Thus an exact state solve alone does not determine the gradient sign. Treating $\widetilde p$ as a contract-valid solver result would violate the adjoint-residual requirement and the proposition's gradient-error certificate [F3].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$ and $R>0$. For every $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$ there exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $d,\alpha,\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega\!\left(\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}\right),$$
where $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the trace quotient and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the constant quotient, and
$$\omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

Let $d\ge3$ and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ for the domain, collar, ellipticity bounds and exponent $0<\alpha<1$ defining that class. Extend $\gamma$ by $1$ outside $\Omega$, using its continuous representative on $\overline\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$, $\gamma_e-1$ has support contained in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and
$$\min\{m,1\}\le\gamma_e\le M,\qquad \sup_{\mathbb R^d}|\gamma_e|\le\max\{R,1\},\qquad \sup_{\mathbb R^d}|\partial_j\gamma_e|\le R,\qquad [\partial_j\gamma_e]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le R.$$
Here the Hölder seminorm is $[f]_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{x\ne y}|f(x)-f(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, and $j=1,\ldots,d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega)$ be a real almost-everywhere class with $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$. Set $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with quotient norm $\|[U]\|_{\mathcal D}:=\inf_{w\in H_0^1(\Omega)}\|U+w\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$, and let $\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$ be its continuous conjugate-linear dual. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, let $u_{\gamma,f}$ be the unique element of the coset $f$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{\nabla z}\,dx=0\qquad(z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)).$$
Define the weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$ by
$$\bigl(\Lambda_\gamma f\bigr)(g):=\int_\Omega\gamma\,\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{\nabla V_g}\,dx,$$
where $V_g$ is any representative of $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$. The trace quotient identification makes $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ the $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data space with its trace quotient norm. Constants lie in the kernel of $\Lambda_\gamma$, and its range functionals annihilate constants; hence $\Lambda_\gamma$ induces $\dot\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1\to(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*$, the quotient Dirichlet-to-Neumann map used for Calderón stability. Well-posedness, independence from the representative $V_g$, boundedness and the induced quotient map are established by the well-posedness result cited below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $0<m\le M<\infty$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with its quotient norm. For every boundary trace class $f\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u_{\gamma,f}\in f$ such that
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla z}\,dx=0\qquad	ext{for every }z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C).$$
For every $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the value $\int_\Omega\gamma
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla V_g}\,dx$ is independent of the representative $V_g\in g$ and defines a bounded linear map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)	o\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$. Constants are in its kernel and its range functionals annihilate constants.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be real measurable conductivities with $0<m\le\gamma_j\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Put $\mathcal D=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $E=\mathcal D/\mathbb C\mathbf1$, both with their quotient norms. For $f_j\in\mathcal D$, let $u_j$ be the weak $\gamma_j$-conductivity solution with trace class $f_j$. Then
$$((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(f_2)=\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}\,dx.$$
The exact norm equality
$$\|\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D,\mathcal D^*)}=\|\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(E,E^*)}=:\delta$$
holds, and consequently the integral above has absolute value at most $\delta\|[f_1]\|_E\|[f_2]\|_E$, and at most $\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. Here $[f_j]$ denotes the coset modulo constants; the stars denote continuous conjugate-linear duals.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $s\ge1$, and let $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^d$ be orthonormal. Put $\zeta=s(e_1-ie_2)$ and
$$p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi.$$
Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$, and set
$$\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p_\zeta(\xi)|^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,\qquad \|u\|_{X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$$
For every fixed Schwartz function $\phi$, a constant $C=C(d,\phi)$ independent of $s,e_1,e_2$ satisfies, for all Schwartz $u$,
$$\|\phi u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{X_\zeta^{-1/2}},\qquad \|\phi u\|_{X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
Consequently
$$\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}},\qquad \|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
The norms are finite on Schwartz space; the values of the weights on the measure-zero characteristic sphere do not affect them. All four maps extend continuously to the completions in the respective input norms.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, a ball $B\subset\mathbb R^d$, and $K>0$. Let $\gamma\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$ be real and positive, equal to $1$ outside $B$, and put $a=\nabla\log\gamma$. Suppose
$$\|a\|_\infty+[a]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le K.$$
Define the compactly supported distribution $q$ and its multiplication form by
$$\langle q,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla v+\frac14\int |a|^2v,\qquad \langle m_q u,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla(uv)+\frac14\int |a|^2uv.$$
These pairings are complex bilinear. For the angular Fourier norms with $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$, there are constants $C,s_0\ge1$, depending only on $d,\alpha,B,K$, such that for every null phase $\zeta$ of length $\sqrt2s$ with $s\ge s_0$,
$$\|m_q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\to\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le Cs^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}\le\frac12.$$
There is $r_\zeta\in\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\cap H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$U_\zeta(x)=e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta(x)),\qquad (-\Delta+q)U_\zeta=0,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le2\|q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}.$$
The equation uses the multiplication form above against compactly supported smooth tests. For the phases $\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)$ associated to $k$ and $P\perp k$, if $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}\}$, then for either sign,
$$\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\left(\|q\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{-1/2}}^2+\|r_{\zeta_\pm}\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{1/2}}^2\right)ds\,d\eta\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $k\in\mathbb R^d$, and fix an oriented two-plane $P\perp k$. For a unit vector $\eta\in P$, let $\eta^\perp$ be its positive quarter turn. For $s\ge|k|/2$, put $r(s)=\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}$ and
$$\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)=\pm s\eta+i(k/2\pm r(s)\eta^\perp).$$
These phases are null, have length $\sqrt2s$, and sum to $ik$. Use the unitary angular Fourier convention and the norms $\dot X_\zeta^b,X_\zeta^b$ with inhomogeneous weight $s+|p_\zeta|$, where $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$. For a fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f):=\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)}^{-1/2}}^2\,ds\,d\eta.$$
Here $d\eta$ is arclength, either sign can be used, and the derivative is distributional. For $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C^d)$,
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\|f\|_2^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,\phi$. If $f\in H^1$, also
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le\frac C\lambda\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$
Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$, put $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$, and define $\omega_2(f,h)=\sup_{|y|\le h}\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2$. For $h>0$ one consequently has
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C_\rho\left[\frac{\|f\|_2^2}{\lambda h^2}+\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\omega_2(f,h)^2\right].$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Extend both coefficients by $1$ using [F1], and fix a ball $B$ containing $[0,1]^d$ and a neighborhood of it. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ and $a_j=
abla\log\gamma_j$. These are globally $C^1$ and $C^{0,\alpha}$, respectively, and $a_j$ has support in $\overline{\Omega'}$. Their supremum and Hölder bounds are uniform: the positive lower bound $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ gives $|a_j|\le C_dR/m_*$; on $|x-y|\le1$, expand $
abla\gamma_j(x)/\gamma_j(x)-
abla\gamma_j(y)/\gamma_j(y)$, using the derivative Hölder bound and $|\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(y)|\le\sqrt dR|x-y|$; on larger distances use twice the supremum. Thus [F4] applies uniformly. Let $q_j=	frac12\operatorname{div}a_j+	frac14|a_j|^2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$, with bilinear distribution pairings as in [F4].

The Liouville form identity is $\int
abla v\cdot
abla w+\langle q_j,vwangle=\int\gamma_j
abla(v/g_j)\cdot
abla(w/g_j)$ for $v,w\in H^1$ on a bounded set. Indeed $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ means $\langle q_j,vwangle=-\int
abla g_j\cdot
abla(g_j^{-1}vw)$; expanding this derivative gives the displayed identity term by term. All products are integrable since $g_j,g_j^{-1},
abla g_j$ are bounded and the factors are in $H^1$. The identity extends from smooth factors by local $H^1$ approximation; multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function with bounded derivative is continuous on $H^1$, as follows from the product rule and the same approximation. Since $g_j=1$ near $\partial\Omega$, the trace of $U_j$ equals that of $u_j:=U_j/g_j$. Testing the form identity with $w=g_jz$, first for compactly supported tests and then in $H_0^1$ by density, shows that each Schrödinger solution $U_j$ yields a weak conductivity solution $u_j$. Define the symmetric bilinear forms $B_j(V,W):=\int_\Omega
abla V\cdot
abla W+\langle q_j,VWangle$ and $b_j(v,w):=\int_\Omega\gamma_j
abla v\cdot
abla w$. Let $v_1$ be the $\gamma_1$-harmonic representative with trace $f_2$. Then $B_1(U_1,U_2)=b_1(u_1,U_2/g_1)=b_1(u_1,v_1)$, because $U_2/g_1$ has trace $f_2$ and its difference from $v_1$ is in $H_0^1$, which is annihilated by the weak equation for $u_1$. This equals $((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}f_1)(\overline{f_2}))$ by the weak DN definition [F2]. By symmetry, $B_2(U_1,U_2)=B_2(U_2,U_1)=b_2(u_2,U_1/g_2)=b_2(u_2,v_2)$, where $v_2$ is the $\gamma_2$-harmonic representative with trace $f_1$; Since $b_2$ is symmetric for real $\gamma_2$, this equals $b_2(v_2,u_2)=((\Lambda_{\gamma_2}f_1)(\overline{f_2}))$. Hence subtraction gives $\langle Q,U_1U_2angle=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(\overline{f_2})$. The compact support of $Q$ makes its whole-space pairing identical to its pairing on $\Omega$. Consequently $|\langle Q,U_1U_2angle|\le\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

Use the paired phases $\zeta_\pm=s(\pm\eta)+i(k/2\pm\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}\,\eta^\perp)$ of [F4]. For fixed $s$ their remainders satisfy $\|r_j\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. To verify this last uniform bound, the symbol inequality $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_{\zeta_j}(\xi)|)\le Cs$ follows by splitting $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. Apply the negative cutoff bound in [F3] to $\operatorname{div}a_j$ and $|a_j|^2$ as in [F4] to obtain $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. The two positive cutoff bounds then give $\|r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le C$ and $\|\nabla r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le Cs$. Multiplication by $g_j^{-1}e^{x\cdot\zeta_j}$ yields $\|u_j\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le Ce^{Cs}s$. Thus step 2.1 bounds the exact interior product by $C\delta e^{Cs}s^2$.

Fix a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\phi=1$ near $\overline{\Omega'}$. We first prove the modulated cutoff bound used for each linear remainder term. Let $u$ be Schwartz and write the Fourier convolution for $\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u$ with $h=\xi-\eta-k$. The symbol comparison and characteristic-sphere estimate proved in [F3] give, uniformly in the center $y$, $\int\langle\xi-y\rangle^{-L}(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})\,d\xi\le C_L$ for sufficiently large $L$, and $s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^2$, where $D_\zeta$ is distance to the characteristic sphere of $p_\zeta$. Since $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})$, these estimates imply $\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta-k)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C\langle k\rangle^2$. Indeed, after substituting $h=\xi-\eta-k$, the integrand is bounded by $C|\widehat\phi(h)|\langle k+h\rangle^2(1+D_\zeta(\eta+k+h)^{-1})$; use $\langle k+h\rangle^2\le C\langle k\rangle^2\langle h\rangle^2$, the rapid decay of $\widehat\phi$, and the uniform-center estimate. The same weighted Schur argument as in [F3] gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|u\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Applying the dual argument of [F3] to $\overline\phi e^{-ik\cdot x}$ yields $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, and hence also the same bound with the homogeneous positive-half norm on the left. Density in the weighted Fourier completions follows by truncating away from the characteristic sphere, as in [F3]. Since $2\le N=d+10$, this proves the modulation estimate used below with the stated exponent. Because $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$.

Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. For each linear or quadratic product, integral Cauchy–Schwarz and [F4] bound its average by $C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$, where $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. The same bound applies when the potential $q_j$ and remainder $r_l$ have different indices, because [F4] holds for either coefficient and either phase. Absorbing the fixed Fourier normalization gives $|\widehat Q(k)|\le C\delta e^{C\lambda}\lambda^2+C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$ whenever $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\langle k\rangle\}$. Replacing $k$ by $-k$ if needed accounts for the negative-sign Fourier convention.

Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For $t\ge1$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $Ct^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|$. The high-frequency contribution of the zero-order field is at most $Ct^{-1}$. For the divergence field $f=a_1-a_2$, split $f=\rho_h*f+(f-\rho_h*f)$ with a fixed nonnegative unit-mass mollifier. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$.

Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. Substituting step 5.1 in step 6.1 therefore gives $\mathcal Q\le C[\delta e^{D t^A}+t^{-\beta}]$ for a fixed $D>0$, after absorbing the polynomial factor $t^{d/2}\lambda^2$ into the exponential. For sufficiently small $0<\delta<t_0$, take $t=(\log(1/\delta)/(2D))^{1/A}\ge1$. The first term becomes $\sqrt\delta$, and the second is $C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\beta/A}$. The former is bounded by a constant times the latter, since $e^{-x/2}x^{\beta/A}$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $\mathcal Q\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\rho}$ with $\rho=\beta/A>0$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $
abla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $
abla\log H\cdot
abla w$. Test this identity with $w$ to obtain $\int H|
abla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hwangle$. The test is legitimate by $H^1$ approximation, since $Q$ is an $L^2$ field plus a divergence of an $L^2$ field and $Hw\in H_0^1(B)$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle Q,Hwangle|\le\mathcal Q\|Hw\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^d)}\le C\mathcal Q\|w\|_{H^1(B)}$. Since $H\ge m_*>0$, Poincaré in [F5] implies $\|w\|_{H^1(B)}\le C\mathcal Q$; if this norm is zero the estimate is immediate, otherwise divide the resulting quadratic inequality by it. Finally the mean value theorem on the bounded interval of possible $\log g_j$ gives $|\gamma_1-\gamma_2|=|e^{2\log g_1}-e^{2\log g_2}|\le2\max\{M,1\}|w|$. Thus $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\mathcal Q$. In particular $\delta=0$ forces equality of the coefficients.

Combine steps 7.1–8.1 for $0\le\delta<t_0$, reducing $t_0$ below $1/2$ if necessary. For $\delta\ge t_0$, use $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$ and enlarge $C$ to at least $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$. This is precisely the saturated modulus in the statement. Every bound used only the fixed class parameters, the geometry and $d,\alpha$, and the zero-data case was proved in step 8.1.

boundaries.evidence: X_d(R) need not be nonempty; all assertions quantify over a supplied pair and are vacuous otherwise. Proof Step 1.1.
delta=0 gives Q=0 by the large-scale limit and then conductivity equality by the coercive logarithmic energy identity. Proof Step 8.1.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $0\le\kappa<1$ and $R,S>0$. For every measurable $\mu$ supported in $D_R=\{|z|<R\}$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa$, there is a unique quasiconformal homeomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\bar\partial\Phi=\mu\partial\Phi,\qquad \Phi(z)=z+O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
Choose any fixed $2<r\le p_\kappa$ from the near-two inversion result, and put $\sigma=r-2>0$. Uniformly over all these coefficients,
$$\|\Phi-z\|_{W^{1,r}(\mathbb C)}+\|\Phi-z\|_\infty+[\Phi-z]_{C^{0,1-2/r}}\le C_{\kappa,r,R},\qquad \int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\,dA\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$
The Jacobian and $\partial\Phi$ are positive and nonzero almost everywhere, respectively, so the negative power is well-defined almost everywhere. In particular, for any $|k|=1$ and $f(z)=e^{ik\Phi(z)}$,
$$\|f\|_{W^{1,r}(D_S)}+\bigl\||\partial f|^{-1}\bigr\|_{L^\sigma(D_S)}\le C_{\kappa,r,R,S}.$$
For $0<\sigma<1$ the displayed $L^\sigma$ quantity means $(\int|\partial f|^{-\sigma})^{1/\sigma}$, without asserting a norm triangle inequality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a Beltrami coefficient on the Riemann sphere with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le k<1$ ([[def-measurable-beltrami-coefficient]]), and let $0,1,\infty$ denote the standard points in the finite and infinity charts ([[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]], [[rem-riemann-sphere-one-point-compactification]]). Then:

(i) **Existence.** There is an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism $f:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ whose Beltrami coefficient is $\mu$ almost everywhere ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]); equivalently, $f$ is a weak solution of $f_{\bar z}=\mu f_z$ ([[def-weak-solution-beltrami-equation]]). Its maximal dilatation is $K_f=K(\mu)\le(1+k)/(1-k)$.

(ii) **Uniqueness up to Möbius maps.** If $f$ and $g$ are two such solutions, then $g\circ f^{-1}$ is a Möbius transformation of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ ([[def-mobius-transformation]]). Thus the solutions are exactly $\{M\circ f:M\text{ is Möbius}\}$, and there is a unique solution fixing $0,1,\infty$.

(iii) **Any normalization.** For every ordered triple $(a,b,c)$ of distinct sphere points, there is exactly one solution with $f(0)=a$, $f(1)=b$, and $f(\infty)=c$ ([[thm-three-point-transitivity-mobius-transformations]]). In particular the solution normalized by $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$, $f(\infty)=\infty$ is unique; denote it by $f^\mu$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism. The following are equivalent.

(a) $f$ is $1$-quasiconformal, in either the geometric or the analytic sense ([[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[thm-geometric-and-analytic-quasiconformality-equivalent]]).

(b) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its weak Wirtinger derivative satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere; under this Sobolev hypothesis this is equivalent to $\mu_f=0$ almost everywhere together with $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere on $\{\partial_zf=0\}$ ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]).

(c) $f$ is holomorphic; equivalently, it is a biholomorphism of $\Omega$ onto $\Omega'$ ([[def-biholomorphic-map]]).

Thus the conformal maps in this library's orientation-preserving sense are exactly the $1$-quasiconformal homeomorphisms; in particular, they preserve angles.

An injective holomorphic map on a complex domain has nowhere-zero derivative and is biholomorphic onto its open image.

Precisely, if $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic and injective on a complex domain, then $f'(a)\ne0$ for every $a\in\Omega$, the set $f[\Omega]$ is a complex domain, and $f:\Omega\to f[\Omega]$ is biholomorphic ([[def-biholomorphic-map]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be an analytically $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]) with Beltrami coefficient $\mu_f$ ([[def-beltrami-coefficient-and-maximal-dilatation]]). Then $g=f^{-1}:\Omega'\to\Omega$ is analytically $K$-quasiconformal, $K_g=K_f$, and
$$\mu_g(f(z))=-\mu_f(z)\,\frac{f_z(z)}{\overline{f_z(z)}}\quad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$
Consequently $|\mu_g|\circ f=|\mu_f|$ almost everywhere, and $f$ is analytically quasiconformal exactly when $f^{-1}$ is, with the same maximal dilatation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be a homeomorphism of complex domains which is $K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense, with $K\ge1$, and let $\lambda,\mu$ denote the extremal length and reciprocal curve-family modulus of [[def-extremal-length-and-curve-family-modulus]].

(i) **Quadrilaterals.** Let $Q$ be a quadrilateral with $\overline Q\subset\Omega$ and marked opposite sides $E_0,E_1$, as in [[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], and let $\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)$ consist of paths in $Q$ joining those sides. Then $f\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)=\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))$ and
$$K^{-1}\mu\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr)\le \mu\bigl(\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))\bigr)\le K\mu\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr),$$
equivalently
$$K^{-1}\lambda\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr)\le \lambda\bigl(\Gamma(f(Q);f(E_0),f(E_1))\bigr)\le K\lambda\bigl(\Gamma(Q;E_0,E_1)\bigr).$$
The same inequalities hold with the other pair of opposite marked sides.

(ii) **Annuli.** Let $\widetilde A\subset\Omega$ be a doubly connected domain, meaning that $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\widetilde A$ has exactly two connected components ([[rem-riemann-sphere-one-point-compactification]]), and put $A=f(\widetilde A)$. Let $\Gamma(\widetilde A)$ and $\Gamma(A)$ be the path families joining the two annular ends. Then
$$K^{-1}\mu(\Gamma(\widetilde A))\le\mu(\Gamma(A))\le K\mu(\Gamma(\widetilde A)),\qquad K^{-1}\lambda(\Gamma(\widetilde A))\le\lambda(\Gamma(A))\le K\lambda(\Gamma(\widetilde A)).$$
For a round annulus $A(r,R)$ the connecting-family extremal length is the conformal parameter $(2\pi)^{-1}\log(R/r)$ and the reciprocal modulus is $2\pi/\log(R/r)$, by [[thm-modulus-rectangle-and-annulus]] and [[thm-round-annulus-conformal-parameter-is-complete-invariant]].

(iii) **Area and null sets.** For every relatively compact Borel set $E\subset\Omega$,
$$\operatorname{area}(f(E))=\int_EJ_f\,dA.$$
In particular, $f^{-1}$ maps Lebesgue-null Borel subsets of $\Omega'$ to null subsets of $\Omega$.

**Annular end-path convention.** In (ii), paths have parameter interval (0,1), are proper, and their tails escape into different ends, defined by the two-collar exhaustion proved below. Local rectifiability means rectifiability on each compact parameter interval. Their nonnegative Borel weighted length is the increasing supremum of those compact-restriction arc-length integrals; a nonrectifiable restriction has infinite length. The displayed extremal-length supremum over finite positive-area densities and reciprocal modulus convention are unchanged. The proof verifies compatibility with ordinary finite-boundary families and transport of the two ends, including punctured and infinite rings.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

If $T\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\Delta T=0$, there is a unique smooth harmonic $h$ with $T=T_h$.

Every bounded entire function is constant.

More explicitly, if $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic and there is a real $M\ge0$ such that $|f(z)|\le M$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$, then $f$ is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Take a solution from [F1] fixing infinity. Outside $D_R$ its coefficient is zero, so it is conformal there. In the infinity chart it is an injective holomorphic map fixing zero with nonzero derivative. Its Taylor expansion there gives $az+b+O(1/z)$ in the original chart, with $a\ne0$. Postcomposition by $(w-b)/a$ gives the principal normalization. Any two principal solutions differ by a Möbius map by [F1]; since both fix infinity this map is affine, and their leading and constant Laurent coefficients force it to be the identity. This proves existence and uniqueness of $\Phi$.

Set $h=\bar\partial\Phi$, which is in $L^2$ and has support in $\overline D_R$ by local quasiconformal Sobolev regularity and the zero coefficient outside. The Cauchy integral for compact $L^2$ data is locally $L^2$: on a fixed target disk the kernel restricted to all differences with $D_R$ is in $L^1$, so [F4] applies; outside a larger disk its bound is $C\|h\|_1/|z|$. Approximating $h$ by smooth functions in a fixed support disk yields distributionally $\bar\partial\mathcal Ch=h$ and $\partial\mathcal Ch=\mathcal Bh$, the latter by Beurling $L^2$ boundedness. Thus $\bar\partial(\Phi-z-\mathcal Ch)=0$. Applying $\partial$ and [F4] makes this distribution smooth harmonic; the original Cauchy–Riemann equation makes its representative holomorphic. It tends to zero at infinity by the principal normalization and the exterior Cauchy bound. Liouville gives $\Phi-z=\mathcal Ch$. Therefore $\partial\Phi=1+\mathcal Bh$, and the Beltrami equation says $(I-\mu\mathcal B)h=\mu$.

Let $h_r=(I-\mu\mathcal B)^{-1}\mu$ in $L^r$. Its norm is at most $C_\kappa\|\mu\|_r\le C_{\kappa,R,r}$ by [F3]. The equation gives $h_r=0$ outside $D_R$, hence $h_r\in L^2$ by Hölder on that disk. Compatibility of the $L^2$ and $L^r$ Beurling actions and uniqueness of the $L^2$ inverse imply $h_r=h$ from step 2.1. Apply the Cauchy bounds in [F3] to $\Phi-z=\mathcal Ch$. This proves its $W^{1,r}$, supremum and Hölder bounds. In particular $\Phi(D_S)$ lies in a disk of radius $S+C_{\kappa,R,r}$, uniformly in $\mu$.

By [F2], $\Psi=\Phi^{-1}$ has coefficient bounded by $\kappa$, supported in $\Phi(\overline D_R)$, and has the same principal expansion at infinity. Step 3.1 puts that support inside a fixed disk; applying step 3.1 to $\Psi$ therefore gives a uniform $L^r$ bound for $\partial\Psi$ on every fixed disk. At common differentiability points, the derivative inverse formula gives $|\partial\Psi(\Phi(z))|=1/[(1-|\mu(z)|^2)|\partial\Phi(z)|]$. Thus $|\partial\Phi(z)|^{-\sigma}\le|\partial\Psi(\Phi(z))|^\sigma$. Change variables with $z=\Psi(w)$ using [F2]; the bound $J_\Psi\le|\partial\Psi|^2$ gives $\int_{D_S}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}\le\int_{\Phi(D_S)}|\partial\Psi(w)|^{\sigma+2}dA(w)$. Since $\sigma+2=r$, step 3.1 and the uniform disk containing $\Phi(D_S)$ bound the right side. Null-set preservation in [F2] justifies all inverse identities and negative powers on common full-measure sets.

On $D_S$, $|\Phi|\le S+C_{\kappa,R,r}$. For $|k|=1$, the exponential and its derivative are bounded on this range. To justify the Sobolev chain rule, set $h=\bar\partial\Phi$ and approximate it in $L^r$ by smooth functions $h_n$ supported in one fixed larger disk; the density and Cauchy bounds in [F3] give $\Phi_n=z+\mathcal Ch_n\to\Phi$ in $W^{1,r}(D_{S+1})$ and uniformly on $D_S$. The Cauchy integrals of these smooth data are smooth, and the uniform convergence keeps their ranges on $D_S$ in a fixed bounded set. The classical chain rule for $f_n=e^{ik\Phi_n}$ gives $\partial f_n=ik e^{ik\Phi_n}\partial\Phi_n$ and the corresponding $\bar\partial$ formula. Uniform convergence of the exponential factors and $L^r$ convergence of the derivatives pass these identities to $f=e^{ik\Phi}$ in $W^{1,r}(D_S)$. Step 3.1 supplies the uniform $W^{1,r}$ bound, while $|\partial f|^{-\sigma}\le e^{\sigma(S+C)}|\partial\Phi|^{-\sigma}$ and step 4.1 supply the negative-power bound. This proves the final assertion, including the case $\sigma<1$ with its stated integral convention. [F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

$f(z)\ne0$ for every $z\in\gamma^\ast$. Then $f\circ\gamma$ is a closed complex
contour with $0\notin(f\circ\gamma)^\ast$, and

$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=n(f\circ\gamma,0).$$

Equivalently, if $\theta$ is any continuous argument of $f\circ\gamma$, then

$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=\frac{\theta(b)-\theta(a)}{2\pi}.$$

If $\gamma$ is also admissible and null-homologous in a larger open set on
which $f$ is meromorphic, then the same integer equals $Z(f,\gamma)-P(f,\gamma)$
by [[thm-argument-principle-null-homologous-cycle]].

For a based loop $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb C^\times$ at $1$, let
$r(z)=z/|z|$ and define

$$W([\gamma]):=\deg(r\circ\gamma).$$

Then $W$ is the standard isomorphism

$$\pi_1(\mathbb C^\times,1)\cong(\mathbb Z,+).$$

If $\gamma$ is rectifiable, then

$$W([\gamma])=n(\gamma,0).$$

Thus the analytic winding number of any rectifiable representative is the
integer classifying its loop class.

A nowhere-zero holomorphic function on a complex domain cannot have an interior local modulus minimum unless it is constant.

Equivalently, if $f$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero on a complex domain $\Omega$ and $|f(z)|\ge|f(a)|$ on some neighbourhood of $a\in\Omega$, then $f$ is constant.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, and let $\sigma,\gamma>0$. Put
$$\rho_\sigma(w)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad p_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du),$$
and define the normalized posterior measure and its mean by
$$\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=\frac{\int_E\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)}{p_\sigma(z)}\quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)),\qquad D_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
The omitted normalizing constant of the $N(0,\sigma^2I)$ likelihood is independent of $u$ and cancels in $\nu_{\sigma,z}$. Writing $U(u)=u$ for the identity random vector under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$, its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u-D_\sigma(z))(u-D_\sigma(z))^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and smooth, each $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ has finite second moment, and $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk $a\mapsto\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)$. Moreover, $D_\sigma$ is smooth and
$$J D_\sigma(z)=\sigma^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)$$
is symmetric positive definite. Hence $D_\sigma$ is injective with open image $X_\sigma=D_\sigma(\mathbb R^n)$ and smooth inverse on $X_\sigma$. Put $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ and, for $x\in X_\sigma$, define
$$h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=-\frac{\|x-D_\sigma^{-1}(x)\|_2^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}q_\sigma(D_\sigma^{-1}(x));$$
set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz

for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would

restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

current_manifest_record.statement: For each integer $m\ge1$, let $\mu_m=(1-2^{-m})\delta_0+2^{-m}\delta_1$ on $\{0,1\}\subset\mathbb R$, where $\delta_a$ is unit mass at $a$, and let the target posterior be $\pi=\delta_0$. For example, this target is the posterior from prior $\delta_0$ and the one-point observation model with likelihood one. The $m$th output law is realized by a one-step instance of the reverse-kernel interface with $N=1$, terminal law $\nu_1=\delta_0$, zero Borel score field, a constant correction into a singleton space, the constant kernel $Q_m(B\mid x,y,a)=\mu_m(B)$, and no projection. Its exact kernel sampler uses at most $m$ independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ draws and returns $1$ exactly when all draws equal $1$, so it has finite budget for every $m$. The output laws $\mu_m$ converge weakly to $\pi$, yet $\mu_m\ne\pi$ at every finite $m$ because $\mu_m(\{1\})=2^{-m}$. This finite-kernel example illustrates the distinction between asymptotic weak convergence and exact posterior sampling; it is not a performance claim about a trained diffusion model.

current_manifest_record.statement: Let $X_0$ take values $-1$ and $1$ with equal probability, let $X_\sigma=X_0+\sigma Z$ with $\sigma>0$ and standard Gaussian noise independent of $X_0$, and let $Y=X_0+\tau W$ for $W\sim N(0,1)$ independent of $(X_0,Z)$, with $\tau>0$. At the observation $y=0$, the exact measurement density $r_\sigma(0\mid x)=\mathbb E[\varphi_\tau(-X_0)\mid X_\sigma=x]$ is constant in $x$, so its score is zero. The exact posterior mean is $m_\sigma(x)=\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_\sigma=x]=\tanh(x/\sigma^2)$, where $\tanh(t)=(e^{2t}-1)/(e^{2t}+1)$. The plug-in density $\varphi_\tau(-m_\sigma(x))$ has score $-m_\sigma(x)m_\sigma'(x)/\tau^2$, which is nonzero for $x\ne0$. Thus evaluating the measurement likelihood at the exact posterior mean does not in general recover the exact measurement score; this example does not rule out equality in special models.

Therefore the posterior mean is $(e^{2x/\sigma^2}-1)/(e^{2x/\sigma^2}+1)=\tanh(x/\sigma^2)$, agreeing with the conditional-mean version in [F1].

At $y=0$, both possible clean states have the same likelihood density: $\varphi_\tau(0-1)=\varphi_\tau(0+1)=\varphi_\tau(1)$. Averaging these equal values over the conditional law from [F2] gives $r_\sigma(0\mid x)=\varphi_\tau(1)$ for every $x$, so its logarithmic derivative and the exact measurement score are zero.

The plug-in log density is $\log\varphi_\tau(-m_\sigma(x))=-\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\tau)-m_\sigma(x)^2/(2\tau^2)$. Differentiating the quotient expression in step 1.1 gives $m_\sigma'(x)=4e^{2x/\sigma^2}/(\sigma^2(e^{2x/\sigma^2}+1)^2)>0$. Hence the plug-in score is $-m_\sigma(x)m_\sigma'(x)/\tau^2$, which is nonzero whenever $x\ne0$.

The exact score in step 1.2 and the plug-in score in step 2.1 disagree for every nonzero $x$. Thus the exact posterior mean does not, in general, make likelihood-at-the-mean guidance equal to the exact measurement score. The calculation permits special cases of equality but refutes a general identity.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, a finite matching affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$ of $\Omega$, and unisolvent reference finite elements assembled on that mesh. Thus the mesh is a finite face-to-face cover by nondegenerate affine simplices with disjoint interiors, and each local finite-element degree-of-freedom map is bijective on its polynomial space. Fix coefficient spaces $\Theta_h=\mathbb R^m$, $V_h=\mathbb R^n$, and $Y_h=\mathbb R^s$ with their standard Euclidean inner products, where $m,n,s\ge1$. Let $Q_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $O_h\subseteq\Theta_h$ be open with $Q_h\subseteq O_h$.

A **finite-element PDE model** in this contract consists of a continuously differentiable residual map $R_h:O_h\times V_h\to V_h$ and a continuously differentiable observation map $G_h:O_h\times V_h\to Y_h$. It must supply a continuously differentiable state branch $S_h:O_h\to V_h$ satisfying $R_h(q,S_h(q))=0$ for every $q\in O_h$. For every $q\in Q_h$, this branch must be the specified unique admissible state and the matrix $D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))$ must be invertible. The discrete forward map is $F_h(q):=G_h(q,S_h(q))$. The unisolvent finite-element degrees of freedom identify $V_h$ with its coefficient space; all matrix transposes below are in the fixed Euclidean coefficient inner products.

For data $y^\delta\in Y_h$, reference parameter $q_0\in\Theta_h$, and $\alpha>0$, the discrete nonlinear Tikhonov objective is
$$
\Phi_h(q):=\frac12\|F_h(q)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2\qquad(q\in Q_h).
$$
Define the finite-dimensional objective before eliminating the state by
$$
J_h(q,u):=\frac12\|G_h(q,u)-y^\delta\|_{Y_h}^2+\frac\alpha2\|q-q_0\|_{\Theta_h}^2.
$$
The symbols $\nabla_uJ_h$ and $\nabla_qJ_h$ denote the Euclidean gradient vectors representing the two partial derivative functionals. At an admissible $q$, the **exact discrete adjoint** $p_h(q)\in V_h$ is the unique solution of
$$
\bigl(D_uR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q)=\nabla_uJ_h(q,S_h(q)).
$$
The associated discrete-adjoint gradient vector is
$$
g_h(q):=\nabla_qJ_h(q,S_h(q))-\bigl(D_qR_h(q,S_h(q))\bigr)^T p_h(q).
$$
The next lemma proves that this vector is the gradient of $\Phi_h$; the definition itself asserts no minimizer exists and no gradient iteration converges.

An **admissibility predicate** is a specified finite-time test $\operatorname{adm}_h(q)$ that decides whether $q\in Q_h$ and checks the model's stated coefficient, boundary, mesh, and time-step hypotheses before a PDE solve. For an explicit time discretization, a Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition (CFL condition) is a method-specific bound relating the time step to the mesh and the discrete evolution operator; no universal CFL threshold is part of this definition. A true predicate result certifies that the declared model hypotheses hold for that input, not merely that a heuristic check passed.

The model must also supply an exact finite-dimensional projection routine which returns $P_{Q_h}(z)$ for a queried $z\in\Theta_h$ in finite time or reports failure only when its declared finite call budget is exhausted. The unique nearest point exists because $Q_h$ is nonempty, closed, and convex, but an operational routine for computing it is an additional part of this contract.

A solver routine with declared nonnegative state and adjoint tolerances $\tau_u,\tau_p$ and a finite solve budget must return either `failure` or approximate state and adjoint vectors $\widetilde u,\widetilde p$ together with certified finite bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p,\eta_u,\eta_p,P,L_{J,u},L_{R,u},M_q,L_{G,u}$. The residual bounds have the exact-system meaning $\|R_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_u$ and $\|(D_uR_h(q,u))^T\widetilde p-\nabla_uJ_h(q,u)\|_{V_h}\le\rho_p$, where $u=S_h(q)$; both must satisfy $\rho_u\le\tau_u$ and $\rho_p\le\tau_p$. In particular, an adjoint residual evaluated at $\widetilde u$ alone does not certify $\rho_p$ unless the model also bounds the resulting state and derivative-data defects. With $u=S_h(q)$ and $p=p_h(q)$, the model must certify
$$
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{V_h}\le\eta_u,\qquad \|p-\widetilde p\|_{V_h}\le\eta_p,\qquad \|p\|_{V_h}\le P,
$$
$$
\|\nabla_qJ_h(q,u)-\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{\Theta_h}\le L_{J,u}\eta_u,
$$
$$
\|(D_qR_h(q,u))^T-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le L_{R,u}\eta_u,\qquad \|(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\|\le M_q,
$$
and $\|G_h(q,u)-G_h(q,\widetilde u)\|_{Y_h}\le L_{G,u}\eta_u$. It then returns
$$
\widetilde g:=\nabla_qJ_h(q,\widetilde u)-(D_qR_h(q,\widetilde u))^T\widetilde p,\qquad \widetilde F:=G_h(q,\widetilde u),
$$
All constants and state/adjoint error bounds must be justified for the chosen model with every derivative-data, geometry, quadrature, and algebraic-solve defect retained. Certified residual bounds $\rho_u,\rho_p$ do not by themselves imply $\eta_u,\eta_p$; a separate model-valid stability estimate is required. The proposition below derives the resulting $\varepsilon_g$ and $\varepsilon_F$ bounds. An objective-evaluation routine must return in its finite budget either `failure` or an interval $[\ell_h(q),u_h(q)]$ containing the exact value $\Phi_h(q)$; `failure` is permitted only when a required state/adjoint solve fails its contract or the evaluation-call budget is exhausted. Exact evaluation is the degenerate-interval case. Projection and objective-evaluation calls consume the algorithm's finite evaluation budget. Each routine must return within its declared budget or report failure.

If a continuous model $F$ is also supplied, an optional mesh certificate $\varepsilon_{\rm mesh}$ must separately bound the claimed continuous-to-discrete error, such as $\|F_h(q)-F(q)\|$ or $\|\nabla\Phi_h(q)-\nabla\Phi(q)\|$. The state and adjoint algebraic residual certificates do not imply this mesh certificate.

Zheng et al.'s InverseBench reports 14 plug-and-play diffusion-prior algorithms and domain-specific baselines on five selected cases: first-Born optical scattering, raw multi-coil knee MRI, black-hole very-long-baseline interferometry, full waveform inversion, and two-dimensional vorticity-form Navier–Stokes inversion. For these experiments, the authors report that diffusion-prior methods often outperform conventional baselines when the training data are suitable, while a classical full-waveform-inversion optimizer initialized from a smoothed ground truth outperforms the tested diffusion-prior methods. In cases with closed-form forward models, methods using more forward-gradient queries can be more accurate and more expensive; the paper reports that this trend fails for its numerical PDE cases. Its Navier–Stokes split has one validation case and ten test cases. The paper reports step-size/Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) failures in its PDE experiments. Its Figure 5 out-of-distribution diagnostics feed digit images to a black-hole prior trained on simulated black-hole images, and nine-cell scattering sources to a prior trained on one-to-six-cell sources; for the black-hole case, the authors report outputs with the prior's characteristic ring feature. These are empirical observations for the named data, solvers, methods, tuning protocol, and hardware; they establish no universal ranking, stability bound, posterior exactness, risk-transfer bound, or robustness theorem.

There is a first-Born notation discrepancy between the paper and its released implementation. Appendix B.1 defines a contrast-dependent total field and then displays a sensor equation with that field multiplied by the contrast, which does not itself exhibit a fixed linear map. The pinned implementation instead passes the fixed incident field into the sensor-propagation routine and constructs its cached linear matrix from that fixed field. This page therefore identifies the implemented benchmark as the first-Born linear case and does not infer linearity from the printed contrast-dependent expression.

current_manifest_record.statement: In the finite-dimensional Gaussian credible-ball question reproduced below, choose $d=n=1$, $R=1$, $\sigma=1$, $T=1$, $\beta(t)=1$, and $\gamma=1/4$, with arbitrary positive $p,s,a$. Take the numerical operator equal to the true operator, so $\delta_A=0$. For every integer $K\ge1$ there is a jointly Borel finite score field with integrated score error exactly zero, whose Euler terminal law is $N(1,K^{-1})$ for every observation. With $M=K$ independent terminal draws, the resulting empirical ball has frequentist coverage tending to zero at truth $\theta=0$, although the stated uniform boundary-margin condition holds with exponent $\kappa=1$. The exact credible-ball baseline satisfies $\delta^0_{1,1/4}<3/4$. Consequently no bound in that question can have $\Phi\to0$ uniformly over its original score class as $(\delta_A,\varepsilon_s,K^{-1},M^{-1/2})\to(0,0,0,0)$. The original formulation is retained verbatim under Original question.

derivations.claim: Completing the square in $e^{-u^2/2}e^{-(Y-u)^2/2}$ gives posterior $N(Y/2,1/2)$, so its exact credible interval is $[Y/2-r,Y/2+r]$. Under truth $\theta\in[-1,1]$, $Y=\theta+G$ and the exact coverage is $c(\theta)=P\{|\theta/2-G/2|\le r\}$. This is a continuous strictly positive function of $\theta$, and is at most one. By compactness of $[-1,1]$ it has a positive minimum $c_*>0$. Therefore $\delta^0_{1,1/4}\le\max\{q-c_*,1-q\}<q$.

Put $h=1/K$ and let $\mathcal G_K=\{1-kh:0\le k<K\}$. Away from this finite set of times, use the exact noised-posterior score. At each $t\in\mathcal G_K$ set $s_t^Y(x)=(1-x)/h-x/2$. This finite-valued jointly Borel field has zero integrated score error: its discrepancy from the exact score is supported on the finite, Lebesgue-null set $\mathcal G_K$ in time. The noised posterior has mean $e^{-t/2}Y/2$ and variance $1-e^{-t}/2$: the integrating-factor solution of the linear forward equation is $e^{-t/2}X_0+e^{-t/2}\int_0^te^{u/2}\,dW_u$, whose independent Gaussian integral has variance $1-e^{-t}$ (use dyadic Brownian-increment sums and pass their Gaussian characteristic functions to the mean-square limit). Its exact score is therefore affine in $x$, so the inner Gaussian error integral is finite at every time. The zero-error conclusion holds for every observation and hence uniformly over all truths.

The variable $\theta/2-G/2$ has a density bounded by $2/\sqrt{2\pi}$ uniformly in $\theta$. The event $\bigl||\theta/2-G/2|-r\bigr|\le u$ is contained in two intervals of total length at most $4u$. Thus its probability is at most $8u/\sqrt{2\pi}$. The required margin holds, for example with $\kappa=1$, $u_0=1$ and $C_{\mathrm{ac}}=8/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

At every Euler step the deterministic update becomes $x+h(x/2+s_t^Y(x))=1$. Thus each new state is $1+\sqrt h\,\zeta_k$, independently of its input and of $Y$, and the terminal law is $N(1,h)$. For $M=K$, write the independent terminal draws as $1+K^{-1/2}G_i$. If $V_K=\max_{i\le K}|G_i|$, then the empirical center differs from one by at most $K^{-1/2}V_K$ and every empirical distance to that center is at most $2K^{-1/2}V_K$. Hence the empirical radius has that same upper bound.

The Gaussian density gives $P\{|G|>v\}\le2e^{-v^2/2}$ for $v\ge1$: integrate $x\phi(x)/v$ on $[v,\infty)$ and use $1/(v\sqrt{2\pi})\le1$. The union bound then gives $P\{V_K>K^{1/4}\}\le2K e^{-\sqrt K/2}\to0$. On the complementary event the center is at least $1-K^{-1/4}$ and the radius at most $2K^{-1/4}$, so for all sufficiently large $K$ the empirical interval excludes truth zero. Its coverage therefore tends to zero, and its deviation from $q$ tends to $q>\delta^0_{1,1/4}$. Since both error norms are zero and $K^{-1},M^{-1/2}\to0$, a uniformly vanishing $\Phi$ would contradict this strict gap.
