current_manifest_record.title: Coverage error under score, forward-solver, and finite-time error
current_manifest_record.statement:
Fix integers $d,n\ge1$, parameters $p,s,a,R,\sigma>0$, a credibility error $\gamma\in(0,1)$, and a continuous schedule $\beta:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ with $T>0$. Let
$$\Theta_s(R)=\left\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\sum_{j=1}^d j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2\right\},\qquad A_p=\operatorname{diag}(1^{-p},2^{-p},\ldots,d^{-p}).$$
Observe $Y_i=A_p\theta+\varepsilon_i$, $1\le i\le n$, with independent $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_d)$. Use the proper Gaussian prior $\Pi_0=N(0,\operatorname{diag}(j^{-1-2a})_{j=1}^d)$, and let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid Y)$ be its exact posterior under the stated forward operator and noise law. Let $m_n(Y)$ be the posterior mean and let $r_{n,\gamma}(Y)$ be the unique radius for which the Euclidean ball
$$C_{n,\gamma}(Y)=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u-m_n(Y)\|_2\le r_{n,\gamma}(Y)\}$$
has posterior probability $1-\gamma$. Define the exact frequentist coverage $c_{n,\gamma}(\theta)=P_{n,\theta}\{\theta\in C_{n,\gamma}(Y)\}$ and its baseline error $\delta^0_{n,\gamma}=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}|c_{n,\gamma}(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|$.

For a deterministic numerical matrix $\widehat A_n\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $\delta_A\ge0$ and $\|\widehat A_n-A_p\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\delta_A$, let $\widehat\Pi_n(\cdot\mid Y)$ be the Gaussian posterior formed with $\widehat A_n$ and the same prior and noise variance. Write $\widehat p_{n,t}^Y$ for the density obtained by applying the forward variance-preserving diffusion $dX_t=-\tfrac12\beta(t)X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t$ to $X_0\sim\widehat\Pi_n(\cdot\mid Y)$, and set $\widehat s_{n,t}^Y=\nabla\log\widehat p_{n,t}^Y$. A jointly Borel learned score field $s_{n,t}^Y$ is required to satisfy
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}E_{Y\sim P_{n,\theta}}\left[\frac1T\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R^d}\|s_{n,t}^Y(x)-\widehat s_{n,t}^Y(x)\|_2^2\widehat p_{n,t}^Y(x)\,dx\,dt\right]\le\varepsilon_s^2.$$
For $h=T/K$, define the reverse-time Euler chain by $Z_0\sim\widehat p_{n,T}^Y$ and, for $k=0,\ldots,K-1$,
$$Z_{k+1}=Z_k+h\left[\tfrac12\beta(T-kh)Z_k+\beta(T-kh)s_{n,T-kh}^Y(Z_k)\right]+\sqrt{h\beta(T-kh)}\,\zeta_k,$$
where the $\zeta_k$ are independent $N(0,I_d)$ vectors independent of $Z_0$ and the observations. Draw $M$ independent copies of this chain conditionally on $Y$ and denote their terminal values by $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(M)}$. Let $\bar X=M^{-1}\sum_iX^{(i)}$, let $\widehat r$ be the empirical $1-\gamma$ quantile of $\{\|X^{(i)}-\bar X\|_2\}_{i=1}^M$ (the smallest order statistic whose empirical cumulative mass is at least $1-\gamma$), and put $\widehat C_{n,K,M}(Y)=\{u:\|u-\bar X\|_2\le\widehat r\}$. Suppose the exact credible-ball boundary satisfies the uniform margin condition
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}P_{n,\theta}\left(\left|\|\theta-m_n(Y)\|_2-r_{n,\gamma}(Y)\right|\le u\right)\le C_{\mathrm{ac}}u^\kappa\quad(0<u\le u_0)$$
for fixed $C_{\mathrm{ac}},u_0>0$ and $\kappa>0$. Determine whether a minimax-sharp nonasymptotic function $\Phi$ exists uniformly over all such score fields and, if it does, find it as a function of $d,n,p,s,a,R,\sigma,T,\gamma,C_{\mathrm{ac}},u_0,\kappa,\delta_A,\varepsilon_s,K^{-1}$, and $M^{-1/2}$ such that
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}\left|P_{n,\theta,\mathrm{sampler}}\{\theta\in\widehat C_{n,K,M}(Y)\}-(1-\gamma)\right|\le\delta^0_{n,\gamma}+\Phi,$$
with matching lower bounds that identify when $\Phi\to0$. The probability includes observation noise and sampler randomness. The target concerns the additional coverage error introduced by the approximate forward operator, learned score, finite reverse discretization, and finite posterior sample; it does not assume that the exact Bayesian credible ball is already calibrated on every truth class.

current_manifest_record.title: Translation and reflection ambiguities for a finite Fourier magnitude map

references.title: Philipp Grohs, Sarah Koppensteiner, and Martin Rathmair, Phase Retrieval: Uniqueness and Stability, arXiv:1901.07911v2, Proposition 3.3

current_manifest_record.statement: Let $C_3=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, put $\omega=(-1-i\sqrt3)/2$, and for a real signal $f:C_3\to\mathbb R$ define its unnormalised discrete Fourier transform by $\widehat f(k)=\sum_{n=0}^{2}f(n)\omega^{kn}$ for the representatives $k=0,1,2$. Its Fourier magnitude data are $(|\widehat f(k)|)_{k=0}^{2}$. Define translation by $(\tau_1 f)(n)=f(n-1)$ and reflection by $(Rf)(n)=f(-n)$, with indices in $C_3$. For $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=2$, and $f(2)=0$, both $\tau_1f$ and $Rf$ have the same Fourier magnitude data as $f$, while neither equals $f$ or $-f$.

citations.quote:
$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Write $s=\sqrt3$. By [F1] and [F2], $\omega^2=(-1+is)/2$, $\omega^3=1$, and $|\omega|^2=1$, hence $|\omega|=1$. Reindexing the finite sum with $j=n-1$ gives $\widehat{\tau_1f}(k)=\sum_j f(j)\omega^{k(j+1)}=\omega^k\widehat f(k)$. Multiplicativity of the modulus [F1] gives $|\omega^k|=1$, so every Fourier magnitude is unchanged.

Since $|\omega|=1$, [F1] gives $\overline\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Reindexing with $j=-n$ gives $\widehat{Rf}(k)=\sum_j f(j)\omega^{-kj}$. Because every $f(j)$ is real, this equals $\overline{\sum_j f(j)\omega^{kj}}=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$ by the conjugation laws in [F1], so reflection preserves every Fourier magnitude.

3.1 The support of $f$ and $-f$ is $\{0,1\}$, while the supports of $\tau_1f$ and $Rf$ are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{0,2\}$ respectively. Thus neither transformed signal equals $f$ or $-f$. Combined with the invariances in steps 1.1 and 2.1, both transformed signals are distinct from the original up to global sign but have identical Fourier magnitude data.

current_manifest_record.title: Wirtinger presentation from a finite diagram code

references.title: Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §§2–3
Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, printed pp. 34–36

current_manifest_record.statement: Define a procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.

current_manifest_record.title: Removing the point at infinity preserves the knot group

references.title: Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §5.3, proof of the Wirtinger Presentation Proposition

current_manifest_record.statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a compact smooth knot and let $b\in\mathbb R^3\setminus K$. The inclusion $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\hookrightarrow S^3\setminus K$ induces an isomorphism
$$\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus K,b)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b).$$

citations.quote:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. For $c>0$, choose the closed tubular disk-bundle neighborhood $N(K)$ formed from one product cap about each underpass and one product tube along each intervening upper arc, attached in the cyclic order of the knot and rounded in disjoint charts. Put $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. There is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, choose a sufficiently small Euclidean normal tube and let $E_K$ be its exterior. The Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In both cases the punctured chosen disk-bundle tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], if $U\cap V$ is simply connected, then the inclusion-induced homomorphisms give an isomorphism

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)*\pi_1(V,x_0)\cong\pi_1(X,x_0).$$

Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and let $x_0\in X$. Composition sends a loop
$\alpha$ at $x_0$ to the loop $f\circ\alpha$ at $f(x_0)$. Using the loop
classes and fundamental group of [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]],
the proposed
**induced homomorphism** is

$$f_*:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(Y,f(x_0)),\qquad f_*([\alpha]):=[f\circ\alpha].$$

The next theorem proves that this value is independent of the representative,
that it is a group homomorphism in the sense of [[def-group-homomorphism]], and
that induced maps respect identities, composition and homotopies that fix the
basepoint.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

derivations.claim: Since $K$ is compact, choose $R>0$ with $K$ and $b$ in the open ball $D=B_R(0)$. Put $U=S^3\setminus(K\cup\{\infty\})=\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ and $V=S^3\setminus\overline D$. Then $V$ is an open ball about infinity, disjoint from $K$, and $U\cap V=V\setminus\{\infty\}$. First verify that $U$ is path-connected without assuming a diagram code. Parameterize the smooth embedded circle by $k:S^1\to K$. For $p\in U$, the cone $$C_p=\{p+t(k(s)-p):s\in S^1,\ t\ge1\}$$ has three-dimensional outer volume zero: on each of finitely many smooth coordinate intervals of $S^1$ and each bounded interval $1\le t\le n$, the defining map is Lipschitz on a compact rectangle; subdividing into $O(N^2)$ squares of side $1/N$ covers its image by balls of radius $O(1/N)$, whose total three-dimensional volume is $O(1/N)$. Thus each truncated image has outer volume zero. For each $n$, the finite chart and derivative bounds give an explicit cover volume $A_n/N$ after mesh size $1/N$; choosing $N_n>2^{n+2}A_n/\epsilon$ makes the $n$th truncated images of both cones have total cover volume below $\epsilon 2^{-n-1}$. These formula-defined mesh sizes give a cover of $C_p\cup C_q$ with total volume below $\epsilon$ for every $\epsilon>0$, so the union has outer volume zero without a choice of covers. An open ball contains a cube of positive volume, so choose $r$ in an open ball outside $C_p\cup C_q$. If the segment $[p,r]$ met $K$ at $k(s)$, then $r=p+t(k(s)-p)$ for some $t\ge1$, contrary to $r\notin C_p$; similarly $[q,r]$ misses $K$. The broken line from $p$ to $r$ to $q$ lies in $U$. Under inversion $J(x)=x/\|x\|^2$, extended by $J(\infty)=0$, the set $V$ is the open ball of radius $1/R$ about $0$. The radial homotopy $y\mapsto(1-t)y$ contracts it to $0$, so it is nonempty and path-connected. Since this ball is convex, every based loop contracts to its own basepoint by the straight-line homotopy inside the ball; [F3] therefore makes $V$ simply connected. The same inversion identifies $U\cap V$ with $0<\|y\|<1/R$. Fix $\rho=1/(2R)$; the puncture-preserving radial homotopy $$y\longmapsto\left((1-t)+t\frac{\rho}{\|y\|}\right)y$$ is a strong deformation retraction of this punctured ball onto the sphere $S^2_\rho$. The punctured ball is path-connected. Choose $y_0\in S^2_\rho$, let $i:S^2_\rho\hookrightarrow U\cap V$ be inclusion, and let $r$ be the radial retraction. Since the radial deformation fixes $S^2_\rho$ pointwise, [F7] and functoriality make $i_*$ and $r_*$ inverse isomorphisms at $y_0$. By [F2], $\pi_1(S^2_\rho,y_0)$ is trivial. For any other basepoint $y$ in the punctured ball, choose a path $\gamma$ from $y$ to $y_0$ and use $[\alpha]\mapsto[\bar\gamma*\alpha*\gamma]$. Concatenation and reparameterization preserve endpoint-fixed homotopies, so this is a well-defined homomorphism. The inverse uses $\bar\gamma$; the inserted pairs $\gamma*\bar\gamma$ and $\bar\gamma*\gamma$ contract by the piecewise retracing homotopy, so the homomorphism is an isomorphism. Thus every basepoint group of the overlap is trivial; its nonemptiness and path-connectedness with [F3] make $U\cap V$ simply connected.

Choose $b_0\in U\cap V$. The open sets $U,V$ cover $S^3\setminus K$; [F4] applies by the path-connectedness in step 1.1. Since $V$ and $U\cap V$ are simply connected by step 1.1, the special case [F5] shows that inclusion induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(U,b_0)\to\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b_0)$.

The inclusion induces the based map by [F6]. Choose a path $\gamma$ in $U$ from $b$ to $b_0$, which exists by step 1.1. The formula $[\alpha]\mapsto[\bar\gamma*\alpha*\gamma]$ defines isomorphisms between the fundamental groups at these basepoints by the concatenation and retracing argument in step 1.1. Using the same path in $S^3\setminus K$ makes the square with inclusion commute, since postcomposing the concatenated path gives the same loop. Thus the inclusion map at $b$ is conjugate by isomorphisms to the isomorphism at $b_0$.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. For $c>0$, choose the closed tubular disk-bundle neighborhood $N(K)$ formed from one product cap about each underpass and one product tube along each intervening upper arc, attached in the cyclic order of the knot and rounded in disjoint charts. Put $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. There is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, choose a sufficiently small Euclidean normal tube and let $E_K$ be its exterior. The Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In both cases the punctured chosen disk-bundle tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

derivations.claim: Take ambient coordinates $(x,y,z)$ with overstrand tangent $+\partial_x$, viewing normal $+\partial_z$, and positive projection basis $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$. Source has $y<0$ and target $y>0$, with the understrand below the overstrand. Parameterize the under-core from source to target by $u$, whether or not this agrees with the knot orientation. Choose its product tube $\Phi(u,v)$ so that the oriented knot tangent followed by the ordered normal frame is ambient-positive; take the first normal-frame vector toward the positive-$z$ side of the understrand and the second to complete that orientation. Thus increasing angle from $\theta_0=0$ gives the positive meridian even when $u$ runs opposite to the knot orientation. Choose a small positive radius $r$. The path used here is the push-off $\beta(u)=\Phi(u,r(\cos\theta_0,\sin\theta_0))$, from source to target; it never lies on the knot core. The two meridian loops are the boundaries $\mu_u(\tau)=\Phi(u,r(\cos(\theta_0+2\pi\tau),\sin(\theta_0+2\pi\tau)))$, based at the endpoints of $\beta$. For exterior paths take $r$ at least the removed tube radius; shrink that radius first if necessary. Choose the product tube disjoint from the overstrand and other arc pieces, and $r$ smaller than the crossing-chart separation bounds. Choose upper-collar paths $\alpha_s,\alpha_t$ to these actual boundary points. In the normal $(y,z)$ plane of the overstrand, their concatenation $\alpha_s\beta\alpha_t^{-1}$ follows a small perturbation of the polygon $(0,H),(-d,-h),(d,-h),(0,H)$, which has positive signed area. The polygon and a sufficiently small surrounding strip avoid the origin; the chosen radius makes the perturbation lie in that strip, so its winding is still $+1$. For explicit complement control, straighten the local under-core to $x=0,z=-h$ in the product chart and take its upper push-off at $z=-h+r$. The access triangle is then entirely above $z=-h$, while the over-core projects to the origin. Radial interpolation of its positive polar-distance function to a sufficiently small circle about the origin stays inside that triangle minus the origin, hence above the under-core as well. Retain the positive-radius angular access in the under-tube until reaching these straightened paths. Thus the resulting homotopy is to one counterclockwise over-meridian and avoids both strands throughout. Thus all paths and homotopies lie in the complement, the loop represents $m_o$, and $\alpha_t\simeq m_o^{-1}\alpha_s\beta$ rel endpoints there.

The positive-radius cylinder $(u,\tau)\mapsto\Phi(u,r(\cos(\theta_0+2\pi\tau),\sin(\theta_0+2\pi\tau)))$ transports the boundary meridians, with its basepoint edge equal to $\beta$. Its image misses the knot core and, by the separated tube choice, the overstrand and every other arc. Reading the boundary of this cylinder gives $\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}\simeq\mu_s$ in the complement; its disk orientation is transported continuously even when the source-to-target direction opposes the knot orientation. Therefore $[\alpha_t\mu_t\alpha_t^{-1}]=m_o^{-1}[\alpha_s\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}\alpha_s^{-1}]m_o=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$. Equivalently the annular-core word $m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}$ bounds the cap of [F1], consistently with [F3]. Reversing the understrand orientation inverts both its meridians, so inversion gives the same side-based equation, rather than a switch of the conjugating direction.

The under-tangent follows $n_o$ exactly when incoming is source and outgoing is target, giving the first incoming/outgoing equation. Otherwise solve the same equation for $m_s$ to obtain the second. A reversed meridian is the inverse loop by [F2]. If a common access path $\alpha$ is replaced by $\lambda\alpha$, the class $[\alpha\mu\alpha^{-1}]$ becomes $[\lambda][\alpha\mu\alpha^{-1}][\lambda]^{-1}$; this holds for each of the three meridians. These observations prove all remaining assertions.

current_manifest_record.statement: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

A **free group on a set $X$** is a group $F(X)$ together with a map
$i:X\to F(X)$ such that, for every group $G$ and every function $u:X\to G$,
there is a unique group homomorphism $\widehat u:F(X)\to G$ satisfying

$$\widehat u\circ i=u.$$

The reduced-word construction supplies such a group; the construction and its
universal property are established in [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]].
When no ambiguity arises, $x\in X$ is identified with its image $i(x)$.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

A homomorphism that kills a normal subgroup factors uniquely through the quotient group.

If $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$, $f:G\to H$ is a homomorphism, and
$N\subseteq\ker f$, then there is a unique homomorphism $\bar f:G/N\to H$
such that $\bar f(gN)=f(g)$ and $f=\bar f\circ\pi$.

The input is a finite record $D$ and a designated starting under-arc $a_0$ of one oriented knot. First check that the vertex, edge, and segment lists are finite; that every vertex, bend, and point on an edge polyline has rational coordinates; and that each polyline has the prescribed incident endpoints. Before geometric tests, delete consecutive repeated coordinates from each polyline; reject an edge with no positive-length segment or a crossing with a zero-length incident ray. Check that every crossing has four incident half-edges, a recorded cyclic order and a pairing into alternating opposite branches, and one designated over-branch; every other vertex must be a valence-two bend. Check that edge orientations agree at bends and continue coherently through each paired branch, and that following these pairings and bends traces one oriented circle. If $a_0$ is not one of the resulting under-arcs, or any structural check fails, return invalid-input.

For every unordered pair of line segments, compute the determinant of their rational direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate intersection equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Reject every self-intersection, every positive-length overlap, and every intersection except a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence. At each crossing, sort the four nonzero incident rays by half-plane and exact determinant comparisons; reject the input if two rays have the same direction, if this geometric cyclic order disagrees with the recorded order, or if the paired branches do not alternate. These checks are finite.

After validation, traverse the oriented knot once from $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. At each crossing, let the outgoing over-half-edge be the ray in the direction of the oriented over-tangent. In the verified counterclockwise cyclic order, the under-half-edge immediately following it is the target side $a_t$; the other under-half-edge is the source side $a_s$. Read the over-arc $a_o$ and append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. This rule uses the positive in-plane normal, which points counterclockwise from the oriented over-tangent, and does not depend on the under-strand direction. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

The crossing pass then visits the finite crossing list once, reads each source and target from its verified cyclic order, appends exactly the corresponding positive-meridian relator, and returns the finite presentation. Thus the procedure terminates with one generator per under-arc and one relator per crossing, as claimed. If $c=0$, the explicit punctured-product model in [F1] gives its fundamental group as infinite cyclic on the positive meridian (the sphere factor is simply connected), while [F6]–[F8] identify the returned one-generator empty-relator presentation with the same free cyclic group. If $c>0$, [F1] and [F5] give the free meridian basis for the meridian region.

Assume $c>0$ and order the crossings $v_1,\ldots,v_c$. Let $b_*$ be the common collar basepoint in $U$, and let $X_0=U$ and $X_i=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_i$. For each $i$, the relative-open cover $X_i=X_{i-1}\cup V_i$ has intersection $A_i=U\cap V_i$, the annulus specified in [F1]. Choose $q_i$ on its core and use the supplied collar access path $\gamma_i$ in $U$ from $b_*$ to $q_i$. Concatenation and reparameterization make $[\alpha]\mapsto[\bar\gamma_i*\alpha*\gamma_i]$ a well-defined homomorphism from loops based at $b_*$ to loops based at $q_i$. Its inverse uses $\bar\gamma_i$, since the inserted path-reversal pairs contract by the piecewise retracing homotopy. The same concatenation formula commutes with inclusion. Apply [F3] at $q_i$: since $V_i$ is contractible, [F4] identifies $\pi_1(X_i,q_i)$ with $\pi_1(X_{i-1},q_i)$ modulo the normal closure of the annular-core image. Rebased to $b_*$, this image is conjugate to the common-based crossing word; conjugation does not change its normal closure. By [F2], that word is exactly the relator emitted for $v_i$. Distinct $V_i$ are disjoint, so these are precisely the intersections at every stage. Repeating over the finite crossing list kills exactly the normal closure of the constructor's relators.

By [F6] and [F7], the quotient in step 2.1 is the returned presentation group; [F8] identifies the quotient map with the homomorphism sending each symbol to its positive meridian. It is an isomorphism onto the group of the covered exterior by the pushout construction.

For $c=0$, step 1.1 already identifies the returned cyclic presentation with the Euclidean complement group on the positive meridian. For $c>0$, step 3.1 identifies the presentation with the covered exterior group, and the compact-tube retraction identifies that group with $\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus K)$. In both cases [F9] then gives the isomorphism to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$, with exactly the stated positive-meridian assignment.

By [F2], replacing the common basing path conjugates every generator image by the same element. Simultaneous conjugation is an inner automorphism of the target group, so the resulting presentation group remains isomorphic to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$.

Changing the designated start arc reindexes the same finite list of under-arcs. The induced bijection of generator symbols carries each crossing's over/under labels, and therefore each constructor relator, to the corresponding relator in the new indexing. It extends to an isomorphism of the free groups and carries one relator normal closure onto the other; [F7] and [F8] give an isomorphism of the presented quotients.

Let $D$ be an oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
regarded as a decorated immersed oriented $4$-valent planar graph, and let
$V$ be its finite set of double points. At each $v\in V$ the two branches of
the diagram cross; the local **Seifert smoothing** of $D$ at $v$ replaces the
crossing by the unique pair of non-crossing arcs in a small disk about $v$ that
joins the four half-edges in the orientation-respecting way: entering along a
strand, one follows the smoothing turn that keeps the travelling direction
consistently on the same side, so that the two oriented arcs through $v$ are
reconnected without crossing. Performing this replacement in pairwise disjoint
small disks, one for each crossing, and leaving the rest of the diagram
unchanged produces the **Seifert smoothing of $D$**: a finite disjoint union of
oriented simple closed curves in $S^2$, its **Seifert circles**. At each
crossing the smoothing reconnects the four half-edges in one of the two
possible non-crossing ways, and exactly one of the two respects the
orientations; hence the smoothing is a well-defined operation on the diagram.
The Seifert smoothing may merge two circles into one or split one circle into
two at a crossing, so its number of circles is a new invariant of the picture
and is not in general the number of components of the link.

The **Seifert picture** of $D$ is the smoothed picture together with one signed
short arc at each former crossing $v$, drawn transversely to the two smoothed
strands and joining the two distinct Seifert circles that passed through $v$; the sign of the arc is the sign of the
crossing, positive or negative. The signed arcs lie in the complement of the
Seifert circles and meet the circles only at their endpoints
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]); every crossing is recorded exactly once. The two smoothed arcs at a crossing
are parallel and equally directed. They cannot belong to the same oriented
Jordan circle: the connecting strip is on opposite local sides of its two
equally directed boundary arcs, whereas a fixed complementary side of an
oriented Jordan circle is consistently on one local side. Thus each signed
arc joins distinct circles, coherently oriented in their common annulus. The orientation of each Seifert circle is the one induced by the
Smoothed strands, and the collection of circles and signed arcs is the object
to which the coherence and height definitions
([[def-coherence-of-seifert-circles-and-the-height-of-a-diagram]]) are applied.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with exactly one component, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Perform the following construction in its projection sphere $S^2$.

1. Choose a point $q\in S^2$ outside the finite diagram. In pairwise disjoint small disks about the crossings, replace each crossing by the unique noncrossing smoothing compatible with the strand orientations. Let the resulting oriented circles be the Seifert circles and let $s$ be their number.
2. For each Seifert circle $C$, take the closure of the component of $S^2\setminus C$ that does not contain $q$. Under the stated choice axiom, each such region is an embedded compact disk. The finite family of disk regions is nested or disjoint. Orient each disk to induce the given orientation of its boundary circle, then place nested disks at distinct nearby heights ordered by inclusion; the resulting disk interiors are pairwise disjoint in $S^3$.
3. For every original crossing, attach one rectangular band along short boundary intervals on the two smoothing arcs. A half-twist means a single $180$-degree turn of the band across the crossing neighborhood. Choose its direction, endpoint orientations, and over/under order to match the original crossing.
4. Return the finite disk-and-band construction data together with $(s,c)$.

The returned data are a finite attached two-dimensional complex. This algorithm's definition alone does not assert that the resulting image is embedded, is a surface, is connected, or has the original knot as boundary; the separate correctness lemma establishes those properties.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a single knot, and let the Seifert algorithm supply its finite disk-and-band construction data. These disks and bands can be realized in $S^3$ as a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F$ with exactly one boundary component, whose oriented boundary is the knot represented by $D$. The bands can be chosen mutually disjoint and disjoint from disk interiors except at their attaching intervals.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a connected compact oriented disk-and-band surface $F$ is built from $s$ disjoint disks by attaching $c$ rectangular bands along boundary intervals and has one boundary component, then $\chi(F)=s-c$ and $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. In particular, if the Seifert algorithm on an oriented knot diagram $D$ has $s$ Seifert circles and $c$ crossings, its output surface has genus $(1-s+c)/2$ and the knot genus satisfies $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. This is an upper bound from one spanning surface, not a minimality assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The word $\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}$ has four crossings. Since $\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_i^{-1}$ both induce the adjacent transposition, its endpoint permutation is $(12)(23)(12)(23)$, a $3$-cycle; [F8] therefore makes its closure one knot component. Smoothing each crossing straightens its adjacent oriented strands, leaving the identity three-strand closure with three cycles. Hence $(s,c)=(3,4)$.

The kinked unknot diagram has one crossing; its oriented smoothing separates the small kink loop from the remaining circle, so $(s,c)=(2,1)$. In the zero-crossing boundary case, the round unknot has one smoothing circle and no bands, so $(s,c)=(1,0)$.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

citations.quote: Let $K$ be finite, $A\subseteq K$ and $B\subseteq L$ subcomplexes, and $f:(|K|,|A|)\to(|L|,|B|)$ continuous. For all sufficiently large integers $r$, there is a simplicial approximation $g:(\operatorname{sd}^rK,\operatorname{sd}^rA)\to(L,B)$, homotopic as a map of pairs to $f b_K^r$. Here $b_K^r$ is the composite barycentric homeomorphism. No pointwise fixing of a positive-dimensional restriction is asserted.

Let $M$ be a compact piecewise linear three-manifold, possibly with boundary, equipped with a finite triangulation in which the boundary is a subcomplex and simplex links have the standard sphere or ball forms. Let $P$ be a subcomplex and let $W$ be any relatively open neighborhood of $|P|$ in $M$. There is a compact piecewise linear three-manifold $V\subset W$, with $|P|\subset\operatorname{Int}_M V$, such that $V$ strongly deformation retracts onto $|P|$. It has a finite triangulation extending a subdivision of $P$. Its trace $V\cap\partial M$ is a compact piecewise linear subsurface of $\partial M$, and its remaining frontier is a properly embedded piecewise linear surface; these surfaces meet along their common boundary. The trace may be empty. If $|P|$ is connected, $V$ is connected.

Let $P$ be a compact subpolyhedron of a polyhedron $Q$. Suppose $P$ is locally piecewise linearly collared in $Q$: each point has a product neighborhood in which $P$ is the bottom of a piecewise linear product with $[0,1)$. Then there is a piecewise linear embedding $c:P\times[0,1]\to Q$ with $c(x,0)=x$ such that $c(P\times[0,1))$ is an open neighborhood of $P$ in $Q$. In particular the boundary of every compact piecewise linear manifold has such a collar.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Let $V$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a finite compatible triangulation $K$, with boundary a subcomplex, and with every simplex link a standard piecewise linear sphere or ball of the appropriate dimension. If $V$ has no connected twofold covering space, every connected component of $\partial V$ is piecewise linearly homeomorphic to the standard two-sphere. This conclusion uses only finite simplicial and cellular calculations and has no choice hypothesis.

All arcs and graphs in this lemma are finite and polygonal: their edges have disjoint interiors except at specified shared endpoints. A simple polygon separates the plane into one bounded and one unbounded component; the closure of the bounded component is a disk. A prescribed piecewise-linear homeomorphism between the boundaries of two such disks extends to a piecewise-linear homeomorphism of the disks, with piecewise-linear inverse after finite subdivisions.

A finite embedded arc has a disk neighbourhood made from vertex disks and edge strips. A finite connected plane graph has a compact disk-and-band neighbourhood; filling its bounded complementary boundary circles produces a closed disk. Subdividing an edge does not change these conclusions. Loops use two distinct attachment germs. No ambient-plane extension is asserted.

Let $M$ be an orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with boundary, let $F$ be a connected subsurface of its boundary, and let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $\pi_1(F)$. Suppose $f:D\to M$ is a proper piecewise linear immersion of a finite polygonal disk, with $f(\partial D)\subset F$, having only regular double curves and with no point having more than two inverse images. More precisely, the double-value set is a finite disjoint union of circles in the interior and arcs properly ending in the boundary; near a double value the two sheets are transverse planes, or transverse half-planes at an endpoint, and there are no other singularities. If the boundary loop of $f$ does not represent an element of $N$, then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $F$ and does not represent an element of $N$.

Membership in $N$ for an unbased boundary loop is interpreted after joining it to a fixed basepoint in $F$. It is independent of that joining path because $N$ is normal. The disk produced need not have the same boundary as $f$.
Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, $H:Y\times I\to B$ a homotopy, and $\widetilde H_0:Y\to E$ a lift of $H(-,0)$. There is a unique lift $\widetilde H:Y\times I\to E$ of $H$ extending $\widetilde H_0$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], replace $f$ by a PL map with boundary homotopic to the original one in $F$. Choose the approximation sufficiently fine on its compact boundary image to keep that image in $\operatorname{Int}F$. Make the map proper without changing its boundary: in a boundary collar $c(u,s)$, a push with parameter $a\ge0$ replaces the height $s$ by $\max(s,a)$ for $s$ below the collar top and is the identity elsewhere, with $a$ smaller than that top. This is a continuous PL function jointly in $(s,a)$. Choose a nonnegative PL function $a$ on the source disk, zero precisely on its boundary and everywhere sufficiently small, and apply that push to the value of the map at each point. Its straight parameter interpolation gives a homotopy relative to the source boundary. After compatible subdivisions the resulting proper PL map $f_0:D\to M$ is simplicial for one fixed finite triangulation of $D$. Its boundary class is still outside $N$. Put $D_0=f_0(D)$ and use [F2] to choose a connected compact manifold neighborhood $V_0$ retracting onto $D_0$ whose trace in $\partial M$ lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$. Let $F_0$ be the component of that trace containing $f_0(\partial D)$.

If $V_0$ has a connected twofold cover $p_1:M_1\to V_0$, lift $f_0$ to $f_1:D\to M_1$ by [F4], put $D_1=f_1(D)$, and choose by [F2] a connected compact manifold neighborhood $V_1$ retracting onto $D_1$. Its trace is chosen inside the relative interior of $p_1^{-1}(F_0)$; let $F_1$ be the component containing $f_1(\partial D)$. Repeat whenever $V_i$ has a connected twofold cover. Write $q_i:V_i\to M$ for the composite of the covers and neighborhood inclusions. Then $q_if_i=f_0$, $q_i(F_i)\subset F$, and $N_i=(q_i|_{F_i})_*^{-1}(N)$ is normal. The boundary class of $f_i$ is outside $N_i$ at every stage. Orientability and the finite compatible PL structures pass to the covers and the neighborhoods.

This tower is finite. Give $D_i$ the simplicial structure obtained by lifting the original image simplices of $D_0$, irrespective of any additional subdivisions used for $V_i$. Its number of simplices is at most the number of simplices in the fixed source disk: each image simplex is the image of at least one source simplex, and each such source simplex has just one lift in the image of $f_i$. Let $\tau_i$ be the deck involution of $p_i$. The inverse image of $D_{i-1}$ is $D_i\cup\tau_i(D_i)$: every point of $D_{i-1}$ is hit by $f_{i-1}$ and its two lifts are interchanged by $\tau_i$. This inverse image is connected, because lifting the deformation retraction of $V_{i-1}$ onto $D_{i-1}$ retracts the connected $M_i$ onto it. The two finite closed sets $D_i$ and $\tau_i(D_i)$ must therefore meet. Since their union is a lifted simplicial complex, their intersection contains a common simplex. Thus $\tau_i$ identifies two distinct simplices of $D_i$ under projection; they are distinct because a deck transformation fixing a simplex would fix its barycenter. Projection takes $D_i$ onto $D_{i-1}$, so $D_i$ has strictly more simplices than $D_{i-1}$. This strict increase is bounded by the fixed finite source count. We reach a last $V_n$ with no connected twofold cover.

Apply [F5] to the last $V_n$ of step 3.1. It has the required finite compatible PL manifold triangulation and orientation by step 2.1 and has no connected twofold cover. Therefore each component of $\partial V_n$ is a PL two-sphere. In particular the endpoint argument uses no general Poincaré duality theorem, singular UCT splitting or unrestricted surface-classification hypothesis; their required finite calculations have been proved in [F5].

The marked $F_n$ is a compact connected subsurface of one of these spheres. It is planar. Its fundamental group is normally generated by its boundary circles: join its finitely many complementary disk regions by disjoint polygonal arcs in the sphere; cutting along the corresponding arcs in $F_n$ gives a polygonal disk, and identifying its paired cut shores expresses each loop as a product of conjugates of boundary loops. The same conclusion follows by collapsing those cut arcs to a finite tree; the unfilled boundary circles supply the remaining generators. If $F_n$ is the whole sphere, its fundamental group is trivial, contradicting the boundary class of $f_n$ being outside $N_n$. Hence some boundary component of $F_n$ has class outside $N_n$. Move it slightly into $\operatorname{Int}F_n$ using [F3], without changing its free homotopy class, and call the resulting embedded polygonal circle $C$. By the PL sphere model of [F6] and the polygonal disk construction there, $C$ bounds a PL disk in $\partial V_n$. Push this disk into $V_n$ relative to $C$ by its boundary collar: in that collar use the graph of a small PL function on the disk, positive on its interior and zero on its boundary. The graph is embedded and proper and is PL after subdivision. We obtain a proper PL embedded disk $g_n:D\to V_n$ with boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F_n$ outside $N_n$.

Suppose a proper PL embedded disk $g_i:D\to V_i$ has been obtained with its boundary class outside $N_i$. Regard it in $M_i$ and perturb it into general position with its deck translate, using the following finite vertex-push construction. Cover its compact image and its translate by finitely many linear coordinate balls $U$ with $U\cap\tau_iU=\varnothing$, together with boundary half-balls. In each ball triangulate the compact disk pieces and the ambient ball, shift one disk vertex a sufficiently small distance, and extend the move by coning to the fixed boundary of its ambient vertex star. The cone construction gives an ambient PL homeomorphism; the disk therefore remains embedded. In $U$, a move of $g_i$ supported in $U$ leaves $\tau_i g_i$ fixed, since that translate changes only in $\tau_iU$. Choose the finitely many shifts in general affine position relative to the fixed translated simplices. Each excluded affine dependence is a proper determinant zero set, so the allowed small open parameter box contains a choice outside their finite union. Applying $\tau_i$ shows that the paired intersection in $\tau_iU$ is also in general position. Process the finite chart pairs in order, retaining the previously treated compact pieces; later moves can be taken sufficiently small to preserve the finitely many nonzero determinants and positive separations already obtained. First do the boundary in its two-dimensional charts, and extend its moves over a small collar by [F3]; then do the interiors relative to that collar. The resulting intersections avoid sheet vertices and pairs of sheet edges. An intersection across one sheet edge and a face of the other has two incident intersection segments, and a face-face intersection is a transverse segment. Thus the double-value set is a disjoint finite union of regular polygonal circles and proper arcs, with the transverse half-plane model at their endpoints. There are no triple values because $g_i$ is embedded and $p_i$ has two sheets. The boundary motions are homotopies in the open marked surface and preserve the class modulo $N_i$. This construction uses only PL coordinate charts and cone moves, without assuming a smoothing of $M_i$.

Apply [F7] in the orientable $V_{i-1}$ to $p_i g_i$ and the normal subgroup $N_{i-1}$. Its boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F_{i-1}$ by the marked-neighborhood construction. Its boundary class is outside $N_{i-1}$ because its further image in $F$ is outside $N$. Thus [F7] gives a properly embedded PL disk $g_{i-1}$ with boundary class outside $N_{i-1}$. Every boundary surgery can be kept inside the open marked surface, so its boundary still lies in $\operatorname{Int}F_{i-1}$. Repeat steps 6.1–7.1 down the finite tower. No embeddedness of an intermediate disk lift is assumed after the double-curve surgeries; at the end of each descent step [F7] gives a new embedded disk, which is the input to the next descent.

We finish with a proper PL embedded disk $g_0$ in $V_0$. Its interior is disjoint from $\partial V_0$, hence from $\partial M$, while its boundary lies in $F_0\subset\operatorname{Int}F$; it is therefore a proper embedded disk in $M$. Its boundary class maps outside $N$ by definition of $N_0$. For the final particular case, take $F$ to be the indicated boundary component and $N$ the trivial subgroup. A nontrivial element of the kernel has a nullhomotopy disk, and the preceding argument gives an embedded disk whose boundary is still nontrivial in that component. This proves the theorem. Every tower has the finite bound proved in step 3.1, and all perturbation, surgery and matrix choices are finite. No countable or arbitrary-index choice hypothesis is introduced.
