In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the standard oriented three-sphere with $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$ and choose $0<r<1$. The standard unknotted Heegaard torus is $T_r=\{|z_1|=r,\ |z_2|=\sqrt{1-r^2}\}$; its two sides are solid tori. In the angular coordinates $(u,v)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ given by $(u,v)\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i u},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i v})$, let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the first and second coordinate classes in $H_1(T_r;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the **oriented torus knot** $T(p,q)$ is the image of $s\mapsto(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$, for $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, oriented by increasing $s$; it represents the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$. The mirror convention is the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$, which sends $T(p,q)$ to $T(p,-q)$ with image orientation, and reversing the knot orientation gives $T(-p,-q)$. For nonzero $p,q$ with $d=\gcd(|p|,|q|)>1$, the corresponding torus link is the union of $d$ disjoint parallel copies of the primitive slope $(p/d,q/d)$; it is not a single embedded curve of class $p\alpha+q\beta$. The exterior is $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ for a chosen closed tubular neighborhood. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and a preferred longitude is a degree-one class on $\partial E_K$ whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

derivations.claim:
**The round-metric tube is an admissible invariant tube.** Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis for the smooth normal-bundle structure by [L1]. Regard $S^3$ as the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ with its round metric, and identify each quotient normal plane $T_xS^3/T_xK$ with its orthogonal complement to $T_xK$ in $T_xS^3$. For $v\in\nu_x(K)$ let $\widehat v$ be that representative and define
$$\Phi(x,v)=\cos(\|v\|)x+\frac{\sin(\|v\|)}{\|v\|}\widehat v,$$
with $\Phi(x,0)=x$. This is the round normal exponential map. Its differential along the zero section sends a tangent-normal pair $(u,w)$ to $u+w$, an isomorphism. By [F5] it is a local diffeomorphism at every zero vector. Compactness of $K$ gives a uniform disk neighbourhood on which its differential stays invertible. After shrinking that radius, $\Phi$ is injective there: otherwise there would be distinct $(x_n,v_n),(y_n,w_n)$ with $\|v_n\|,\|w_n\|\to0$ and equal images; compactness gives subsequences converging to $(x,0),(y,0)$, equality gives $x=y$, and a local inverse near $(x,0)$ contradicts distinctness. Thus, for some $R>0$, $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism from the open normal disk bundle of radius $R$ onto an open neighbourhood of $K$. Choose $0<\epsilon<R/2$ also smaller than $\pi$ and than the distance from $K$ to either coordinate circle. The closed metric $\epsilon$-neighbourhood of $K$ equals $\Phi(\{v:\|v\|\le\epsilon\})$: a nearest point of $K$ exists for every point in that neighbourhood, and minimizing round distance is equivalent to maximizing the Euclidean dot product with that point; differentiating along $K$ shows the corresponding short great-circle segment is normal to $K$. Conversely, each normal vector of length at most $\epsilon$ gives a geodesic of that length, and injectivity on the radius-$R$ disk bundle rules out a closer nearest point. Hence this $N(K)$ is the closed tubular neighbourhood required by [F2], is disjoint from the two coordinate circles, and is invariant under $\rho_t$, since these maps are orthogonal and preserve $K$. Finally, the local product charts of $\Phi$ and compactness of $K$ allow $\epsilon$ to be decreased so that $N(K)\cap T_r$ is an annular neighbourhood of $K$ in the Heegaard torus; its two halves are boundary collars on the two solid-torus sides.

The primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$ is essential on the Heegaard torus. Removing a small annular neighborhood of $K$ from that torus leaves a closed annulus $A$. On either side, removing the corresponding half of the tube from a solid torus only removes a boundary collar, so the two pieces retract to solid tori $W_x,W_y$ and their overlap retracts to $A$. Thicken the pieces by half-collars to obtain path-connected open sets covering $E_K$ whose intersection retracts to $A$. The core of $A$ winds $p$ times around the core generator $x$ on one side and $q$ times around $y$ on the other. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F2] by [L1].

The generic orbits of $\rho_t$ have slope $(p,q)$ and trivial stabilizer: if both coordinates are nonzero, a stabilizing parameter $t\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ satisfies $pt,qt\in\mathbb Z$, hence $t=0$ because $\gcd(p,q)=1$. The stabilizer orders on the coordinate circles $z_1=0$ and $z_2=0$ are $|q|$ and $|p|$, respectively. The orbit space is a sphere: on each intermediate torus $|z_1|=r$ with $0<r<1$, quotienting by the primitive circle orbit leaves a circle, and at $r=0,1$ that quotient circle collapses to the corresponding coordinate-orbit point. The invariant tube from step 1.1 lies in the free-orbit region, and its quotient is a disk: every orbit in its normal disk bundle meets the fiber over one chosen point of $K$ exactly once. Removing its interior therefore removes a disk from the orbit sphere, leaving a disk. The quotient map is a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ with the two stated core multiplicities. Multiplicity one is regular; multiplicity greater than one is exceptional.

The three fundamental groups in this cover are $\pi_1(W_x)=\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, $\pi_1(W_y)=\langle y\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, and $\pi_1(A)=\langle a\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with inclusion maps $a\mapsto x^p$ and $a\mapsto y^q$. By [F4], $\pi_1(E_K)$ is their pushout. A group receiving maps from the two cyclic factors is determined by images of $x,y$; the maps agree on the intersection exactly when $x^p=y^q$. Hence the pushout has presentation $\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$.

A regular orbit parallel to $K$ represents the annulus core $x^p=y^q=h$. This element commutes with $x$ because it is $x^p$, and commutes with $y$ because it is $y^q$; as $x,y$ generate the group from step 3.1, $h$ is central.

Choose integers $c,d$ with $pd-qc=1$ and let $L=c\alpha+d\beta$. With the coordinate orientation determined by $\alpha$ followed by $\beta$, the ordered intersection number $K\cdot L=pd-qc=1$, so $L$ is a simple curve meeting $K$ once. At the intersection, the boundary $m$ of a small normal disk splits into arcs $\gamma_x,\gamma_y$ on the two solid-torus sides, while $L$ splits into its crossing arc and complementary arc $L_1$. Inserting $L_1L_1^{-1}$ into $m=\gamma_x\gamma_y$ gives $m=(\gamma_xL_1)(L_1^{-1}\gamma_y)$. The first factor winds $c$ times around the $x$ core and the second winds $-d$ times around the $y$ core, hence $m=x^c y^{-d}$. Its abelianization under $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is $cq-dp=-1$, so it is opposite the positive normal-disk meridian, whose class is the positive generator by [F3]. Thus $\mu=m^{-1}=y^d x^{-c}$. Setting $\alpha=d$ and $\beta=-c$ gives $p\alpha+q\beta=1$ and the stated word; another Bezout solution changes the exponents by $(qk,-pk)$, so the word is unchanged because $y^{qk}=h^k=x^{pk}$ and $h$ is central.

Abelianizing the presentation in step 3.1 gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is surjective because $\gcd(p,q)=1$, and its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the relation vector; hence it identifies this quotient with $\mathbb Z$. Step 4.2 sends the positive meridian to $1$, so by [F3] it is the positive generator of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Thus $[h]=p[x]=pq[\mu]$. The regular orbit $h$ is a degree-one parallel of $K$ under the equivariant normal-bundle projection from step 1.1, and $\mu$ has degree zero there, so $\lambda=h\mu^{-pq}$ has degree one and zero image in $H_1(E_K)$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies it with the preferred longitude; [F3] also proves that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so each is primitive.

references.title: Allen Hatcher, Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology

current_manifest_record.statement: For every nontrivial companion knot and every pattern in its solid torus, the companion torus in the satellite exterior is essential.

citations.quote: Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

derivations.claim: Take the core pattern $P=S^1\times\{0\}\subset V$ and choose its tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ to be a smaller concentric solid torus. The companion embedding sends this core to $K$, so $P(K)=K$ with the smaller chosen tube, while the companion torus is the boundary of the larger tube.

Radial interpolation in the $D^2$ coordinate identifies the shell between the two concentric tubes with $T^2\times[0,1]$. It lies in the satellite exterior and has the companion torus and the satellite exterior boundary as its ends. Thus the companion torus is boundary-parallel and is not essential by [F2]. This refutes the unrestricted statement.

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume full AC. Let $M=E_{P(K)}$ be a satellite knot exterior with companion torus $T_c$. Suppose the pattern hypotheses of the essential-companion-torus lemma hold, both components of $M$ cut along $T_c$ are atoroidal or Seifert-fibered, and $M$ itself is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Then the inclusion-minimal JSJ system of $M$ consists of a torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. Cutting along that torus identifies the companion exterior $E_K$ as the component on the outside of the embedded companion solid torus. No conclusion is made for an essential companion torus that is absorbed into a Seifert-fibered union.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a nontrivial smooth knot with a specified companion solid torus $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$, let $P\subset\operatorname{int}(S^1\times D^2)$ be a pattern, and assume the outer torus of its pattern exterior $X_P$ has no compressing disk and is not product-parallel to the inner pattern torus. Let $T_c=\partial V=e(\partial(S^1\times D^2))\subset E_{P(K)}$ be the companion torus. Then $T_c$ is incompressible and is not boundary-parallel in $E_{P(K)}$; hence it is essential.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. There exists a finite inclusion-minimal collection $\mathcal T$ of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori in the interior of $E_K$ such that every component of $E_K$ cut along $\mathcal T$ is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Any two such inclusion-minimal collections are ambient isotopic in $E_K$. Atoroidal pieces in this statement are not asserted to be hyperbolic.

citations.quote: Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every nonempty compact
connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold is homeomorphic to exactly one
of the following types: the sphere $S^2$, a connected sum of $g\geq1$ tori,
or a connected sum of $k\geq1$ real projective planes. The connected sums here
are the explicit polygonal models with their chosen disk removals and boundary
gluings ([[def-connected-sum-of-compact-surfaces]]). The integer is unique
within its type. Equivalently, two such surfaces are homeomorphic if and only
if they have the same integral orientability and Euler characteristic.

The canonical one-face words are respectively the sphere digon $aa^{-1}$
(whose *reduced notation* is empty), the $g$-fold commutator word
$\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1}$, and the $k$-fold square word
$\prod_{j=1}^k c_jc_j$. The empty notation is not an empty polygonal schema.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected irreducible Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold, and let $F\subset M$ be a connected, two-sided essential annulus or torus, neatly embedded at its boundary (the condition is vacuous for a torus). Then $F$ is ambient isotopic to either a vertical surface, meaning a union of regular fibers, or a horizontal surface, meaning a surface transverse to every fiber. For a horizontal surface $F$ with $n$ sheets over the base orbifold $B$ and exceptional-fiber multiplicities $q_1,\ldots,q_m$, the Euler characteristics satisfy
$$
\frac{\chi(F)}{n}=\chi(B)-\sum_{i=1}^m\left(1-\frac1{q_i}\right).
$$
If $F$ is two-sided and horizontal, cutting $M$ along $F$ gives an interval bundle over a surface.

For a smooth boundary-preimage embedding without the neatness condition, the same vertical-or-horizontal normal form is attained by a smooth isotopy of embeddings, fixed on the original boundary during its preliminary neatification, and by a topological ambient isotopy. The Euler count and interval-bundle conclusions apply to the resulting horizontal representative. A smooth ambient isotopy is asserted for the neat inputs above.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a nontrivial smooth knot with a specified companion solid torus $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$, let $P\subset\operatorname{int}(S^1\times D^2)$ be a pattern, and assume the outer torus of its pattern exterior $X_P$ has no compressing disk and is not product-parallel to the inner pattern torus. Let $T_c=\partial V=e(\partial(S^1\times D^2))\subset E_{P(K)}$ be the companion torus. Then $T_c$ is incompressible and is not boundary-parallel in $E_{P(K)}$; hence it is essential.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth oriented knot with a specified orientation-preserving companion embedding $e:V=S^1\times D^2\to S^3$ that sends the oriented core to $K$ and identifies the product meridian and longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. Let $P\subset\operatorname{int}V$ be a smooth oriented pattern with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)\subset\operatorname{int}V$. Put $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$ and assume that no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ has essential boundary on $\partial V$, and that $X_P$ is not a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with ends $\partial V$ and $\partial N(P)$. Put $P(K)=e(P)$, $M=E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$, and $T_c=e(\partial V)$. Suppose both components of $M$ cut along $T_c$ are atoroidal or Seifert-fibered, and $M$ itself is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Then every inclusion-minimal JSJ system of $M$ consists of one torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. Cutting along $T_c$ has the companion exterior $E_K$ as its outside component. No conclusion is made for an essential companion torus that is absorbed into a Seifert-fibered union.

Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. There exists a finite inclusion-minimal collection $\mathcal T$ of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori in the interior of $E_K$ such that every component of $E_K$ cut along $\mathcal T$ is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Any two such inclusion-minimal collections are ambient isotopic in $E_K$. Atoroidal pieces in this statement are not asserted to be hyperbolic.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth Seifert-fibered three-manifold and let $T$ be a boundary torus whose inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups. Fix one Seifert fibration and a based regular fiber $h\in\pi_1(T)\subset\pi_1(M)$. Suppose the quotient $\pi_1(M)/\langle h\rangle$ is isomorphic to a finite free product of at least two nontrivial groups, excluding the free product of two groups of order two. Then every Seifert fibration of $M$ has the same unoriented regular-fiber slope on $T$ as the fixed fibration. No choice hypothesis is introduced. The notation $\langle h\rangle$ denotes the cyclic subgroup, which is normal as proved below.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Let $G=G_1*\cdots*G_k$, where $2\le k<\infty$ and every factor is nontrivial. If $k=2$, assume the two factors are not both cyclic of order two. Then every cyclic normal subgroup of $G$ is trivial. No choice hypothesis is required.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

derivations.claim: The circle action $t\cdot(z,w)=(e^{4\pi i t}z,e^{2\pi i t}w)$ on $S^1\times D^2$ has generic orbit slope $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$. The given pattern is one such orbit. The core $S^1\times\{0\}$ has stabilizer of order $2$, while generic points have trivial stabilizer. Removing a tube about the regular orbit $P_{2,1}$ therefore gives a Seifert fibration of $X_{P_{2,1}}$ over an annulus with one exceptional point of multiplicity $2$. On the outer torus its regular-fiber slope is $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$.

Remove a small neighborhood of the exceptional point from the annulus base. The remaining pair of pants has fundamental group freely generated by a loop $a$ around the outer boundary and a loop $c$ around the removed cone point; its third boundary loop is $(ac)^{-1}$. The circle bundle over this pair of pants has a section: it retracts to a graph, and a section over that graph is obtained by choosing one point in the fiber at the vertex and extending over each edge. Thus its group has generators $a,c,h$, with $h$ the fiber and $[a,h]=[c,h]=1$. The order-two local model $(z,w)\mapsto(-z,-w)$ around the exceptional core identifies the filled meridian with $c^2h$ after replacing $c$ by $ch^k$ if necessary: one circuit of the cone-point boundary lifts from $(z,w)$ to $(-z,-w)$, so two circuits equal one inverse fiber turn, and the twisting coefficient is odd. Filling that neighborhood kills this meridian. By [F3],
$$
\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})=\langle a,c,h\mid [a,h]=[c,h]=1,\ c^2h=1\rangle.
$$
Its quotient by $\langle h\rangle$ is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, which is nonabelian by reduced normal forms [F4]; hence $X_{P_{2,1}}$ is not $T^2\times I$. Its outer boundary subgroup is generated by $a,h$. The abelianization is free on $[a],[c]$ with $[h]=-2[c]$, so $a^m h^n=1$ implies $m=0$ and $n=0$. Thus the outer torus group injects into $\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})$ and has no compressing disk.

For the trefoil, [F2] gives $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^2=y^3\rangle$ and regular fiber $h_K=x^2=y^3$. Its quotient by $\langle h_K\rangle$ is $C_2*C_3$, nonabelian by [F4], and $h_K$ is infinite because its abelianization is $6$ times the generator of $H_1(E_K)\cong\mathbb Z$. The group maps onto $S_3$ by $x\mapsto(12)$ and $y\mapsto(123)$, so it is nonabelian and $K$ is not the unknot, whose exterior group is $\mathbb Z$.

The peripheral formula in [F2] gives $h_K=\lambda_K+6\mu_K$. The companion embedding identifies $(\mu_V,\lambda_V)$ with $(\mu_K,\lambda_K)$. Therefore the two Seifert fibrations on the cut sides induce slopes $2\lambda+\mu$ and $\lambda+6\mu$ on the companion torus. Their determinant in the ordered basis $(\mu,\lambda)$ is $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&6\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=-11$, so the slopes are not parallel.
By [F7], the companion torus $T_c$ is essential. Hence the whole exterior $M=E_{P_{2,1}(K)}$ is not atoroidal. Both pieces cut along $T_c$ are Seifert-fibered by steps 1.1 and 1.3.

The horizontal case is impossible. The interval-bundle bases inherit smooth transverse charts from the horizontal surface and the fiber charts. For any such compact connected surface with nonempty boundary, [F10] gives a finite triangulation. Root a spanning tree of its triangle-adjacency graph at a boundary edge. Delete each triangle across its exposed parent edge, starting at the root; this collapses the surface to a finite connected graph. Its group is therefore free, with rank equal to the rank of its abelianization, by collapsing a graph spanning tree. For a closed surface, the polygon models of [F5] give abelianization $\mathbb Z^{2g}$ in the orientable genus $g$ case and $\mathbb Z^{k-1}\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ in the nonorientable genus $k$ case, by adding the signed edge occurrences in its single face word. Hence a compact surface group with torsion-free rank-two abelianization is either the torus group $\mathbb Z^2$ or the free group of rank two; with torsion-free rank-one abelianization it is infinite cyclic. The cable group has abelianization $\mathbb Z^2$, is nonabelian because its quotient is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, and has the nonidentity central element $h$ since $[h]=-2[c]$ in its abelianization. It is neither $\mathbb Z^2$ nor the free group of rank two, whose center is trivial by [F11]. The trefoil group has abelianization $\mathbb Z$ and is nonabelian by step 1.3, so it too is not a surface group with that abelianization. Thus neither cut piece can be an interval bundle over a surface.

Suppose $M$ had a Seifert fibration. By [A2], countable choice holds, so [F13] makes $M$ irreducible. Then [F6] makes $T_c$ ambient isotopic to a vertical or horizontal torus. Isotopy preserves the homeomorphism types of the cut pieces. In the horizontal case, cutting along $T_c$ gives interval bundles over compact connected surfaces, so each side group is a surface group.

Suppose instead that $T_c$ is vertical after isotopy. Pull the hypothetical fibration back by that ambient isotopy, so the original $T_c$ is vertical and the original cut-piece markings are retained. Restriction gives a Seifert fibration on each cut piece with one common regular-fiber slope on $T_c$. Their boundary groups inject independently of any general knot-boundary incompressibility theorem. For the cable side this was proved in step 1.2. For the trefoil side, the peripheral formula of [F2], with $2(-1)+3(1)=1$, gives $\mu=y^{-1}x$ and $\lambda=h_K\mu^{-6}$. Thus $(\mu,h_K)$ is also a basis for its boundary-torus group. In the quotient $C_2*C_3$ the word $y^{-1}x$ is cyclically reduced of length two, so all its nonzero powers are nonidentity by [F4]. If $\mu^a h_K^b=1$, quotienting forces $a=0$, and the infinite order of $h_K$ from step 1.3 forces $b=0$. This proves injectivity of that boundary group. The two original fiber quotients are $\mathbb Z*C_2$ and $C_2*C_3$, respectively, by steps 1.2 and 1.3; neither is the two-order-two exception. Apply [F9] separately to the restricted hypothetical fibration on each side. Its common boundary-fiber slope must equal both original slopes, contradicting their determinant $-11$ in step 2.1. This rules out the vertical case; together with step 2.3 it proves that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered.

Steps 2.2 and 4.1 verify the nonamalgamation hypotheses of [F8], so the companion torus is a JSJ torus and the component outside the companion solid torus is $E_K$. The smooth ambient uniqueness in [F8] carries the original marked outside component to the outside component for any isotopic minimal JSJ torus.

derivations.claim: Put $M=E_K$ and $T=\partial M$. By hypothesis $M$ is compact, connected, orientable and irreducible, and $T$ is its single torus boundary component. If $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(M)$ had nontrivial kernel, [F1] would supply an essential simple curve in $T$ bounding a proper disk in $M$, contradicting boundary incompressibility. Hence $\pi_1(M)$ contains the injected group $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ and is infinite.

The given embedded-torus atoroidality and the hypothesis that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered allow [F2] to be applied. Therefore every $\pi_1$-injective torus map is homotopic into $\partial M$. Together with the incompressible torus boundary and infinite $\pi_1$ from step 1.1, these are the actual hypotheses of [F3]: AFW supplies hyperbolization, and the finite-volume conclusion for this incompressible-boundary case is the separately cited Rubinstein statement. Thus $\operatorname{int}(M)$ admits a complete finite-volume metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$. This applies to fibered knot exteriors as well as nonfibered ones; no additional non-interval-bundle assumption has been introduced.

The interior of a compact connected manifold with one connected boundary component has one end: a boundary collar gives a cofinal family of connected complements of compact subsets, namely $T\times(0,\epsilon)$. By [F4], every end of the metric from step 2.1 is a rank-two horoball quotient, so there is exactly one torus cusp. It belongs to the unique original boundary end. This is an existence assertion for a metric on the original interior; no prescribed horosphere scale, meridian–longitude translation vectors, or separately marked peripheral conjugacy is asserted. No conclusion is used outside the four topological hypotheses of the Statement.

current_manifest_record.title: Closed square-integrable adjoint one-forms on a cusped hyperbolic three-manifold are exact

references.title: Pere Menal-Ferrer and Joan Porti, Twisted cohomology for hyperbolic three manifolds
references.locator: Section 2, particularly Corollary 2.12 and Lemma 2.14; the required complete-manifold analytic implication is also proved locally below

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be an oriented hyperbolic three-manifold with compact complement to finitely many standard torus cusp ends, each isometric to $(T^2\times[0,\infty),dt^2+e^{-2t}g_T)$ for a flat metric $g_T$. The compact case is allowed. Let $E=\mathbb H^3\times_\Gamma\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ be the adjoint flat bundle. Give its fiber at a basepoint the Hilbert–Schmidt Hermitian product and transport this product by the homogeneous $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)/\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ construction. Write $d_E$ for its flat differential and $\delta_E$ for the metric formal adjoint.

There is $c>0$, depending only on the model normalization, such that every compactly supported smooth $E$-valued one-form satisfies
$$\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2.$$
Every smooth $E$-valued one-form $\alpha$ with $d_E\alpha=0$ and $\|\alpha\|_2<\infty$ has a smooth square-integrable primitive $b$, with $d_Eb=\alpha$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

derivations.claim: Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$, $K=\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ and $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$. Choose $X_1=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $X_2=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $X_3=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $\mathfrak k$, and put $Y_j=iX_j$. These $Y_j$ are an orthonormal tangent basis for curvature $-1$ hyperbolic space; for example $\exp(tY_1)$ moves the basepoint distance $|t|$, and the $K$ action rotates this basis. The matrix commutators give $[X_i,X_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ and $[Y_i,Y_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}Y_k$. On $V$ let $R_j=\operatorname{ad}Y_j$. Each $Y_j$ is Hermitian, so $R_j$ is self-adjoint for $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)$, by cyclicity of trace. The $K$ action is unitary for this product.

Represent $E$-valued forms by horizontal $K$-equivariant $V$-valued forms on $Q=\Gamma\backslash G$, expressing their coefficients in the left Maurer–Cartan frame. Indeed a frame $g$ identifies the fiber over $gK$ with $V$ by $\operatorname{Ad}g$, and replacing $g$ by $gk$ changes these coefficients by $\operatorname{Ad}k^{-1}$ and rotates the tangent indices. In these coefficients write $\varepsilon_j$ for exterior multiplication by the dual of $Y_j$ and $\iota_j$ for contraction by $Y_j$. The ordinary covariant differential of the $K$ connection is $D=\sum_j\varepsilon_jY_j$, because the horizontal part of $[Y_i,Y_j]$ is zero. Differentiating the fiber change $\operatorname{Ad}g$ gives $d_E=D+T$, where $T=\sum_j\varepsilon_jR_j$. These are actual coefficient formulas on all degrees, not definitions of a different connection.

The invariant volume on $Q$ is the product of hyperbolic volume and normalized compact-fiber volume. Integration in a local bundle chart and then a subordinate smooth partition of unity [F2] shows that integration of a $K$-invariant coefficient norm on $Q$ equals its integration on $M$. The left invariant fields $Y_j$ have zero divergence for this volume: $G$ is unimodular, since $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}Z)=0$ for the displayed Lie algebra basis, hence for all $Z$, and $\det\operatorname{Ad}(\exp Z)=1$. Right translation therefore preserves its Haar volume. Integration by parts on compact supports now gives $D^*=-\sum_j\iota_jY_j$ and $T^*=\sum_j\iota_jR_j$. The relations $\varepsilon_i\iota_j+\iota_j\varepsilon_i=\delta_{ij}$ show that $DT^*+T^*D+TD^*+D^*T=0$: the two anticommutator sums are respectively $\sum_jR_jY_j$ and its negative, since coefficient differentiation commutes with the constant matrices $R_j$. Thus $d_E\delta_E+\delta_Ed_E=DD^*+D^*D+H$, where $H=TT^*+T^*T$. All statements are $K$-equivariant and descend from $Q$ to $M$.

On one-form coefficients $a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in V^3$, the exterior-contraction relations give $(Ha)_i=\sum_jR_j^2a_i+\sum_j[R_i,R_j]a_j$. This finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator is positive definite. If $Ha=0$, positivity of $TT^*+T^*T$ gives $Ta=0$, namely $R_ia_j=R_ja_i$ for all $i,j$. Since $[R_i,R_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, the commutator sum in the displayed formula is a multiple of $R_ka_j-R_ja_k$ and vanishes. Consequently $0=\langle Ha,a\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\|R_ja_i\|^2$. Each $a_i$ commutes with all $Y_j$, which span $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ over $\mathbb C$. A matrix commuting with all traceless matrices is scalar, and a traceless scalar is zero. Thus $a=0$. Compactness of the unit sphere in $V^3$ supplies $c>0$ with $H\ge cI$.

For a compactly supported smooth one-form, integration by parts in step 3.1 and step 4.1 give $\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2=\|D\alpha\|_2^2+\|D^*\alpha\|_2^2+(H\alpha,\alpha)\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2$. We next extend this inequality to the joint weak graph domain. On each cusp choose a smooth cutoff equal to one for $t\le R$, zero for $t\ge2R$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set it equal to one on the compact core. These cutoffs $\chi_R$ have compact support and $|d\chi_R|\le C/R$. For a weak graph-domain form $v$, the product formulas $d_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_Rd_Ev+d\chi_R\wedge v$ and $\delta_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\delta_Ev-\iota_{\nabla\chi_R}v$ show convergence to $v$ in the joint graph norm. The same conclusion holds separately for each differential and codifferential and for forms of every degree. In the compact case take the cutoff identically one.

Here are the local smoothing details needed to finish that graph-density argument. In a finite collection of trivializing charts around the support of $\chi_Rv$, every differential or codifferential is a first-order matrix operator $P=\sum_jA_j(x)\partial_j+B(x)$ with smooth coefficients. Multiplication by a subordinate smooth partition [F2] reduces to forms supported inside individual charts. For convolution with a smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho_\epsilon$, the difference $P(v*\rho_\epsilon)-(Pv)*\rho_\epsilon$ is a sum of integral operators with kernels $(A_j(x)-A_j(y))\partial_j\rho_\epsilon(x-y)+(\partial_jA_j)(y)\rho_\epsilon(x-y)$ and a zero-order coefficient commutator. The $L^1$ kernel bounds are uniform on the compact chart, by the mean-value bound for $A_j$ and scaling of $\rho_\epsilon$; thus these commutators are uniformly bounded on $L^2$. They tend to zero on smooth functions by differentiation of convolutions, hence on all $L^2$ functions by the smooth-density fact in [F2] and the uniform bound. Therefore local mollification converges in each asserted graph norm, also for the direct sum operator $(d_E,\delta_E)$. The partition contributes only fixed zero-order commutators, so a finite sum completes the approximation by compactly supported smooth forms. Together with step 5.1 this proves the coercive inequality on the maximal joint graph domain. It also proves that maximal differentials are the adjoints of maximal formal codifferentials, since their compact-support integration-by-parts identities extend by this graph density.

Let $\mathcal H_p=L^2(\Lambda^pT^*M\otimes E)$ and let $d_p$ be the maximal weak differential. It is closed: convergence of a form and its differential in $L^2$ preserves the weak test-function identity. Flatness gives $d_1d_0=0$ distributionally. Put $Z=\ker d_1$, a closed subspace of $\mathcal H_1$, and $\delta=d_0^*$. Every $w\in Z^\perp$ belongs to $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ with $\delta w=0$, because it is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}d_0\subseteq Z$. Hence the orthogonal projection $P_Z$ maps $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ into itself and $\delta P_Zv=\delta v$. On $Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, steps 5.1 and 6.1 give $\|v\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\delta v\|_2$. In particular $A=\delta|_{Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta}$ is injective with closed range: a Cauchy sequence of its images is, by this estimate, the image under the closed operator $\delta$ of a convergent sequence in $Z$.

Fix a weakly closed $\alpha\in\mathcal H_1$, so $\alpha\in Z$. On the closed range of $A$ define $\ell(Av)=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$. It is well defined and bounded, with norm at most $c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$, by step 7.1. Extend it to $\mathcal H_0$ by zero on the orthogonal complement of that range and use [F1] to obtain $b\in\mathcal H_0$ with $\langle Av,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$. For arbitrary $v\in\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, replace $v$ by $P_Zv$; its $\delta$ image is unchanged and its pairing with $\alpha$ is unchanged. Thus $\langle\delta v,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ on the full domain of $\delta$. By the adjoint definition and the graph-density conclusion of step 6.1, $b\in\operatorname{Dom}d_0$ and $d_0b=\alpha$. This proves the primitive assertion in the weak sense without an external closed-range or harmonic-representative theorem.

If $\alpha$ is smooth, the primitive $b$ is smooth. In a flat parallel frame on a coordinate ball, $d_Eb=\alpha$ is the ordinary componentwise distributional equation $db=\alpha$. A smooth closed one-form on a smaller star-shaped coordinate ball has a smooth primitive $b_0$, given by integrating along straight radial segments; differentiating the integral and using closedness verifies $db_0=\alpha$. Then $d(b-b_0)=0$ distributionally. Mollification on still smaller balls makes this difference a sequence of constants, so its distributional limit is constant as well. Thus $b=b_0+\text{constant}$ is smooth locally and hence globally. Its $L^2$ norm and the bound from step 8.1 remain unchanged.

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the chosen smooth knot-exterior data. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, with one boundary component. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose positive normal push-off of its core has linking number $+1$ with the core; a negative Hopf band has linking number $-1$. A square plumbing identifies a square in the boundary collars of the annuli with the four boundary edges alternating between the annuli, then smooths corners. Let $F$ be this plumbed surface, and choose the compact exterior by deleting the interior of the binding neighborhood $N(K_8)\cong\partial F\times D^2$ supplied by the open book; on every page this neighborhood meets the page in an annular collar of $\partial F$. Let $a,b$ be the core curves, ordered so that $a$ is the positive-band core and $a\cdot_F b=+1$. The exterior $E_{K_8}$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $F$. With the twist convention that the positive twist $R_a$ sends $a\mapsto a$, $b\mapsto a+b$, and the negative twist $L_b$ sends $a\mapsto a+b$, $b\mapsto b$, the monodromy is $R_a\circ L_b$. After capping $\partial F$ by a disk, its action on the ordered homology basis $([a],[b])$ is represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: In $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$, the standard Hopf link is $H=\{z_1z_2=0\}$. On its complement, $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2/|z_1z_2|$ is a submersion to $S^1$. Writing $r=|z_1|^2$, $\theta=\arg z_1$, and $\phi=\arg z_2$, a fiber is $0<r<1$, $\phi=-\theta+\text{constant}$, hence an annulus. For base angle $s\in[0,2\pi]$, transport by $\theta_s=\theta+\chi(r)s$, $\phi_s=\phi+(1-\chi(r))s$, where $\chi=1$ near $r=0$ and $\chi=0$ near $r=1$, fixes both boundary circles at $s=2\pi$ and makes one full annular twist between them. The sign is determined by the signed linking of the positive normal push-off of the core with the core: changing the handedness of the Hopf band reverses the twist. With $a\cdot_F b=+1$, the positive twist about $a$ acts by $b\mapsto a+b$, while the negative twist about $b$ acts by $a\mapsto a+b$. Hence the two band monodromies have the stated actions $R_a$ and $L_b$.

The square plumbing is the Murasugi sum in Construction 5.37 of [F3]. Theorem 5.38 of [F3] gives a fibration with fiber $F$ and return map the composition of the two Hopf-band monodromies extended by the identity; in the stipulated order, step 1.1 identifies it as $R_a\circ L_b$. Example 5.39 of [F3] identifies the boundary of the opposite-handed sum as the standard figure-eight knot. Deleting the binding neighborhood as in [F1] therefore gives the stated exterior as the mapping torus.

Each annulus has Euler characteristic $0$, and the plumbing square has Euler characteristic $1$, so $\chi(F)=0+0-1=-1$. The plumbing is connected, oriented, and has one boundary component by the stated gluing; hence $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ gives $g(F)=1$. Thus $F$ is a once-punctured torus.

In the ordered basis $([a],[b])$, the columns of $R_a$ are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, while the columns of $L_b$ are $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$. Their product is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Inclusion of the once-punctured torus into the torus obtained by capping its sole boundary induces an isomorphism on $H_1$, since attaching a disk along the boundary adds no 1-cycle or 2-cycle relation in degree one. Extending the boundary-fixing monodromy by the identity on that disk therefore has the same displayed action.

current_manifest_record.statement: Let $N$ be the complement of finitely many disjoint open solid tori in a connected oriented three-manifold, and suppose its interior has a hyperbolic metric. Fix one boundary torus $T$ with primitive peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$. Assume that a neighborhood of this end, after developing into $\mathbb H^3$, is isometric to a punctured radius-$\varepsilon$ tube about a geodesic axis, modulo a translation of length $L>0$ along that axis. Assume that $\lambda$ is the axial translation direction and that $\mu$ is the angular direction making one full turn of angle $2\pi$ about the axis; equivalently, its peripheral holonomy is the identity isometry with the full-turn lift. Then the hyperbolic metric extends smoothly over the ordinary Dehn filling along $\mu$, adding the axis quotient as the core geodesic of length $L$. The same conclusion holds simultaneously for any finite set of ends satisfying these conditions.

citations.quote:
Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

Let an oriented finite ideal triangulation of the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold have $k\ge1$ ideal vertices, each with torus link. Assign a positive ideal-tetrahedron shape to every tetrahedron. Suppose that around every finite edge the product of its incident complex shape parameters is $1$ and the sum of its dihedral angles is $2\pi$. For each ideal vertex $v$, choose a basis $(\alpha_v,\beta_v)$ of the fundamental group of its torus link and suppose the cusp multipliers satisfy $H(\alpha_v)=H(\beta_v)=1$. Then the face gluings define a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the manifold interior, with one rank-two cusp for each ideal vertex.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

derivations.claim: In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta,z)$ about a geodesic in $\mathbb H^3$, the metric is $ds^2=dr^2+\sinh^2(r)\,d\theta^2+\cosh^2(r)\,dz^2$. The full-turn condition makes $\theta$ have period $2\pi$, while the axial translation identifies $z$ with $z+L$. Thus the developed tube quotient is $(0,\varepsilon)\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$, and its meridian is exactly the $\theta$ circle representing $\mu$.

Set $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$. Then $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)d\theta^2=dx^2+dy^2+\frac{(\sinh^2r-r^2)}{r^4}(x\,dy-y\,dx)^2$. The coefficient has the convergent even-power expansion $1/3+O(r^2)$ at $r=0$, and $\cosh^2(r)$ is smooth in $x^2+y^2$. Hence the metric extends smoothly across $x=y=0$; the added set is the circle $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z$ and is the core of a solid torus. The extended metric has curvature $-1$ on the dense punctured tube by [F2], so its smooth curvature tensor has curvature $-1$ on the core by continuity.

First use the model attaching map from step 1.1; by step 2.1 it gives a smooth hyperbolic extension over that filled solid torus. For any specified ordinary filling map with the same meridian slope, [F4] supplies an oriented homeomorphism from that filling to the model filling, equal to the identity on the complement. Transport the smooth structure and extended metric across this homeomorphism. The transported structure agrees with the original smooth structure on the complement, so this gives the asserted extension on the specified topological filling. For finitely many ends the tube neighborhoods are disjoint, and these identifications and extensions can be made independently.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [A1], the needed countable-choice hypothesis [F1] holds. Let $F$ be the fiber from [F5]. Cutting the exterior along $F$ gives $F\times[0,1]$, with its interval ends reidentified by the monodromy $\varphi$; because $\varphi$ fixes $\partial F$ pointwise, the boundary torus is identified with $\partial F\times S^1$.

The curve $\partial F$ on the peripheral torus is an essential parallel of the knot and bounds the fiber in the exterior, so its homology class maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_8};\mathbb Z)$. It is primitive because it is a simple essential curve. By uniqueness in [F4], it represents $\lambda$ up to orientation, hence it is exactly the unoriented filling slope $0$ by [F3].

For the model gluing, use the second coordinate of $D^2\times S^1$ as the mapping-torus direction and identify the meridian disk boundary with $\partial F\times\{t\}$. The filled space is the mapping torus of $\overline F=F\cup_{\partial F}D^2$: extend $\varphi$ over the disk by the identity, which is continuous and fixes the seam since $\varphi|_{\partial F}=\mathrm{id}$. The actual filling map has the same meridian slope by [F3]; [F7] extends the transition map over the filling solid torus, so the actual filling is oriented-homeomorphic to this model mapping torus.

The surface $\overline F$ is obtained from a once-punctured torus by capping its sole boundary component with a disk, so it is a closed torus. The mapping torus of the extended homeomorphism $\overline\varphi$ is consequently a torus bundle over $S^1$. Inclusion $F\hookrightarrow\overline F$ induces an isomorphism on first homology, and the extension is the identity on the cap, so its matrix remains the matrix in [F5].
