current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be an oriented hyperbolic three-manifold with compact complement to finitely many standard torus cusp ends, each isometric to $(T^2\times[0,\infty),dt^2+e^{-2t}g_T)$ for a flat metric $g_T$. The compact case is allowed. Let $E=\mathbb H^3\times_\Gamma\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ be the adjoint flat bundle. Give its fiber at a basepoint the Hilbert–Schmidt Hermitian product and transport this product by the homogeneous $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)/\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ construction. Write $d_E$ for its flat differential and $\delta_E$ for the metric formal adjoint.

There is $c>0$, depending only on the model normalization, such that every compactly supported smooth $E$-valued one-form satisfies
$$\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2.$$
Every smooth $E$-valued one-form $\alpha$ with $d_E\alpha=0$ and $\|\alpha\|_2<\infty$ has a smooth square-integrable primitive $b$, with $d_Eb=\alpha$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $Z$ be a reduced complex analytic space with point $o$, and suppose $u_i,v_i,a_i,b_i$ are holomorphic germs on $Z$ for $1\le i\le k$, with $k<\infty$, $u_i(o)=v_i(o)=0$, $a_i(o)\ne0$ and $\tau_i^0=b_i(o)/a_i(o)\notin\mathbb R$. Suppose the affine maps
$$L_i(w)=e^{u_i}w+a_i,\qquad P_i(w)=e^{v_i}w+b_i$$
commute at every parameter point. Then, after shrinking around $o$, there are holomorphic germs $\tau_i$ such that $v_i=\tau_i u_i$, $\tau_i(o)=\tau_i^0$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\ne0$ throughout. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and $v_i/u_i\to\tau_i^0$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u_i\ne0$. No smoothness, dimension or rank hypothesis on $Z$ is required.

For $u_i\ne0$, there is a unique real pair $(p_i,q_i)$ solving $p_iu_i+q_iv_i=2\pi i$. With
$$\widetilde u_i=\frac{2\pi i}{p_i+\tau_i^0q_i},$$
one has
$$|\widetilde u_i-u_i|\le\frac{|\tau_i-\tau_i^0|}{|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0|}|u_i|.$$
Set $\widetilde u_i=0$ when $u_i=0$. The functions $\widetilde u_i$ are continuous at such points, and $\|\widetilde u-u\|=o(\|u\|)$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u\ne0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a boundaryless Riemannian manifold. An open set $W\subseteq M$ is called **strongly geodesically convex** here when, for every ordered pair $(x,y)\in W\times W$, there is a unique affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to M$ that globally minimizes length from $x$ to $y$, its image lies in $W$, and $(x,y,t)\mapsto\gamma_{x,y}(t)$ is smooth.

Every point of $M$ has a strongly geodesically convex neighbourhood. More precisely, the neighbourhood may be chosen inside any prescribed open neighbourhood of the point, and it may be chosen so that every piecewise smooth curve attaining the global minimum between two of its points is a monotone reparametrization of the displayed connector. Every nonempty intersection of a positive finite family of strongly geodesically convex open sets is again strongly geodesically convex.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Every open cover of a smooth manifold has a countable cover by coordinate balls with compact closures, each closure contained in one member of the original cover.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(U_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a countable cover of a smooth manifold $M$ by coordinate balls with compact closures. Then there is an at-most-countable index set $I$ and families of open sets $(W_k)_{k\in I}$ and coordinate balls $(V_k)_{k\in I}$ such that $M=\bigcup_{k\in I} W_k$, each $\overline{W_k}\subseteq V_k\subseteq \overline{V_k}\subseteq U_{n(k)}$ for some index $n(k)$, and the family $(V_k)$ is locally finite. The index set may be finite or empty.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

derivations.claim: The complete holonomy is irreducible and its adjoint invariants vanish. Indeed one cusp subgroup is a rank-two translation lattice fixing $\infty$. If all of $\Gamma$ fixed $\infty$, its elements would be similarities $z\mapsto az+b$. An element with $|a|\ne1$ would conjugate a fixed nonzero lattice translation to translations tending to the identity, contradicting discreteness. An element with $|a|=1$ and $a\ne1$ is elliptic about a vertical line, impossible in a torsion-free discrete group. Hence all elements would be translations, and the quotient would have infinite volume as height tends to zero. This contradicts the finite-volume hypothesis. Thus some element does not fix $\infty$. A traceless matrix invariant under the cusp group is a multiple of $E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, by direct commutation with a nontrivial unipotent. A nonzero such matrix invariant under all of $\Gamma$ would force preservation of its kernel line, hence of $\infty$, a contradiction. Thus $H^0(M;E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0})=0$. The same argument excludes a common invariant line for the holonomy matrices. The group centralizer in $G$ is trivial as well: a Möbius map commuting with the cusp translations fixes $\infty$ and is itself a translation, by its affine formula; a nonidentity such translation has unique fixed point $\infty$, so commuting with the entire group would force the whole group to fix $\infty$.

We specify the cohomology comparisons being used. The flat adjoint bundle has local parallel frames, obtained on simply connected balls by trivializing its defining covering construction. In such frames its differential is the componentwise ordinary exterior differential; integration of forms over simplices is compatible with the constant transition matrices and with Stokes. The usual local Poincaré contraction is explicit: integrate contraction by the radial vector along radial coordinate segments. A locally finite good cover by sufficiently small strongly convex metric balls therefore gives a Čech double complex whose form columns resolve the parallel local sections. Its positive Čech rows are contracted by $(hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}=\sum_j\phi_jc_{ji_0\ldots i_{r-1}}$, for a subordinate partition of unity. The small-singular-cochain double complex has the same degree-zero columns, since every intersection is contractible; subdivision makes singular simplices subordinate to the cover, and the Čech rows contract by assigning a containing index to each small simplex. The two edge comparisons identify flat de Rham cohomology with singular cohomology with this local system, naturally for restrictions. These constructions also apply to compact support and to collars, so relative classes are represented by forms supported away from the ends. Finally $M$ is aspherical, with universal cover $\mathbb H^3$ contractible. Its lifted cellular or singular chains form a free resolution of $\mathbb C$ as a $\mathbb C\Gamma$-module; comparison of free resolutions by successive lifts gives the same cohomology as group cocycles. In degree one, this comparison is concretely integration of an equivariant closed form along a lifted group loop. These arguments establish the coefficient comparisons, rather than invoking an unproved twisted de Rham theorem.

The representation scheme of a torus is smooth near its noncentral complete peripheral pair. Use local $SL_2$ lifts $A,B$ of the two generators, both near nontrivial commuting unipotents; their commutator is $I$ because its sign is locally constant and is positive at the basepoint. Choose a fixed vector $v$ with $v,Av$ independent at that point and hence nearby. For a commuting matrix $B$, write $Bv=av+bAv$; commutation then forces $B=aI+bA$ by applying both sides to the basis $v,Av$. This argument works over truncated power-series rings too, because the basis determinant is a unit. Put $C=A-(\operatorname{tr}A)I/2$ and write $B=\alpha I+\beta C$. Its determinant condition is $\alpha^2-\beta^2((\operatorname{tr}A)^2/4-1)=1$. At the complete pair $\alpha=1$, so [F3] solves uniquely for $\alpha$ in terms of $A$ and $\beta$. Thus the commuting-pair scheme is locally a smooth four-dimensional space, parametrized by the three coordinates of $A$ and one of $\beta$. In particular every representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ near this pair extends one order further.

Write $E_0=E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0}$. The restriction $r_1:H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)$ is injective. If a closed smooth form represents a class in its kernel, on each cusp tail it equals $d_{E_0}b_i$ for a smooth section, by step 1.2. Subtract $d_{E_0}(\chi_i b_i)$ using a cutoff equal to one sufficiently far along that end and zero near the core. The resulting cohomologous closed form is compactly supported, hence square integrable, and is exact by [F1]. Thus the original class is zero. Equivalently the map $H^1(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^1(N;E_0)$ vanishes. By [F2], its transpose, up to the harmless cap-boundary sign, is the map $H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N;E_0)$, so that map also vanishes. The pair sequence therefore gives $r_2:H^2(N;E_0)\to H^2(\partial N;E_0)$ injective. It is onto because its cokernel embeds in $H^3(N,\partial N;E_0)$, which is dual to $H^0(N;E_0)=0$ by step 1.1.

We give the full obstruction construction. Suppose $\rho^{(n)}$ is a representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ with constant term $\rho_0$. Choose arbitrary one-order lifts $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ of its values. The defect is uniquely $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)\widetilde\rho(\delta)\widetilde\rho(\gamma\delta)^{-1}=I+t^{n+1}c(\gamma,\delta)$ modulo $t^{n+2}$, with $c$ in the adjoint Lie algebra; this expression is read in the identity chart of $G$. Associativity gives $c(\gamma,\delta)+c(\gamma\delta,\epsilon)=\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}c(\delta,\epsilon)+c(\gamma,\delta\epsilon)$, exactly the group two-cocycle relation. Replacing the lift at $\gamma$ by $(I+t^{n+1}b(\gamma))\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ changes $c$ by $b(\gamma)+\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}b(\delta)-b(\gamma\delta)$. Hence a one-order extension exists if and only if the class $[c]\in H^2(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ vanishes. The formulas commute with restriction to every subgroup.

At a cusp the adjoint invariants are $\mathbb CE$, of dimension one. Torus duality and the Euler characteristic of a finite cellular local system give $\dim H^0(T_i;E_0)=\dim H^2(T_i;E_0)=1$ and $\dim H^1(T_i;E_0)=2$. Indeed every cell contributes three coefficient dimensions, so the alternating chain dimension is $3\chi(T_i)=0$. The pair sequence and step 2.1 give a short exact sequence $0\to H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to0$. The last group is dual to the first by [F2]. Consequently $\dim H^1(N;E_0)=k$, while $r_2$ identifies $H^2(N;E_0)$ with $\mathbb C^k$. All these spaces are finite dimensional by the finite CW model in [F2].

On each peripheral subgroup the obstruction in step 2.2 is zero by the smooth formal chart of step 1.3. The map on $H^2$ restricting to all peripheral subgroups is injective by step 2.1 and the comparisons in step 1.2, so the global obstruction vanishes. Starting with any first-order cocycle, repeat step 2.2 and choose corrections at each order. AC supplies this countable recursive sequence. Every first-order representation tangent vector therefore has a full formal representation curve with that tangent. No convergence assertion about this curve is needed.

We compute the cusp classes and trace derivatives. Normalize the cusp lattice as $z=x+\tau_i^0 y$, with deck translations $x\mapsto x+1$ and $y\mapsto y+1$, and put $F=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and $n(z)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The forms $\eta_i=dx\otimes E$ and $\omega_i=dz\otimes\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F$ are equivariant and closed: $E$ is translation invariant and the polynomial $\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F=F+zH-z^2E$ depends only on $z$, so its derivative wedges to zero with $dz$. Their trace-paired cup product is $\operatorname{tr}(\eta_i\wedge\omega_i)=\tau_i^0dx\wedge dy$, while each self-pairing is zero. Thus these two classes are independent and form a basis by step 3.1. The form $\eta_i$ is square integrable on its cusp: at height $t$, $|dx|$ grows as $e^t$ and the homogeneous norm of $E$ decays as $e^{-t}$, whereas volume decays as $e^{-2t}$.

Let $L$ be the span of the $k$ classes $\eta_i$ in $H^1(\partial N;E_0)$. The image of $r_1$ meets $L$ only in zero. If a global closed form restricts cohomologically to a combination of these $\eta_i$, subtract exact cutoff terms on the ends as in step 2.1 to arrange equality with that combination on each tail. The resulting global form is square integrable by step 4.1 and compactness of the remaining core, hence exact by [F1]. Since both $H^1(N;E_0)$ and the span of the $\omega_i$ have dimension $k$, there is a global cohomology basis whose boundary images are $\omega_i+\sum_jc_{ij}\eta_j$.

A group one-cocycle $a$ represents the infinitesimal representation $(I+\epsilon a(\gamma))\rho_0(\gamma)$ modulo $\epsilon^2$, as direct multiplication verifies; infinitesimal conjugacies are precisely coboundaries. Thus representation tangent vectors modulo infinitesimal conjugacy are $H^1(N;E_0)$. For the positive local lift of the normalized cusp meridian, $\rho_0(\mu_i)=n(1)$, integration in step 1.2 gives $a_{\eta_i}(\mu_i)=E$ and $a_{\omega_i}(\mu_i)=\int_0^1(F+xH-x^2E)\,dx=F+H/2-E/3$. Therefore $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\eta_i)=\operatorname{tr}(En(1))=0$ and $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\omega_i)=1$. For trace squared the latter derivative is $4$, since the complete trace is $2$. Classes supported at other cusps contribute only their own restrictions. By the basis in step 5.1, $(ds_1,\ldots,ds_k)$ is an isomorphism from $H^1(N;E_0)$ to $\mathbb C^k$. This is a tangent calculation; smoothness is proved next.

Here is why formal integrability implies analytic smoothness in this setting, without an approximation theorem for formal solutions. Take a finite presentation from [F2] and express its relators near $\rho_0$ as an analytic map $R:\mathbb C^{3g}\to\mathbb C^{3r}$ by using local coordinates on $G$ for the generators and the identity logarithm for each relator. Put $K_0=\ker dR_0$, choose a complement $W$ in the source and a projection $\pi$ onto $\operatorname{im}dR_0$ in the target. By [F3], the equation $\pi R(z,w)=0$ has the unique solution $w=\psi(z)$, with $z\in K_0$, $\psi(0)=0$ and $d\psi_0=0$. Thus the representation germ is the zero set of $\kappa(z)=(I-\pi)R(z,\psi(z))$. If $\kappa$ were nonzero, let $P_d$ be its first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term. A formal representation curve of arbitrary tangent $a\in K_0$, supplied by step 3.2, has $z(t)=ta+O(t^2)$ and $w(t)=\psi(z(t))$; the latter identity follows recursively from the invertible partial Jacobian defining $\psi$. Its relators then give $P_d(a)=0$. This holds for every $a\in K_0$, contradicting that $P_d$ is a nonzero polynomial. Hence $\kappa$ vanishes identically by convergence of its analytic Taylor series. The representation scheme is smooth with tangent $K_0=Z^1(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ and dimension $k+3$: $H^1$ has dimension $k$, and the coboundaries have dimension three because the invariants vanish in step 1.1.

To pass to ordinary conjugacy, choose three linear coordinate conditions transverse to the conjugation orbit at $\rho_0$. The orbit derivative is injective by step 1.1. The analytic inverse theorem, equivalently [F3] applied to the conjugation map, gives a local product of a three-dimensional identity neighborhood in $G$ and a slice $S$ of dimension $k$. This slice represents the actual conjugacy quotient germ. To exclude extra identifications by large conjugations, suppose instead that arbitrarily near $\rho_0$ there were conjugate pairs requiring conjugators away from the identity in $G$. Choose such a sequence, lift its conjugators to nonzero matrices and normalize their Euclidean matrix norms to one. After a subsequence the normalized matrices have a nonzero limit $P$. Choose local lifts of the finitely many generator matrices. Their intertwining equations have signs $\pm1$; after another subsequence each sign is fixed. If $P$ had rank one, these equations would make its kernel a common invariant line of the limiting holonomy matrices, contradicting step 1.1. Thus $P$ is invertible, and its projective class centralizes the complete holonomy. That projective centralizer is trivial by step 1.1, so the conjugators tend projectively to the identity, a contradiction. The local product uniqueness therefore excludes all extra slice identifications after shrinking. This proves smoothness of the ordinary quotient germ. By step 6.1 the trace-squared map on $S$ has invertible differential, and [F3] makes $(s_1,\ldots,s_k)$ its holomorphic coordinates.

Let $u\in\mathbb C^k$ be small. Step 8.1 gives a unique slice representation $\rho(u)$ whose trace-squared coordinates are $s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2)$; it depends holomorphically on $u$. Choose local $SL_2$ lifts $A_i(u)$ of $\rho(u)(\mu_i)$ with trace near $2$. Their traces equal $2\cosh(u_i/2)$, because their squares agree and the near-$2$ branch is unique. Thus $e^{u_i/2}$ is an eigenvalue. The matrix $A_i(u)-e^{u_i/2}I$ has rank one throughout a small neighborhood, including $u_i=0$, since it has zero determinant and stays near a nonzero rank-one matrix. A fixed nonzero column of its adjugate gives a holomorphic kernel line $\ell_i(u)$ after shrinking. This line is invariant under the whole peripheral subgroup by commutation. Conversely, given a nearby slice representation with a chosen peripheral line, its meridian eigenvalue on that line is holomorphic and near $1$; its unique near-zero ratio logarithm defines $u_i$. The trace relation forces precisely the representation just constructed, and the rank-one kernel forces precisely its chosen line. Both constructions are holomorphic: the eigenvalue is read by applying the matrix to a local nonzero vector of the line. They are inverse maps on the augmented germ. Hence that germ is smooth of dimension $k$ with coordinates $u$.

The local lift of $\rho(u)(\lambda_i)$ commutes with $A_i(u)$: the commutator sign is locally constant and positive at the complete point. It acts on $\ell_i(u)$ by a nonzero holomorphic eigenvalue near its complete value; choose its sign to make this value $1$, and define $v_i$ as twice its near-zero logarithm. Choose a holomorphic change of frame sending $\ell_i(u)$ to $\mathbb Ce_1$, by adjoining a fixed complementary vector and normalizing the determinant locally. The resulting peripheral Möbius maps fix $\infty$ and act on its finite complement as $z\mapsto e^{u_i}z+a_i(u)$ and $z\mapsto e^{v_i}z+b_i(u)$. At $u=0$, their translations satisfy $a_i(0)\ne0$ and $b_i(0)/a_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Apply [F4] to get $v_i=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\tau_i$ holomorphic and $\tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Positivity of the imaginary part persists on a sufficiently small common neighborhood. For one cusp the holomorphic Taylor expansion gives $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. All constructions used representation matrices and cusp models; none used an ideal triangulation, or a positivity assumption about tetrahedra.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact oriented smooth $1$-manifold and give $\partial W$ the outward-normal-first orientation ([[def-induced-boundary-orientation]]). The boundary is a finite $0$-manifold, so its orientation at a boundary point $p$ is a sign $\varepsilon(p)\in\{+1,-1\}$; then $$\sum_{p\in\partial W}\varepsilon(p)=0.$$ On each closed-interval component the two boundary points carry opposite signs; circle components contribute nothing. With the standard orientation of $[a,b]$ the outward-normal-first convention gives $\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}$.

If $X$ is a nonempty contractible topological space, then for every $n\geq 0$
and every abelian group $G$,
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\cong H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\ast;G),$$
where $\ast$ denotes a one-point space.

Let $X$ be a compact oriented smooth $x$-manifold without boundary, let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed oriented embedded $z$-submanifold with $x+z=n$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). For a smooth $f:X\to M$ transverse to $Z$, the **oriented intersection number** is the finite sum

$$I(f,Z):=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(Z)}\varepsilon(p)\in\mathbb Z,$$

with the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]; the sum is finite by [[lem-compact-transverse-complementary-intersections-are-finite]]. For an arbitrary smooth $g:X\to M$, choose a transverse $f$ homotopic to $g$ ([[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], under Countable Choice; the homotopy is a smooth family in the sense of [[def-smooth-family-of-maps-and-evaluation-map]]) and set $I(g,Z):=I(f,Z)$; independence of the choice is [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], not assumed here. For compact oriented complementary-dimensional submanifolds $A,B\subseteq M$, where one is compact and the other closed, one sets $I(A,B):=I(i_A,B)$ with $i_A$ the inclusion, so the first factor is the submanifold $A$. If the source is not compact, or the target submanifold is not closed, the sum may fail to be finite or invariant; the safe extension by properness with compact trace is recorded in the remark on properness later on this page. Countable Choice is assumed for selecting transverse representatives and for the classification used to prove independence of that selection; the signs, the finite sum and the empty case (which contributes $0$) are choice-free.

For transverse maps $f:X^x\to M$, $g:Z^z\to M$ with compact oriented boundaryless sources and $x+z=\dim M$, define $I(f,g)$ as the sum of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]] over $X\times_MZ$. This set is closed in the compact product because $M$ is Hausdorff, and discrete by [[def-transverse-complementary-dimensional-intersection-set]], so the sum is finite. If $g$ is an inclusion this recovers $I(f,Z)$. Ambient compactness is unnecessary in either construction.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $f:X^x\to M$ and $g:Z^z\to M$ be smooth maps from oriented smooth manifolds, with $x+z=n$ and $f,g$ transverse in the sense of [[def-transverse-smooth-maps]]. Let $a\in X$, $b\in Z$ satisfy $f(a)=g(b)=y$. Then $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ and $T_yM$ have the same dimension, and transversality says that

$$(df_a,dg_b):T_aX\oplus T_bZ\longrightarrow T_yM,\qquad (v,w)\mapsto df_a(v)+dg_b(w),$$

is surjective, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-transverse-linear-subspaces]]); the sum is direct because the dimensions add up. The ordered direct sum $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ carries the product orientation with the first factor $T_aX$ and the second factor $T_bZ$ ([[def-product-orientation]]), and the three tangent spaces carry their manifold orientations ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

The **local oriented intersection sign** $\varepsilon(a,b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is $+1$ when this isomorphism carries the product orientation of $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ to the orientation of $T_yM$, and $-1$ otherwise; equivalently it is the orientation sign of the induced isomorphism of determinant lines ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

For transverse oriented embedded submanifolds $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ with $a+b=n$ one takes $f$ and $g$ to be the inclusion maps ([[def-transverse-embedded-submanifolds]]); the sign at $p\in A\cap B$ then compares $T_pA\oplus T_pB\to T_pM$ with $A$ first. The empty intersection is allowed and carries no signs. In dimension zero the sign compares the two orientation rays directly, and for $x=z=n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_X(a)\varepsilon_Z(b)\varepsilon_M(y)$, the product of the two source point signs and the ambient point sign. The factor order is part of the definition: with the two factors exchanged the signs are multiplied by $(-1)^{ab}$, exactly the graded-commutativity sign measured later on this page by the factor-interchange theorem. No compactness, closedness hypothesis or choice axiom is used in this local definition.

For an oriented manifold with boundary, orient $T_p\partial M$ by the **outward-normal-first** rule: an outward vector first, followed by a positive boundary determinant, is a positive determinant of $T_pM$.

For oriented vector spaces use the ordered determinant isomorphism $\det(V\oplus W)\cong\det V\otimes\det W$ and take the tensor product of the selected rays. Fibrewise this defines the product orientation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary. Let $f:D=\Delta^n\to N$ be continuous. On each codimension-one face $D_i$, prescribe a smooth simplex $g_i$ and a continuous homotopy $H_i:D_i\times[0,1]\to N$ from $f|_{D_i}$ to $g_i$. Require the homotopies to agree on every common face at every time. Then there are a smooth simplex $g:D\to N$ and a continuous homotopy $H$ from $f$ to $g$ whose restriction to each $D_i\times[0,1]$ is exactly $H_i$, with unchanged time parameter. If $f$ is already smooth and every $H_i$ is constant, one may take $g=f$ and $H$ constant. The boundaryless hypothesis cannot be removed: for the boundary target $[0,\infty)$ there are compatible smooth faces of a $3$-simplex, an explicit continuous filling, and compatible constant prescribed face homotopies, for which no filling with a $C^2$ scalar extension to an affine neighbourhood exists. In particular there is no smooth filling in the sense of [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. This counterexample requires no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: **Finite-chain model and independence.** Write each rational chain as a finite rational sum of parametrized singular simplices. Within each labeled intersection factor, take the finite family of its simplices and iterated faces, identifying equal parametrized faces so that cancellations remain exact. Never identify simplices across the two factors merely because their maps agree: their perturbations must be independent. Preserve the given smooth product end collars and truncate at a smaller positive collar level. The remaining target is the boundaryless interior $B^{4\circ}$. Apply [F7] inductively over the finite face family, extending compatible face homotopies and fixing prescribed smooth faces. This gives a smooth chain replacement respecting the boundary operator, with the same rational coefficients; the homotopy prisms give relative homology. Applying [F7] with any prescribed open neighborhood as target keeps the replacement there. For general position, keep the two labeled families separate and make each pair of their open face strata transverse to the diagonal in $B^{4\circ}\times B^{4\circ}$. Choose faces in increasing dimension, fixing their previously treated subfaces. In Euclidean coordinates a cutoff-supported translation of the unfixed map is submersive in its parameter where the cutoff is positive; near the fixed part the pair is already transverse. The relative and parametric clauses of [F6] therefore give the required perturbation. Extend a chosen face homotopy consistently to all incident simplices in that factor, but not to the other factor. Finitely many face-pair conditions can be imposed simultaneously. Subdivision into finitely many compact coordinate pieces and sufficiently small parameters keep all changes inside prescribed open neighborhoods and away from the end collars. For complementary two-chains the diagonal preimages are finite signed sets; lower-dimensional face pairs are empty. Define the intersection by summing these signs with the rational product coefficients. This agrees with the given transverse interior count. Now fix $Q$ and two choices $P,P'$ bounding $\alpha$, using facewise-transverse representatives with their identical end collars. Their difference $C=P-P'$ is a smooth rational two-cycle compactly supported in $B^{4\circ}$. By [F3], choose a finite continuous rational three-chain $Z$ there with $\partial Z=C$. Smooth $Z$ relative to its prescribed boundary $C$ by [F7], identifying faces within the $Z$ family only. Keeping $Q$ independent and fixed, perturb the remaining $Z$ faces relative to $C$, whose intersections with $Q$ are already transverse. Each simplex-pair diagonal preimage is a compact oriented one-manifold; codimension-one faces give its endpoints, while codimension-two faces have negative expected dimension. The local half-space model and [F4] give the boundary signs. Sum with the rational product coefficients: internal face endpoints cancel because the same face map occurs with opposite boundary coefficients. What remains is $(\partial Z)\cdot Q=C\cdot Q$, together with the term from $Z$ and $\partial Q$. That latter term is empty since $Z$ is compactly supported in the interior and $\partial Q=\beta\subset S^3$. By [F2] the total signed boundary count is zero, so $P\cdot Q=P'\cdot Q$. Apply the same finite construction to homotopy prisms to obtain independence of the replacements. Interchanging the two two-dimensional factors introduces no sign and proves independence of the second chain. All operations are rational-linear, giving the same assertions for finite rational combinations. No embedded-manifold realization of $Z$ is used.

By [F5], choose an oriented Seifert surface $S_\beta\subset S^3$ for each knot component of $\beta$, and similarly choose a cap for each component of $\alpha$. It suffices by bilinearity to consider one knot component of each. Choose a collar depth $0<\epsilon$ in $B^4$. Make $Q$ a graph of $S_\beta$ in the boundary collar with depth zero on $\beta$ and strictly between $0$ and $\epsilon/2$ on its interior. To give this graph a literal product end collar, choose $0<\delta<\epsilon/2$, attach $\beta\times[0,\delta]$, and join its inner edge to the graph inside a tubular neighborhood of $\beta$ disjoint from $\alpha$, leaving the graph unchanged outside that neighborhood; choose the join below depth $\epsilon/2$. This adds no intersections with $P$ and changes none of the signs computed below. Make $P$ consist of the product collar $\alpha\times[0,\epsilon]$ followed by a cap at depth $\epsilon$. Then $P$ and $Q$ intersect exactly above $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. At each such point, the oriented tangent basis of the collar of $P$ is $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a)$, where $a$ is the positive tangent to $\alpha$ and $n_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward normal of $B^4$; the tangent basis of $Q$ is a positive basis $(s_1,s_2)$ of $S_\beta$, up to radial components which do not change the determinant. By [F4], $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive exactly when $(a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive in the boundary orientation. Thus the $4$-dimensional intersection sign is exactly the $3$-dimensional sign of $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. Hence $P\cdot Q=\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ by [F1].

Step 1.1 shows the intersection number is independent of admissible collared bounding chains, and step 1.2 computes it for one convenient choice. Hence the equality holds for all such $P,Q$ when the boundaries are knots. Expanding finite rational cycles into their oriented knot components and using bilinearity of both signed intersection and linking proves the stated equality.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

derivations.claim: Double $B^4$ across $S^3$ to $S^4$ and double $D$ across its product boundary collar to a locally flat sphere $N\cong S^2$. A smooth tubular neighborhood of the smooth knot $K$ in $S^3$, crossed with the doubled collar coordinate, gives an actual rank-two normal bundle germ over a closed seam annulus $C=K\times[-a,a]\subset N$. Away from the seam the pair is locally flat by hypothesis; at the seam its chart is the product pair $(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\{0\})$. The local complement is homotopy equivalent to $S^1$, so its fundamental group is infinite cyclic and its local $\pi_2$ vanishes. Also $S^4$ is a boundaryless ANR homology $4$-manifold, $N\times\mathbb R\cong S^2\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold, and $S^4\setminus N$ is a manifold. Apply [F2] relative to $C$ to obtain a normal disk bundle over $N$ that agrees with the displayed germ on a smaller seam annulus. Restrict it to one copy of $D$. Agreement near the seam and compactness of the remaining disk allow its radius to be shrunk so that the whole tube lies in the original $B^4$ and is product-shaped on a boundary collar.

The oriented normal plane bundle over the disk is trivial. Choose a nowhere-zero section, and make its restriction to the seam smooth by a homotopy in the prescribed smooth tube, extending that homotopy across a smaller collar of $D$. Its parallel disk $D'$ is disjoint from $D$, and its boundary $K'$ is a smooth push-off of $K$. Represent the two disk parametrizations by finite continuous singular chains. Their disjoint compact supports have disjoint relatively open neighborhoods in the standard smooth ball. The relative finite-chain construction in [F4] replaces them by smooth rational chains within those respective neighborhoods, fixing their already smooth knot boundaries and standard end collars; hence their intersection count is zero, without smoothing either TOP disk embedding. By [F4], $\operatorname{lk}(K',K)=D'\cdot D=0$. The push-off determined by the Seifert surface $F$ also has linking number zero, since it is disjoint from $F$, by [F5]. In the smooth normal tube, the class of a framed push-off differs from the zero longitude by its winding number times the positive meridian. Thus the degree of the transition map between these two oriented framings is their linking-number difference, namely zero. This degree-zero map $K\to SO(2)$ extends over $D$; adjust the section by that extension. The resulting framed tube agrees with the zero-longitude marking from $F$. Remove its interior and round the product corners to obtain the compact topological disk exterior $X$. The collared decomposition $B^4=X\cup(D^2\times D^2)$ has overlap retracting to $D^2\times S^1$. Mayer–Vietoris [F6] gives $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the positive normal meridian $\mu$. The boundary of $X$ is the zero surgery $M(K)=E_K\cup_{T^2}(D^2\times S^1)$, with disk slope the zero longitude and circle coordinate the positive meridian; by [F8], its $H_1$ is also generated by $\mu$, and its inclusion into $X$ sends this generator to $\mu$.

Truncate $F$ at the knot tube and cap its boundary by $D^2\times\{1\}$ in the inner solid torus. This gives a closed connected surface $\Sigma_0\subset M(K)$. On a product neighborhood of the $F$ portion, let $u$ be the signed normal coordinate in the positive Seifert direction and put $f_0=\exp(2\pi i u)$. On the inner solid torus put $f_0(x,z)=z$. The zero-longitude marking makes these definitions agree in the peripheral product collar. Cut the remaining knot exterior along $F$. The two copies of $F$ receive real phases $\epsilon$ and $1-\epsilon$; on the remaining peripheral annulus use the lifted angular coordinate between these values. Extend this real phase over the compact cut exterior by finitely many collar cutoffs and a partition of unity, keeping every value in $(0,1)$ away from the prescribed collars and equal to $1/2$ off them. Exponentiating gives a continuous boundary map $f_0:M(K)\to S^1$ whose fiber over $1$ is exactly $\Sigma_0$, with a product neighborhood and positive coorientation on $F$. Its induced homomorphism sends the positive meridian to $1$, as required by the angular coordinate $z$.

The exterior $X$ is connected: the overlap $D^2\times S^1$ and the tube are connected, and the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the decomposition of connected $B^4$ forces $H_0(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. By [F7], $X$ has a connected CW model. The homomorphism $\pi_1(X)\to\mathbb Z$ obtained by abelianization and sending $\mu\mapsto1$ is realized by a continuous map $g:X\to S^1$. The maps $g|_{M(K)}$ and $f_0$ induce the same homomorphism because $H_1(M(K))\to H_1(X)$ sends the positive meridian generator to $\mu$, by steps 2.1 and [F8]. Choose a boundary basepoint and multiply $g$ by a constant in $S^1$ if needed so its value there equals $f_0$; this leaves the induced homomorphism unchanged. Hatcher's classification in [F7] then makes the restrictions based homotopic. Use the collar [F6] and its homotopy extension property to replace $g$ by a continuous map $f:X\to S^1$ equal to $f_0$ on a whole smaller boundary collar. This step uses only a continuous map; it invokes no smooth structure or regular-value theorem on $X$.

Let $Y=X\times S^1$, let $Z=X\times\{1\}$ with its specified trivial circle-normal line microbundle, and let $M=\{(x,f(x)):x\in X\}$ be the graph. It is a proper locally flat submanifold, since the homeomorphism $(x,z)\mapsto(x,zf(x)^{-1})$ takes it to $Z$. On a closed collar of $\partial X$, $f=f_0$ and $1$ is a product-transverse value, so $M$ is microbundle-transverse to $Z$ there. Choose nested closed collars $C_0\subset\operatorname{Int}C$ of the whole boundary in $Y$, with $M$ transverse near $C$. Apply [F3] with $D=Y$ and with support in a neighborhood of $(Y\setminus C)\cap M\cap Z$ disjoint from $C_0$. The resulting proper submanifold $M'$ is transverse to $Z$ and unchanged on $C_0$. Parametrize it by its isotopy image $j:X\to M'$ and put $f'=\operatorname{pr}_{S^1}\circ j$. Then $R_0=(f')^{-1}(1)$ is a compact locally flat $3$-manifold, its boundary is exactly $\Sigma_0$, and its whole boundary product and coorientation are those prescribed by $f_0$. Quinn's conclusion identifies its normal microbundle in $M'$ with the restriction of the trivial normal line of $Z$; pulling back by $j$ gives an actual two-sided product neighborhood of $R_0$ in $X$, agreeing with the prescribed product on $C_0$. Discard any closed components of $R_0$; since $\Sigma_0$ is connected, exactly one component has boundary.

The fiber $\Sigma_0$ contains the cap disk $D^2\times\{1\}$ in the inner solid torus. Attach the radial sector $D^2\times[0,r]$ at the fixed angular value $z=1$ down to the zero section $D$ of the tube. Its top disk matches the cap disk, and its side annulus matches the peripheral product collar because the tube frame is the zero framing from step 2.1. In these product coordinates the sector's normal is the angular coordinate; it agrees with the circle-normal coorientation of $R_0$, and on $F$ that coorientation is the positive Seifert direction from step 3.1. Glue the product neighborhoods along their common products and flatten the explicit quadrant corners. To perform the collar push in the Statement, use the product chart near $F$ and choose a small smooth function $h:F\to[0,\epsilon/4)$ that vanishes on $K$, is positive on $\operatorname{int}F$, and has the boundary profile of the matched seam collar. Choose $\rho:[0,\epsilon)\to[0,1]$ with $\rho(0)=1$, $\rho=0$ for $s\ge\epsilon/2$, and $\|h\|_\infty\|\rho'\|_\infty<1/2$. On the adjacent collar product define $(x,s,u)\mapsto(x,s+h(x)\rho(s),u)$. For each $x$, the collar coordinate has derivative $1+h(x)\rho'(s)>1/2$; the map fixes the seam $K$ and is the identity at the inner edge, so it embeds the product neighborhood while preserving the normal coordinate and coorientation. Choose the disk sector collar to agree with this same seam product. The result is a compact connected oriented locally flat $3$-manifold $R\subset B^4$ with boundary the collar-adjusted $F\cup_KD$. Its two-sided product neighborhood places the positive push-off of $F$ on the complementary side of $R$. Thus all conclusions hold for a locally flat disk, including the smooth case.

current_manifest_record.title: Integral half-solutions, Strebel classes, and L²-signatures
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

current_manifest_record.title: The boundary kernel of a rational homology ball is a linking metabolizer
current_manifest_record.statement: Assume AC. Let $W$ be a compact connected smooth oriented $4$-manifold with rational homology of a point and connected boundary $Y$. Then $Y$ is a rational homology sphere, and $P=\ker(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W;\mathbb Z))$ is a metabolizer for the torsion linking form $\lambda_Y$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

Assume AC. If $Y$ is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, then the bounding-chain torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ is symmetric and nonsingular: its adjoint $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.

Let $Y$ be a closed oriented $3$-manifold and let $x,y\in\operatorname{Tor}H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For choices of an integer $n>0$ and an integral $2$-chain $C$ with $\partial C=nx$, the bounding-chain expression is $(C\cdot y)/n\bmod\mathbb Z\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, where $C$ and $y$ are placed transversely and intersection signs use the orientation of $Y$. This expression is the torsion linking pairing when its independence of the choices is established.

A finite nonsingular linking form is a pair $(A,\lambda)$, where $A$ is a finite abelian group and $\lambda:A\times A\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is symmetric and induces an isomorphism $A\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. For $P\le A$, put $P^\perp=\{a\in A:\lambda(a,p)=0\text{ for every }p\in P\}$. A metabolizer is a subgroup $P$ with $P=P^\perp$; equivalently, $\lambda$ vanishes on $P\times P$ and $|P|^2=|A|$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;R)$, $c\in C_n(X;R)$, $p,n\ge0$, over a commutative unital ring,
$$\partial(\varphi\cap c)=(-1)^p\bigl(\varphi\cap\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap c\bigr).$$
Consequently cap induces an $R$-bilinear map
$$H^p(X;R)\otimes_R H_n(X;R)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;R).$$
Negative chain groups are zero, and no AC is assumed.

Let
$$0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in an abelian category. Then
there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(A)\to H^n(B)\to H^n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial^n}H^{n+1}(A)\to H^{n+1}(B)\to H^{n+1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

derivations.claim: The rational homology-pair sequence and [F1], with $H_i(W;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $i>0$, give $H_1(Y;\mathbb Q)=H_2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$; connectedness gives $H_0(Y;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, and orientation gives $H_3(Y;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. Thus $Y$ is a rational homology sphere. By [F4] and [A1], both $W$ and its smooth boundary $Y$ have finite CW type, so their integral homology groups are finitely generated. The groups $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, $H_1(W;\mathbb Z)$ and $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ have vanishing rationalizations and are therefore finite.

Put $A=H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, $B=H_1(W;\mathbb Z)$, and $C=H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Since $A$ is finite by step 1.1, the universal coefficient sequence [F3] gives $H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$; [F7] then gives $H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$. Also $H_3(W;\mathbb Z)=0$: [F1] identifies $H_4(W,Y)$ with $H^0(W)=\mathbb Z$, and its fundamental-class boundary maps to the generator of $H_3(Y)=\mathbb Z$; since $H_3(W,Y)\cong H^1(W)=0$, exactness forces $H_3(W)=0$.

By [F3], $H^2(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(B,\mathbb Z)$ and $H^3(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(C,\mathbb Z)$, because $B,C$ are finite and $H_3(W)=0$. Their orders are $|B|$ and $|C|$. Under [F1], these are the orders of $H_2(W,Y)$ and $H_1(W,Y)$, respectively. The pair sequence [F2] shows that $P=\ker(A\to B)$ is the cokernel of the injective map $H_2(W)\to H_2(W,Y)$, while $B\to H_1(W,Y)$ is onto because the next map $H_0(Y)\to H_0(W)$ is an isomorphism. Hence $|P|=|B|/|C|$ and $|A/P|=|B|/|C|$, so $|A|=|P|^2$.

To prove isotropy, [F2] and the naturality in [F7] identify $P$ under Poincaré duality with the image of $H^2(W;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For $x,y\in P$, choose lifts $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Since $W$ is a rational homology ball, the coefficient Bockstein $H^1(W;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is onto by [F8]: the adjacent groups $H^1(W;\mathbb Q)$ and $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$ vanish. Choose $\gamma\in H^1(W;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with Bockstein $\widetilde y$. The Bockstein–duality formula in [F5] evaluates $\lambda_Y(y,x)$ as the restriction of $\gamma\smile\widetilde x$ on $[Y]$; symmetry of $\lambda_Y$ then gives the same value for $\lambda_Y(x,y)$. This class extends over $W$, and the inclusion sends $[Y]$ to zero in $H_3(W)$ because $Y=\partial W$. Thus $\lambda_Y(x,y)=0$.
The isotropy from step 3.2 gives $P\subseteq P^\perp$. Nonsingularity [F5] implies $|P^\perp|=|A|/|P|=|P|$ by step 3.1. Therefore $P=P^\perp$, so $P$ is a metabolizer by [F6].

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume full AC. The unknot has the empty Seifert matrix, Alexander polynomial $1$, and a smooth slice disk. The right-handed trefoil has positive-push matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and Alexander polynomial $t^2-t+1$, so the Alexander-one theorem gives no conclusion for it and does not prove it nonslice. Let $Wh^+(T)$ denote the satellite of the right-handed trefoil $T$ by the positive-clasped, untwisted Whitehead pattern, embedded using the preferred longitude. This knot has Alexander polynomial $1$; by topologically slice we mean that it bounds a locally flat embedded disk in $B^4$. The established theorem gives that topological conclusion, not a smooth slice disk.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose two boundary components, with their induced orientations, have linking number $+1$. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Assume full AC. If a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ has Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, then there is a locally flat proper embedding $D^2\hookrightarrow B^4$ whose boundary is $K$. Here **topologically slice** means bounding such a locally flat proper disk; the conclusion asserts no smooth slice disk.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

derivations.claim: For the unknot, the Seifert surface is a disk, so $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)=0$ and the empty determinant is $1$; the standard flat disk in $B^4$ proves sliceness. For the trefoil, [F1] and [F2] give $\det(V-tV^T)=t^2-t+1$, which is not a Laurent unit.

Construct the actual surface inside the preferred-longitude tube of $T$ from [F3]. Take a narrow annulus $A$ about its core with the zero product framing. In a small ball meeting $A$ in one square $Q$, plumb $A$ to a positive Hopf annulus $H$: identify their squares so the two annular core arcs are the two crossing coordinate axes in $Q$, and place the parts outside the square on opposite sides. Smooth the four square corners. Outside that ball the boundary is the two oppositely oriented zero-framed parallels of $T$; inside the ball the positive Hopf band joins them by its positive clasp. This is precisely the positive-clasped untwisted Whitehead pattern in the specified tube. The untwisted condition is the zero framing of $A$, and the construction uses the preferred longitude rather than an arbitrary longitude. It is also the $k=0$ surface of the cited Figure 2; that figure identifies the convention but is not a substitute for the following matrix calculation.

Let $a$ be the annulus core and $b$ the Hopf core, with orientations chosen so their sole square intersection has $a\cdot_F b=1$. The plumbed surface is connected and oriented. Its Euler characteristic is $0+0-1=-1$, and tracing the alternating four attaching edges gives one boundary component. The two annuli retract to their two core loops with the square intersection identified, so $(a,b)$ is an integral handle basis and the surface has genus one. Choose the plumbing side in which the positive push of the $a$-arc is above the square. The unknotted Hopf core $b$ has a spanning disk in the local ball lying below the square except for its boundary arc; use the lower side for the remainder of $H$. Thus this disk misses $a^+$, including the part of $a^+$ outside the ball. This is a local disk for $b$, and does not assert that the companion $a=T$ bounds a disk.

The positive push of $a$ is a small parallel with the product annulus framing; its linking with $a$ is zero because that product longitude is the preferred longitude. Equivalently move the push to the annular side direction through nonzero normal directions, keeping it disjoint from $a$. The local square does not add a twist to this annular framing. Hence $V_{11}=0$. The two boundary components of the positive Hopf annulus, with induced orientations, link $+1$. Equally oriented core parallels therefore link $-1$, since one induced boundary orientation is reversed. Moving one core parallel to the positive normal push preserves this linking, so $V_{22}=-1$. The local spanning disk from step 2.1 and symmetry of linking give $V_{12}=\operatorname{lk}(a^+,b)=0$. Finally [F5] gives $V_{21}=-1$. Thus the ACTUAL Whitehead double of $T$, not just the pattern applied to the unknot, has matrix $V_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$.

Direct calculation gives $\det(V_0-tV_0^T)=t$. This is a Laurent unit, with inverse $t^{-1}$, so [F2] gives $\Delta_{Wh^+(T)}\doteq1$. Applying [F4] proves the stated locally flat proper slice disk in the standard $B^4$. The argument establishes the announced topological conclusion; it contains no smooth slice-disk construction and no inference that the trefoil is nonslice from its nonunit Alexander polynomial. Every claim in the example follows without a general satellite determinant theorem.
