**Section11: Dual model and the singular collar parameterization.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data.

Fix a FINITE model tower, before its extra plumbings are mapped into the ambient manifold. The entire disk-like capped model has regular neighborhood D^2 times D^2. Deleting the caps instead leaves the complement of disjoint dual two-handles H_m=(D^2 times D^2,D^2 times S^1). The latter convention for their attaching solid torus is the dual one; it is not the original attaching S^1 times D^2. This statement is checked at one elementary surface move: replace the disk by its self-tube along a short arc. Its complement acquires a one-handle, and the two caps supply its cancelling dual two-handle pair. Slice the tube by a normal three-disk. The two cap dual disks run on opposite sides of that slice; outside the tube they are two parallel strips, while inside it their strips pass once on opposite normal sides. Gluing the slice back gives the two linked solid tori in the original D^2 times S^1. Replacing one cap by another capped surface repeats exactly this operation INSIDE its own dual handle. Multiple handles on a surface give disjoint stacks of this pair. Finger moves on a cap, and its added Whitney/accessory disks, give further dual handles contained in those already present. Thus successive finite stories give nested finite families H_(n,m), and the neighborhood of their body is
(D^2 times D^2) minus union_m int H_(n,m).
The elementary pair of linked tori just described is the Bing pair in this argument; its specified strips, rather than a link name alone, determine the relevant pattern.

Here is the finite shortening operation on that pattern. Cut the longitude of the parent solid torus at a small box. After the first doubling each core has a long forward-and-return pair of strands, monotone in the longitude coordinate, with the remaining clasp confined to the cut box. A 'monotone loop of length r' means one strand runs monotonically through an interval of length r and the other returns through that same interval; the rest has longitude diameter<a. If r>a, place a doubling clasp a short distance a along the forward strand and its mate a short distance a from the far turn on the return strand. On either child the two middle opposite parallel runs bound an empty ribbon: they are the two sides of the same normal strip, with its clasp endpoints outside that ribbon. Cancel these two runs by pushing across this ribbon. The remaining child has one forward-and-return pair of longitude length at most r−a; its two short joining pieces and clasp have longitude diameter<a. Perform the cancellation for the two children in different normal levels of the parent strip. Their supports are disjoint, and the old single linked passage between the children stays in their short clasp boxes. This is an isotopy of the doubled pair inside the parent torus: the moving ribbon is in its product normal disk, its endpoints are fixed on the two clasp boxes, and at each intermediate time the strands remain in their prescribed separate normal levels. It does not cut a linked component or pass it through the other one.

Iterate the shortening. The initial forward-and-return length is less than the circumference of the longitude circle, say2pi. After more than2pi/a steps every child core has longitude diameter<a. Compress the transverse disk widths as well, with an isotopy in the solid-torus product coordinates. Hence sufficiently many grope stages put every boundary solid torus of the dual handles in a ball of arbitrarily small prescribed diameter about a point of the longitude core. Further Whitney/accessory handles lie inside the preceding dual handles, so also satisfy that bound. All moves are in the finite MODEL, with its actual normal strips; no assertion is made that an arbitrary linked family can be made small componentwise without that iterated pattern.

Apply this to the convergent tower of Section8. At the n-th step use replication and squeezing to add two stories: choose the grope height of the first high enough for the preceding dual-boundary shortening to the next required model tolerance, and put the ambient next-story pieces in balls of diameter<2^−n. For each dual handle H_(n,m):D^2 times D^2→D^2 times D^2, choose its collar on the attaching D^2 times S^1. The precise two model bounds are diam H_(n,m)(D^2 times S^1)<2^−n and diam H_(n,m)(D^2 times ((1/2+2^−n)D^2))<2^−n. The former follows from the boundary shortening; the latter is arranged by compressing the radial disk factor toward the center, leaving the attaching collar fixed. Arrange the new collars to agree with the old collar on the outer interval [2^−n,1]; this is accomplished by product interpolation inside the old dual handle. The changes at step n are supported over the part of the old collar below height2^−n. All attaching parts and their ambient images have the same shrinking bounds.

Distinct branches are disjoint at a finite level; their limit points cannot coincide. A branch point and a finite-stage point also separate at a finite level. This proves injectivity. The complement of the body in the finite dual model is the union of the interiors of the H_(n,m). q:D^2 times D^2 → C'

whose nontrivial fibers are precisely those wild-collar intervals. A continuous disk filling with its supplied smooth boundary collar first admits a smooth approximation. To keep the collar fixed, use the Euclidean embedding and smooth neighborhood retraction constructed in the actual Whitney-approximation proof: interpolate in the ambient Euclidean coordinates between the old map and its smooth approximation with a cutoff which is zero on a smaller boundary collar and one outside the region where the old map is already smooth, then apply that retraction. Its pointwise approximation bound keeps the whole interpolation inside the retraction neighborhood. This gives a smooth filling and homotopy fixed on the smaller collar. In a target with boundary, first push any unwanted interior boundary contacts into the target collar's positive side, fixed on the prescribed source collar; double the target only for the approximation, and choose its error smaller than half the positive target-boundary distance on the remaining interior. Thus the final filling stays in the intended manifold with its prescribed proper collar.

For genericity, cover the remaining compact disk interior by finitely many coordinate patches and add small affine coordinate polynomials times cutoffs. Their parameters independently vary values and first derivatives on smaller patches. The evaluation into first-jet coordinates is therefore submersive, for parameters in a sufficiently small common ball. The rank-one derivative stratum has codimension(2−1)(4−1)=3 and the rank-zero stratum codimension8, both exceeding the domain dimension2. Parametric transversality consequently makes the perturbed map an immersion. Compactness gives a common local-injectivity scale for this immersion and for sufficiently small subsequent C1 perturbations. Off that scale the pair configurations form a compact set. At two distinct points choose disjoint bump patches, so the two-value evaluation is submersive. Transversality to the diagonal in V times V makes its double locus zero-dimensional and compact, hence finite. At three distinct points use three disjoint bumps; the three-value diagonal has codimension8>6, so triple points are absent. Interior-point/boundary-point coincidences likewise have expected dimension2+1−4<0 and are removed while the boundary collar is fixed. The finite products of parameter balls have dense sets of good parameters by the actual parametric-transversality theorem. No assertion that ordinary pointwise transversality alone proves a jet statement is being used: the independent affine-jet parameters supply the required submersion explicitly.

These finite operations also apply to Whitney and accessory fillings with their fixed local corner models: perform the perturbations off those closed collars and keep their prescribed normal directions. The same finite multi-evaluation argument gives pairwise transversality of the different new disks and the old sheets.

The given maps and collars here are smooth in the supplied neighborhood. The TOP-generic interpretation of the broader disk-data Definition requires a later relative smoothing bridge and is not inferred from ambient smoothness. First record the finite geometric Casson move. Let two immersed surfaces F,G have an opposite-sign pair p,q with a framed Whitney disk W. For every interior point of G intersection W choose an arc in W from its preimage to the interior of the G Whitney boundary arc. Choose these arcs away from the finite preimages of F intersection W and from the double-point preimages of W, and use separate parallel widths where they share an endpoint region. Push the G sheet along that arc and past the G boundary arc. This removes the selected G intersection W and introduces only G self-intersections near that boundary arc. It misses F, since the interior of the G Whitney arc misses F and all arcs avoided the F preimages. After the finite pushes, the interior of W misses G. Perform the immersed Whitney move on F across W. It removes p,q; its only new intersections are F self-intersections coming from W self-points or F intersection W. No F–G points remain from the operation. It is a regular homotopy supported in a neighborhood of W, so all algebraic intersection and self-intersection numbers and boundary framings are preserved. For a finite family, exclude the other prescribed body sheets from the support by first clearing W using their geometric duals whenever that is stipulated below. This is the actual finite separation move, not a smooth embedded-Whitney-disk assertion.

Apply it to the input disks f_i and framed spheres g_i. The excess f_i–g_j points can be paired by framed immersed Whitney disks because their group-ring coefficients cancel. The required boundary circle is null: equal group labels, with the sheet choices matched, are exactly the equality making that Whitney loop trivial. A relative smooth generic filling supplies the disk; boundary twisting corrects its Whitney framing. Use the preceding move on the two collections, so it creates only self-intersections within either collection and removes all excess mutual points. This makes g_i geometrically dual to f_i. Since the original f_i already have zero mutual lambda and mu, no spherical tubing which changes their homotopy classes is required. They have only undergone regular homotopies.

The inclusion M'=M minus an open framed plumbing neighborhood of the f_i into M induces a pi1 isomorphism. Surjectivity follows by moving loops off a finite two-dimensional image. For injectivity, put a nullhomotopy in general position with respect to that image; after deleting small disks at its finitely many intersections, its extra boundary circles are meridians of the f_i sheets. Each meridian is null in the complement using the punctured immersed geometric dual g_i. This fills all punctures and gives the nullhomotopy in M'. The same argument handles both sheets at a double point. Hence M' has the given good fundamental group.

Choose framed Whitney disks D_j for all intersections within and among the f_i, and tube their interiors over separate parallels of g_i to remove their intersections with every f_i. Thus D_j are immersed proper disks in M'. At one paired double point take its Clifford torus T_j in the local product normal chart. Its two meridional caps each intersect exactly one f sheet; tube each cap at that point to a punctured parallel g_i. This gives capped tori T_j^c entirely in M'. Their bodies lie arbitrarily close to the corresponding component of the boundary of the plumbing neighborhood, and are geometrically dual to D_j. Their caps have zero mutual lambda and mu: the local meridional interiors are disjoint, their attaching collars meet only in their prescribed boundary crossing, and the remaining points are exactly those among the framed g_i parallels, with the same cancelling group labels. The input zero Wall numbers therefore give zero coefficients before augmentation. Contract separate parallel capped tori to get geometric dual spheres for D_j, push D_j off these contractions, and tube intersections of the ORIGINAL torus caps with D_j into those parallel spheres. The resulting T_j^c are genuinely dual capped surfaces, meaning their caps also miss D_j. This cleanup preserves the cap Wall hypotheses: the contraction sphere is built from two oppositely oriented parallels of each cap and the torus body, so its intersection with any old cap is a signed sum of the old cap–cap coefficients, hence zero; its self-number is a sum of the same zero self/cross coefficients. The sesquilinear and quadratic sphere-sum formulas therefore leave all cap lambda/mu numbers zero when a cap is tubed to those spheres. The bodies stay in their chosen boundary collar.

Here is the collar reservation which prevents the old gap. Parameterize the actual boundary collar by t in [0,1], with boundary t=0, and put the initial T_j bodies in5/6<t<1. Only attaching collars of D_j and of the torus caps enter this collar otherwise. Tube all D_j mutual/self-points over full parallels of T_j^c in this outermost slab. The resulting bottom surfaces D'_j are embedded, mutually disjoint, and have the same framed boundaries; their caps C' are the two appropriate torus-cap parallels at every tube. If C denotes the torus caps, lambda(C,C')=mu(C)=0 by the preceding coefficient calculation and parallel-copy identities. Take a fresh family of capped-torus parallels with bodies in4/6<t<5/6 and contract it, pushing nothing off, to obtain spheres S_j geometrically dual to D'_j.

Pair the C–C' points by framed immersed Whitney disks. Their boundaries lie above t=4/6, and their nullhomotopies can be chosen there: deleting t<4/6 from a boundary collar is a homotopy equivalence with an explicit collar-push inverse. Tube these disks over S_j to make their interiors disjoint from all D'_j. The tube paths and spheres stay above the fresh lower collar slabs. Apply the geometric Casson move to C and C'. Its supports miss D'_j and all unused torus BODIES below4/6. Thus the new caps miss each other as the two collections, while arbitrary self/intersections within each cap collection are still allowed and remain algebraically cancelling.

Push the C' self/mutual points down D'_j and tube full capped-torus parallels with bodies in3/6<t<4/6. This adds the second surface stages, producing height-two capped gropes D''_j. Their body is embedded by the same scorecard as Section3. Separate their new caps C'' from C exactly as before, now using contracted parallels in2/6<t<3/6 and Whitney nullhomotopies outside t<2/6. All remaining torus bodies may now be taken in0<t<2/6. They and their caps are geometrically dual to the entire height-two gropes, including their caps. Raise the latter to any required finite height, keeping their first two stages, and successively contract one extra top stage to make their caps pairwise disjoint, with their self-points in canonical cancelling pairs. These neighborhood operations miss the dual capped surfaces because those were made disjoint from the whole starting grope except at the bottom transverse point.

Now the actual good-group Definition applies in its exact place. Choose grope height n+2.5. Each disjoint top height-1.5 component is a supplied disk-like framed grope. Apply goodness to its homomorphism into pi1(M') to obtain the framed null disk in that canonical model. Section14 smooths it within a neighborhood with trivial group image while retaining its attaching frame; thus it supplies the smooth immersed disk required here, with double-point loops null in M'. Distinct replacement disks lie in disjoint component neighborhoods. The retained grope has height n+1. Contract one top stage symmetrically: the new cap double loops are parallel copies or differences of the null loops, hence null; the cap self-points come in algebraically cancelling finger pairs. The first n stages have been kept EXACTLY. Taking n≥4 is sufficient for Sections7–12.

Fill those double-point loops by framed immersed accessory disks. Their boundaries miss t<2/6, so their fillings may be pushed off that collar. Hence they miss the torus BODIES reserved there, although they may intersect its caps and the grope arbitrarily. Contract fresh dual capped surfaces with bodies in1/6<t<2/6 to get spheres S''_j. Correct the accessory framings, push their body intersections down, and tube over S''_j to clear the whole grope body. The resulting accessories are the proper tower top caps. Finally take the LAST capped-torus parallels with bodies in0<t<1/6 and contract them, pushing every tower-cap sheet off the contraction. Their bodies already miss the accessories by the collar choice. The resulting spheres R_j therefore miss the ENTIRE tower except for their prescribed bottom transverse point. This final contraction/push-off is the step which the uncontrolled use of the original spheres in Section6 could not provide.

The R_j are nullhomotopic in the ORIGINAL M. Indeed symmetric contraction of a fixed capped surface is independent up to homotopy of its caps: it is regularly homotopic to surgery on only the first cap of each pair; switch the unused second caps; it is also homotopic to surgery on only the second caps; then switch the first caps. Thus in M replace the caps built from g_i by the original small meridional caps. The contracted Clifford torus is now contained in the original double-point four-ball, and is null there. This proves [R_j]=0 in pi2(M), despite its being a useful nonzero class in pi2(M').

Remove intersections of the original g_i with the towers by pushing them down the tower to the bottom and tubing over R_j. They still meet the f_i only at their one original dual point, since all these changes lie in M'. They now miss the entire tower. The changes of g_i are homotopies and additions of whiskered R_j, which are null in M, so preserve their original homotopy classes. Perform Sections7–12 inside neighborhoods of the towers disjoint from these g_i, with their one dual intersection moved into the protected attaching collar. The resulting embedded framed Whitney disks are disjoint from every g_i. Their Whitney moves on the f_i give disjoint properly locally flat embedded disks, regularly homotopic rel boundary/framing to the original f_i, and with the g_i still geometrically dual. They also provide the product normal charts required in the final surface-compression application: on the untouched pieces keep the old smooth disk frames; on each Whitney replacement use the pulled-back standard two-handle frame, glued by the Whitney framing along its two boundary arcs. This is a finite construction of a normal disk bundle over the resulting disk, trivialized by those compatible frames. Compactness permits sufficiently small widths so different patches overlap only by their prescribed bundle transitions and the resulting total-space map is injective. Thus the constructed disks have their OWN product tubes, without using the later general TOP normal-bundle theorem. Thus the original disk theorem's homotopy conclusion is supplied by WHITNEY MOVES, rather than assumed from an arbitrary standard-core choice.
**Section14: Smoothing a framed null disk inside a canonical grope neighborhood.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit.

This operation addresses the category of the disk obtained from GOODNESS, whose boundary is the canonical smooth attaching region of the framed model grope. It does not smooth an arbitrary original boundary knot or a TOP-generic disk in an unrelated ambient manifold. Its input is a generic immersed disk with the supplied extending framing/product germs which make its boundary the model attaching region. If 'framed boundary' were read as an arbitrary external integer without an extending framed immersion, the following parity argument would not apply; that is not the framed-disk convention used here.

Let Q be the smooth framed model neighborhood, phi:pi1(Q)→Gamma, and d:D^2→Q the supplied generic framed disk with phi-null double-point loops. Its compact image A is homeomorphic to a finite polyhedron P: subdivide the parameter disk with the finitely many paired double-point preimages as vertices and with their stars disjoint, identify those vertex pairs, and subdivide once more. The resulting finite quotient complex maps continuously bijectively onto A and hence homeomorphically, by compactness and the Hausdorff target. Its fundamental group is generated by the finitely many double-point loops, since the disk before identifying the pairs is simply connected. Thus phi kills the entire image of pi1(A).

Here is an explicit neighborhood-retraction argument, avoiding a general normal-bundle theorem. Realize P as a finite subcomplex of a standard simplex, subdivide barycentrically, and note that its subdivision is FULL: a simplex whose chain of face-vertices all belong to P belongs to P. On the open star of P in that subdivided simplex, delete the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside P and normalize the remaining positive sum. Fullness makes this a continuous retraction onto P. A small neighborhood in Euclidean space first retracts to the simplex, by taking nonnegative coordinates and normalizing their sum. Composing gives a Euclidean neighborhood retraction onto P.

Extend the finitely many coordinates of the inverse homeomorphism A→P continuously to Q as follows. For a residual continuous scalar function r_n on compact A with sup norm at most c_n, choose the least positive integer L_n such that
|r_n(a)−r_n(b)| ≤ c_n/2 + L_n dist(a,b)   for all a,b in A.

Uniform continuity and boundedness give such an integer. Put h_n(x)=inf_(a in A)(r_n(a)+L_n dist(x,a)), clamped to[−c_n,c_n]. It is bounded and L_n-Lipschitz; on A its error from r_n lies between0 and c_n/2. Define r_(n+1)=r_n−h_n|A and c_(n+1)=c_n/2. The uniformly convergent sum of the h_n extends the original coordinate function exactly. All constants are suprema/infima or least integers, so this is a definable recursion. For a zero starting function use the zero extension. The finite coordinate extensions give a map Psi:Q→R^N. On the inverse image of the preceding Euclidean retraction neighborhood, compose with its retraction and P→A. This gives a continuous retraction r:U→A from an actual open neighborhood U of A.

Form the smooth double $Q^{\mathrm{dbl}}$ from the two copies of the supplied smooth grope neighborhood, using its given product boundary collar, as in Section13. Use the proper Euclidean embedding j of this BOUNDARYLESS double and its smooth neighborhood retraction R supplied by the actual Whitney-approximation proof. There is a continuous fold c:Q^{dbl}→Q: it is the identity on the first copy, identifies the second copy with the first by the doubling identification, and in the shared collar is (x,t)→(x,|t|). For x in a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood U' of compact A in U⊂Q, the segment between j(x) and j(r(x)) stays in the domain of R. Indeed r fixes A, and compact j(A) has positive distance from the closed complement of that domain. The formula c(R((1−t)j(x)+t j(r(x)))) is a continuous homotopy IN Q from the inclusion U'→Q to r|U', fixed on A. Hence every loop in U' has phi-trivial image in Q. No smooth retraction onto the boundary of Q is used, and no smoothness of the fold is claimed.

Carry out the smooth relative approximation and finite jet perturbation of d in the DOUBLE, fixing its supplied smooth attaching collar pointwise. Choose a smaller closed source boundary collar inside the collar where d is already smooth; keep a neighborhood of that smaller collar fixed by the cutoff. The complement of that neighborhood in the compact parameter disk is a compact set mapped into IntQ, since d is proper. Its image therefore has positive distance from the boundary of Q in the doubled metric. It also has a positive tolerance for remaining in U', by relative openness and compactness. Choose the approximation and subsequent finite perturbations below both tolerances. On the fixed collar the map remains d; everywhere else it stays in IntQ∩U'. Thus the resulting map is a smooth proper generic disk IN Q, with the original attaching collar and framing, and all its double-point loops lie in U'. The continuous fold used in1.127 is NOT applied to this smooth approximation. For the framing, take the supplied framed parallel of the original d with its disjoint boundary parallel. Its ordinary relative intersection with d is twice the signed self-point count, and is therefore even; the normal-zero term is absent because that frame extends. The relative intersection number is unchanged under homotopy fixing these boundary parallels. For the smooth approximation it equals2mu+e, by the local parallel-sheet count and the zeros of a generic normal section. Thus its relative Euler number e is even. Interior cusps change e by2, so finitely many restore e=0 and the required frame. Their new loops are trivial in the same small coordinate balls, so phi-nullness survives. The resulting SMOOTH framed generic null disk has the original attaching region.

This operation shows why the goodness step can be consumed in the canonical smooth grope model with the framed-disk convention, without using arbitrary TOP neighborhood smoothing, stable5 integration, or the full boundary/collar smoothing needed for an unrelated original TOP-generic input. That boundary/collar bootstrap is not claimed here.
**Section15: Countable Choice versus the successive tower choices.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit.

Countable Choice is not being identified with Dependent Choice. Saying 'choose a next tower at each stage' would not justify this foundation claim. The geometric selections in this particular smooth-model construction can instead be made by a single-valued least-code rule, after fixing the Euclidean embedding/retraction of the smooth neighborhood once.

For a new disk with a specified smooth boundary collar, list pairs consisting of a dyadic collar width and a finite tuple of rational polynomials on the standard parameter disk. Use its supplied boundary-collar map b and a fixed smooth radial cutoff alpha, equal to1 on a smaller collar and0 off that collar. Form the Euclidean candidate alpha j(b)+(1−alpha)P and apply the fixed neighborhood retraction R. The term alpha j(b) is extended by zero only where alpha already vanishes; it is smooth there. Candidates are retained only when the Euclidean values lie in the retraction domain and the resulting map has the required proper boundary collar, genericity, support and finite intersection conditions. Framed candidates are listed simultaneously: project rational polynomial vector fields to the smooth normal plane of the candidate disk, blend them with the prescribed boundary frame on the same collar, and retain those with oriented linearly independent normal vectors everywhere. Orthogonal projection is computed from the ambient embedding metric and the derivative matrix, so is part of the fixed formula.

Whenever an admissible smooth framed filling exists, some listed candidate exists. Choose the dyadic collar inside a collar on which that filling agrees with b. Rational polynomials approximate its Euclidean coordinates and its normal frame uniformly with the required first derivatives. Here is the needed C1 density calculation. Extend each smooth coordinate function slightly past the compact disk, using its finitely many local extensions and a finite smooth partition, and restrict to a containing square rescaled to[0,1]^2. Its Bernstein polynomial is the finite sum of f(k/n,l/n) times the two binomial basis polynomials. Uniform convergence follows from uniform continuity: the binomial weights are probabilities, and the weight outside a fixed distance eta of(x,y) is at most1/(2n eta^2) by the sum of their variances. Its x derivative is the analogous degree(n−1,n) sum of n(f((k+1)/n,l/n)−f(k/n,l/n)), each an average of the x derivative on an interval of length1/n; uniform continuity of that derivative and the same variance bound give uniform derivative convergence. The y derivative is identical. Approximate the finitely many coefficients by rationals with error smaller than the desired C1 tolerance divided by4n: the basis sums to1 and the derivative difference has bound2n times that error. Restrict back to the disk. This proves the claimed rational-polynomial C1 density rather than assuming an analytic power series for an arbitrary smooth function. The values stay in the open retraction domain; properness away from the fixed collar, the normal-frame determinant and the finite transversality angles have positive compact lower bounds. Thus sufficiently close candidates preserve them. Near a generic immersion the double points and their labels persist in disjoint coordinate balls and no new double points occur outside them, by compactness off the local-injectivity diagonal. For a group-null filling use Section14's open neighborhood with null group image: sufficiently close candidates lie there, so retain all null-loop conditions. Candidates which are required to lie in a prescribed relative homotopy class do so for sufficiently close approximations, by the straight retraction homotopy fixed on the boundary collar.

The least natural-number code satisfying these actual predicates therefore specifies the disk and its frame uniquely. Decidability of the predicates is not asserted or needed for set-theoretic definability. This is not a choice function on arbitrary subsets of a mapping space: it is minimization in a specified COUNTABLE list which has just been proved nonempty for each geometric step.

The other choices have the same form. Paths and finger arcs are finite polygonal/rational smooth approximations in the already specified charts, with endpoint templates and finite disjointness conditions. Parallel widths and modification balls use the first dyadic radius meeting the strict compact separation conditions. Finite orderings of double points can be obtained lexicographically from their distinct parameter preimage coordinate tuples, and every finite tree or interval subdivision is chosen in that ordering. The local shrinking Baire step of Section5 has its own explicit countable rational bump rule, preserving every earlier finite avoidance margin. The successive approximations of Sections9–12 use least cofinal story levels and least integer tolerances. No choice is made over an uncountable family of possible future branches.

Thus each next finite stage is a uniquely defined function of the previous finite stage, the original input and the fixed embedding/retraction. Ordinary recursion on the natural numbers constructs the entire sequence. The single fixed smooth embedding/retraction and the actual transversality/approximation suppliers use their stated Countable Choice hypothesis; once those are fixed, no additional Dependent Choice principle is introduced by the tower or shrinking recursion. This is the precise foundation claim of the current smooth-input candidate. It does not turn the open unrestricted problem into a theorem and does not supply a TOP smoothing theorem.

references.title: Michael H. Freedman and Frank Quinn, Topology of 4-Manifolds

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The infinite cyclic group $\mathbb Z$ is good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem, in the sense of the $\pi_1$-null disk property defined for a good fundamental group.

citations.quote: Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is a proper framed generic immersion $d:D^2\looparrowright G^c$ of a disk into the grope's actual four-dimensional framed block. Its boundary is the core attaching circle, with the normal framing specified by the attaching solid-torus neighborhood, and each double-point loop of $d$, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: **Section1: Precise input.** A finite framed four-dimensional capped-grope neighborhood is supplied, with its usual product collars and self-plumbing charts. Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input.

**Operation.** Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Consequently, if all designated labels lie in an interval [a,b], every new label has absolute value at most b−a.

**Proof of the contraction operation.** Cut the top surface at each pair of symplectic attaching curves. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. Cutting a genus-g one-boundary surface along its complete symplectic system leaves the disk region with paired edges; the four parallel cap sectors and this square fill each pair of edges. Thus this replaces the surface with its contracted disk. All replacements take place in the supplied framed block. Parallel copies are made in its chosen normal coordinate; the central square uses the untwisted product collar, so the external attaching framing is unchanged. The result may be immersed, which is allowed.

For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. Finitely many paths on one cap can be chosen with disjoint interiors by an embedded finite tree and small parallel offsets. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. In a product rectangle around the path, this is just the rectangle between the two parallel copies, closed by the boundary square. Its interior is disjoint from the old body and all unmodified sheets. A generic sufficiently small choice of the finitely many product widths is possible because their unwanted incidences are finitely many closed disjoint compact sets. No appeal to a normal bundle over an arbitrary TOP surface occurs.

Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Ribbons on the same cap have been chosen parallel and disjoint, and ribbons belonging to different handles have disjoint block neighborhoods. Therefore every new intersection has exactly the stated two designated ancestors. Repeating for all parallel descendants removes the designated old point altogether. This is a finite sequence of ordinary finger/Whitney operations in explicit smooth block charts; a small relative perturbation makes the resulting intersections transverse.

Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. A path to the new intersection follows the first pushed sheet along the ribbon to its second-sheet cap, crosses the common central square, and returns along the other ribbon in reverse. Cancel the common paths in the old body. The resulting word is g h^{-1}; changing starting path conjugates it and exchanging the two resulting sheets inverts it. This is a calculation in the original supplied neighborhood, since every ribbon and push lies there. Its Z label is consequently ±(phi(g)−phi(h)). An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. The construction, classification of new intersections and claimed bound follow.

**Section2: Halving and the finite stopping bound.** Suppose there are h top surface stages available for contraction and the absolute labels of all the actual cap-point generators are at most an integer N. Contract the top stage, designating all points whose labels are in [N/2,N]. Their new labels have absolute value at most N/2 by Section1. The unmodified old positive labels are less than N/2; old negative labels may still range to −N. Contract the next top stage and designate the labels in [−N,−N/2]. Again new labels have absolute value at most N/2. Old labels outside this interval already have absolute value at most N/2. Thus two contractions reduce the bound to N/2. The same construction works when N is odd, since inequalities refer to real bounds and labels remain integers.

After q pairs of contractions the bound is N/2^q. Choose the least integer q with 2^q>N; if N=0 take q=0. This is a finite integer algorithm. At that point every cap-point generator has label zero. The neighborhood group is generated by these loops: the abstract disk-like capped grope is simply connected (its symplectic basis loops are killed by its attached higher stages/caps), and each self-plumbing identifies two small simply connected sheet neighborhoods, adding its one double-point loop. Cutting the finite plumbing neighborhoods restores the abstract source. Van Kampen, adding them back one at a time, gives precisely these generators, with no assertion that an arbitrary ambient group is free. Hence the entire neighborhood image has zero Z label.

Contract the remaining body stages to a disk. Every operation stays in this neighborhood, so all double-point loops of the final framed immersed disk have zero image under the original homomorphism. Its boundary and framing are unchanged. This proves null-disk production **when sufficiently many actual stages have been constructed**; it does not yet manufacture those stages from height1.5.

In the symmetric height-raising construction, the precise quantitative target can be stated without the harmless factor-of-two compression in FQ2.9. If 2k raising steps give height at least 2^k and each resulting cap-point loop has word length at most 5^{2k} in the original finite cap-point generators, their absolute labels are at most 5^{2k}B. It suffices that
2^(−floor((2^k−1)/2)) · 5^(2k) · B < 1.

Reserve one bottom surface stage; the other stages supply the indicated number of contraction pairs. The displayed quantity tends to zero because its base-two logarithm is at most −2^(k−1)+O(k)+log2 B. Thus a least successful k is obtained by a terminating integer search. No infinite choice or convergence theorem is hidden in this numerical step. Sections3–4 prove the required height and word-length estimates starting from the asymmetric height1.5 input.

**Section3: The asymmetric bootstrap.** Start with one symplectic pair above the bottom surface: on the positive side a framed capped surface R of positive genus, on the negative side a framed immersed cap W. The same construction is repeated for the finitely many pairs; their body blocks are disjoint, and interactions between cap systems are allowed. All operations fix a neighborhood of the original bottom surface and its attaching region.

Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. The annulus and the single crossing are read in the supplied symplectic handle block, not in a hypothetical neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface.

Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. This includes the original caps of F, the caps of R and the remaining parts of W. All intersections newly produced by those pushes are between those cap sheets. The sphere T is therefore disjoint from both R and the body/caps of F, and from the caps of R, and meets W at its one prescribed point only. Self-intersections of T are allowed. The ribbons have support near cap arcs and their central squares, away from the lower body, so they do not alter any of the displayed body intersections.

Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. Thus they may create cap intersections but no body intersections. Their original intersections with R or the body of F are empty, and sufficiently small parallel copies retain that property. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W.

For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections.

This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections.

**Section4: Height raising and word length.** Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section3 gives (1,0) to (1,1). The following side extension, used only finitely often in this bootstrap, supplies (1,1) to (2,1) to (2,3). Let P be the side to be raised and Q its other side, of heights p,q at least one. Construct F transverse to the bottom surface of P by taking two normal parallels of Q and closing their rims with the normal annulus. It is sphere-like of height q. Its body is embedded, meets P only at the specified first-stage point, and misses all other body stages; intersections of its caps with the old caps are allowed.

First make a contracted parallel sphere T transverse to the bottom of P, using Section1 and pushing off all original cap sheets and the caps of F. Its only body intersection is that prescribed transverse point. To make the caps of F disjoint from the old P caps, push an F-cap sheet at each intersection down the old P cap to its attaching stage and then down successive P stages to its bottom. A finger across one attaching collar replaces one intersection with two on the immediately lower stage; this is two parallel paths around the two ends of that collar. After p stages there are finitely many points on the bottom of P. Tube them off over parallel copies of T. These changes affect only caps of F. They cannot reintroduce intersections with old P caps because T misses those caps and the finger paths on the old caps avoid the other finitely many double-point preimages. The new intersections are among caps of F and possibly the old Q caps, which are still caps. All old body stages are fixed.

Now for an intersection of an old P cap with a Q cap, push the Q-cap sheet down the P stages and tube it off over T. The Q cap is still an immersed disk; its boundary and framing are fixed. It may acquire self/intersections with other caps, which are allowed. It remains disjoint from the old P caps and all body stages: the punctured T used in the tubing has had its unique bottom-P intersection removed. Crucially T is also disjoint from the body of F, so the Q caps miss every body piece to be added in the next step.

Finally treat every self/mutual intersection among the old P caps by pushing one of its P sheets down the P stages and tubing it off over copies of the full F, rather than T. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope: its first added stage is the old disk with punctured bodies of F attached, followed by the higher stages of those copies of F. Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All old P-cap intersections have been removed; the added bodies are embedded and disjoint from each other because distinct body parallels of F are disjoint, and the tube paths avoid all other old preimages. The new caps are copies of F's caps. Those were made disjoint from ALL old P caps before this step, and properness makes them disjoint from F's parallel bodies. Consequently every new intersection is among caps, not on a new body. A cap with no intersections may be regarded as a genus-zero stage with no attached higher surface, as in the disk-like model. We have obtained side heights at least (p+q,q), with the previous body and its attaching framing preserved. The first and second steps are needed: merely asserting that tubing adds height would leave the old cap intersections on the new body.

All choices involve finite paths, parallels and normal widths in supplied framed blocks. Use the move first with p=q=1, then exchange the two sides and use p=1,q=2. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap.

Once both sides have height at least two, there is an efficient variant which contracts only the TOP stage of a transverse grope. For the side P to be extended, form the transverse grope from the opposite side Q. Its height is that of Q. Contract its top stage and push the old caps off that contraction by Section1. The transverse grope now has height one less and its caps are disjoint from all old caps. Push each intersection on a P cap down the P stages, and at the bottom tube off over this transverse grope. The same body/cap scorecard as Section4 applies: new bodies consist of separate parallel copies of the old embedded opposite-side bodies, and all cap intersections have been removed from the new body before it is declared a body. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope with the height of the contracted transverse grope. In terms of full path heights a,b INCLUDING the shared bottom, the updated path height is a+b−2. Alternate the sides. Starting with a_{−1}=a_0=3, the successive updated path heights obey a_n=a_{n−1}+a_{n−2}−2. The uniform height is the smaller of the two current path heights. Writing a_n−2 as a Fibonacci recursion gives, after 2k steps, uniform height at least 2^k: consecutive pairs increase the smaller Fibonacci term by at least a factor two. Additional initial height only improves the bound.

For clarity, the required estimate concerns WORDS, not numbers of double points. Base every old cap-point loop by a path in the old grope. Body-stage paths contribute no new plumbing generator. Contraction copies an old point without changing its generator. A push off a contraction creates the difference loop of Section1, a word of length at most two in the OLD cap-point generators. A new intersection among caps of the parallel transverse grope has length one, since its sheets are old parallel sheets. The only remaining type is a loop using a newly pushed-down finger: follow its first sheet across at most two old cap-point loops to the parallel transverse copy, cross its new cap intersection (one old generator), and return across at most two old loops on the other finger. The two bottom-stage paths cancel, as do the parallel collar paths. This is a concatenation of at most 2+1+2 old generators or inverses. These exhaust the new intersections: they occur on unchanged parallels, on a contraction push, or between two inserted fingers. Thus each step sends every NEW generator to a word of length at most five in the PRECEDING generators. Induction gives length at most 5^(2k) after 2k steps, and absolute Z label at most 5^(2k)B. No count of the possibly much larger number of points is substituted for this word bound.

Choose the least k satisfying Section2's displayed stopping inequality (if B=0 no raising is needed). Height supplies the required number of contraction pairs, and the label estimate supplies their initial bound. Section2 then gives zero image on every cap-point loop, and final contraction produces a framed immersed disk with the original framed attaching circle. Everything occurs in the original supplied grope neighborhood. For an arbitrary homomorphism to Z this is the pi1-null disk property of the existing goodness Definition. The construction is finite for each input: no countable-stage choice, limiting disk, tower standardization or arbitrary TOP normal-bundle theorem has been used in this cyclic part.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Let $W$ be a connected Hausdorff space with a supplied basis of contractible open neighborhoods, $o\in W$, $\pi=\pi_1(W,o)$, and $N\triangleleft\pi$. Put $G=\pi/N$ and let $k$ be any commutative unital ring. Use first-loop-first concatenation in $\pi$. There is a canonical based normal path-class cover $p:W_N\to W$ with $\pi_1(W_N)=N$, whose right deck action is
$$[\gamma]\cdot g=[a^{-1}*\gamma]\quad\text{when }a\in\pi\text{ represents }g.$$
Let $\mathcal R_x$ be the free $k$-module on $p^{-1}(x)$, with its induced right $k[G]$ action and transport along lifted paths. Each fiber is free of rank one as a right $k[G]$-module. Its base fiber is identified with $k[G]$ by the constant-path lift. Thus transport around a based loop $a$ is left multiplication by its quotient image $g^{-1}$.

For this specified right local system, the actual singular chain complex is naturally isomorphic to $C_*(W_N;k)$ as a complex of right $k[G]$-modules, and there is a natural isomorphism
$$H_1(W;\mathcal R)\cong (N/[N,N])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k.$$
The right action on the last group is $[u]\otimes c\mapsto[a^{-1}ua]\otimes c$ for $g=[a]\in G$. A based loop $u\in N$ with coefficient $1$ corresponds to $[u]\otimes1$. In particular it represents zero in $H_1(W;\mathcal R)$ exactly when it lies in the kernel of $N\to(N/[N,N])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k$. Taking $N=P^s\pi$ gives exactly the next mixed-series kernel $P^{s+1}\pi$ with coefficient ring $k$. For a based continuous map carrying $N$ into a normal subgroup $N\prime$ of the target fundamental group, these identifications commute with its induced homology maps and quotient-group coefficient maps. This includes every connected Hausdorff manifold, with boundary allowed, and every connected finite polyhedron. No finite CW structure, compactness, finite generation of $\pi$, or choice principle is assumed.

derivations.claim: The supplied contractible basis consists of path-connected open sets, so connectedness implies path-connectedness: path components are open and their complements are open. Form the set of paths $\gamma:o\to x$, identifying two with the same endpoint when the loop $\gamma*(\gamma')^{-1}$ belongs to $N$. The subgroup laws make this an equivalence relation. For a member $U$ of the supplied contractible basis and a path $\gamma$ ending in $U$, let $U_{[\gamma]}$ consist of $[\gamma*\eta]$ for paths $\eta$ lying in $U$ and starting at that endpoint. The projection to $U$ is bijective because any two such paths with the same endpoint are homotopic rel endpoints in $U$. If two such sets over $U$ meet they coincide; for two different basis neighborhoods, a smaller basis neighborhood of a common endpoint shows their intersections contain a basic set of this same form. They therefore define a topology for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets each homeomorphic to $U$. Surjectivity uses a path to each individual endpoint, rather than selecting all such paths. Thus this is an actual covering space constructed without a representative section.

For completeness the degree-one constant-coefficient calculation needs no universal-coefficient theorem. For any path-connected based space $Y$, concatenate paths by the first-loop-first rule. A constant edge is the boundary of a constant triangle; a path homotopy gives the boundary of its two-triangle prism up to constant endpoint edges; and $uv$ is homologous to $u+v$ by mapping a triangle to the concatenated path with vertex parameters $0,1/2,1$. A reversed path is homologous to the negative path, since its concatenation with the original contracts by retracing. These finite relations show that $[u]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c\mapsto c[u]\in H_1(Y;k)$ is a well-defined additive balanced map $S:\pi_1(Y)_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k\to H_1(Y;k)$. For a fixed finite cycle $z=\sum_e c_e e$, choose paths $\gamma_v$ from the basepoint to the finitely many endpoint images and put $$T_\gamma(z)=\sum_e [\gamma_{e(0)}*e*\gamma_{e(1)}^{-1}]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c_e.$$ Finite choice follows by finite induction in ZF, so these paths exist without an axiom of choice.

A path $\gamma$ lifts from the constant-path point by $t\mapsto[\gamma|_{[0,t]}]$, with the restricted path reparametrized and held stationary after its endpoint. This is continuous on the basic sets of step 1.1, and reaches $[\gamma]$, so $W_N$ is path-connected. For any fixed starting lift, path lifting exists uniquely by finite subdivision into evenly covered basis neighborhoods. A homotopy lifts uniquely by the same finite-grid construction on its compact square: choose a finite fine grid subordinate to the inverse-image cover and extend sheet by sheet, with uniqueness on overlaps. The square is compact metric, so this finite construction uses no choice principle. Hence $p_*$ is injective on fundamental groups, and its image consists exactly of based loops whose lifted endpoint is the constant-path point, that is, exactly $N$. This identifies $\pi_1(W_N)$ with $N$ by the actual projection. The same lifting statement for a singular simplex follows directly by sending a point to the lift obtained along the straight segment from its first vertex; segments joined by a triangle are homotopic inside the simplex, so this gives the unique continuous lift with prescribed first vertex.

Another finite path family changes each loop term by $d_{e(0)}-d_{e(1)}$ in the abelianization. After tensoring, its total coefficient at a vertex is that of the cycle boundary, hence zero. Thus $T_\gamma(z)$ has one uniquely defined value $T(z)$, independent of paths or enlargement of the finite endpoint list. On a singular triangle the loops for edges $01,12,02$ satisfy $L_{01}L_{12}=L_{02}$ because the triangle fills their concatenation, so $T$ kills its signed boundary. For any finite two-chain use the finite union of its vertex images to get the same conclusion termwise, with its $k$ coefficients. Thus $T$ descends to homology. The relations in step 1.2 say $\gamma_{e(0)}*e*\gamma_{e(1)}^{-1}$ is homologous to $\gamma_{e(0)}+e-\gamma_{e(1)}$; in the weighted sum the extra path terms cancel by the cycle condition. Hence $ST=\mathrm{id}$. On a based loop use the constant connector at its endpoint, giving $TS=\mathrm{id}$ on every generator $[u]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c$. This proves the natural isomorphism $H_1(Y;k)\cong\pi_1(Y)_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes k$. Naturality follows by mapping a finite connector family forward; independence then removes that family from the map. No paths to all points of $Y$ and no basis of an infinite vector space were chosen.

For $g\in G$ and any representative loop $a$, define the right action by $[\gamma]\cdot g=[a^{-1}*\gamma]$. Replacing $a$ by another representative gives the same path class, since $N$ is normal; replacing $\gamma$ by an equivalent path also does. The action law follows from $b^{-1}*a^{-1}=(a*b)^{-1}$, and its maps carry the basic sets in step 1.1 to basic sets. On each fiber it is free and transitive: for paths $\gamma,\delta$ to the same endpoint take the quotient class of $\gamma*\delta^{-1}$, which sends $[\gamma]$ to $[\delta]$. The formula specifies the action uniquely without choosing representatives for all quotient elements. Free $k$-linearization of each fiber gives $\mathcal R_x$; path transport commutes with this right action because it appends a path at the end, while deck action prepends $a^{-1}$. Thus it is a right-$k[G]$ local system, each fiber individually having a torsor point as a free basis. At the basepoint the constant-path point is a specified basis, and transport along $a$ sends it to $[a]=[1]\cdot g^{-1}$, giving exactly the stated inverse convention and a right-linear map.

A basis generator in the local chain group consists of a base singular simplex $\sigma$ together with one point of the covering fiber over its first vertex and a scalar in $k$. Send it to the unique lift of $\sigma$ with that first vertex, given in step 2.1, with the same scalar. Pairs of this kind are in bijection with covering singular simplices: projection gives the inverse map. Both directions are uniquely specified on generators, hence define inverse maps on all finite chains without selecting a lift for each base simplex. For the face omitting the first vertex, the first point of the lifted face is the transport of the old first point along that edge, exactly the local coefficient boundary rule. The other faces keep the first point. Thus the bijection commutes with all signed boundary terms. It commutes with the right deck action on generators too, so gives the claimed actual chain isomorphism of right $k[G]$-module complexes.

Apply steps 1.2 and 2.2 to $Y=W_N$ and combine with steps 2.1 and 4.1. A based loop $u\in N$ lifts to the based loop whose projection is $u$, so its coefficient-one class maps precisely to $[u]\otimes1$. For the right action, move the constant-path base lift by $g=[a]$. The lift of $a^{-1}$ joins the old base lift to that new one. Rebase the translated lift of $u$ by this path and its inverse; its projection is $a^{-1}ua$. Connector contributions cancel in first homology by step 1.2, so this gives the stated conjugation action on $N_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes k$. Different representatives of $g$ change it by an inner automorphism of $N$, trivial on $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$. The zero criterion is now exactly the displayed isomorphism and its coefficient-one formula; for $N=P^s\pi$ in the finite mixed series defined in the Statement, it is the next kernel $P^{s+1}\pi$. For a based continuous map $f:(W,o)\to(W',o')$ between spaces with the stated connected, Hausdorff and contractible-neighborhood hypotheses, if $f_*(N)\subseteq N'\triangleleft\pi_1(W',o')$, the covering map is explicitly $[\gamma]\mapsto[f\circ\gamma]$; the equivalence relation makes it well-defined. It commutes with endpoint projection, the induced quotient-group action and simplex lifting, so step 4.1 is natural for its coefficient maps. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 already prove naturality of the constant-coefficient identification, yielding the stated commutative homology comparison. All covering, chain and homology maps were explicit quotient maps or uniquely defined finite-lift maps, so the full coefficient and choice scope in the Statement is proved.

current_manifest_record.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, the following are equivalent: $K$ bounds a ribbon immersion of a disk in $S^3$; and $K$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball for which squared radial distance is Morse in the interior with only critical points of indices zero and one. In the second presentation the boundary collar in $D$ is parametrized by $c_D(y,s)=(1-s)y$ for $y\in\partial D\subset S^3$ and $0\le s<\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and let $K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$ be a smooth oriented knot, meaning the image of an orientation-preserving smooth embedding of a circle. A **ribbon immersion** for $K$ is a smooth immersion $f:D^2\to S^3$ whose boundary restriction is an embedding onto $K$ and whose only multiple points form finitely many pairwise disjoint transverse double arcs $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m$. For each $i$, the full preimage of $\gamma_i$ consists of two disjoint embedded arcs $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ in $D^2$: $\alpha_i$ is properly embedded, with its two endpoints on $\partial D^2$ and its interior in $\operatorname{Int}D^2$, while $\beta_i$ is compact and lies in $\operatorname{Int}D^2$. There are no triple points or other self-intersections. A **ribbon disk** for $K$ is such a ribbon immersion, and $K$ is a **ribbon knot** if it admits a ribbon disk.

A **band** on a link in $S^3$ is the image of a smoothly embedded rectangle whose two opposite attaching edges lie on the link and whose remaining points are disjoint from it. A **band move** removes the attaching edges, inserts the other two edges, and rounds the corners; the embedded band, including its half-twist data, is part of the move. A **no-maximum disk movie** is the family of regular level links of a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$ whose boundary collar in $D$ is parametrized by $c_D(y,s)=(1-s)y$ for $y\in\partial D\subset S^3$ and $0\le s<\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ is Morse in the disk interior with only index-$0$ minima and index-$1$ saddles. A minimum creates a split unknot and a saddle performs an oriented band move; there are no maxima. The no-maximum disk movie is a second presentation convention used by the design for explicit ribbon examples. This movie model and the ribbon-immersion definition above describe the same class of knots: a finite birth-and-band induction converts the movie to an immersion, and cutting the proper double-arc preimages converts an immersion to a disk-and-band movie. The local resolution lemma proves only that a ribbon immersion pushes rel boundary to a smooth proper disk in $B^4$. The slice-ribbon conjecture asks whether every smooth slice knot admits a ribbon immersion as defined above.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. On a compact collared triad $(W;M_0,M_1)$, every adapted excellent Morse function determines a finite handle decomposition relative to $M_0$, with one handle of index $\operatorname{ind}(p)$ per critical point. Given an adapted field, the attaching sphere is the boundary of its local unstable disk transported to the lower regular level. Conversely every finite handle decomposition relative to $M_0$ is realized by an adapted excellent Morse function with one critical point per handle, of the same index, ordered by the prescribed handle order.

If $M$ is a compact smooth manifold and $f:M\to\mathbb R$ is a Morse function,
then $f$ has only finitely many critical points.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

derivations.claim: Start with a no-maximum disk movie. On its stipulated boundary collar, $\rho(c_D(y,s))=(1-s)^2$, so there are no radial critical points for $0<s<\varepsilon$. The critical set is therefore a compact discrete subset of the disk interior, hence finite by [F2]. On each regular radial interval, radial projection to the unit three-sphere gives an isotopy of the level link, extended by [F3]. A local minimum has the usual disk model and creates a split round unknot in a small ball; a local saddle has the rectangle model and changes the link by its framed band move. These assertions follow in coordinates from the Morse equations $x^2+y^2$ and $x^2-y^2$: the first level is a small circle born in a ball, and in the second the two attaching sides of the rectangle are replaced by the other two sides. Critical points sharing a value have disjoint small ambient neighborhoods, so the corresponding local events may be processed successively. Thus there is a finite sequence of births, band attachments, and boundary-link isotopies, whose abstract disk and band handles give exactly the original disk. We will realize this same sequence by immersed surfaces in $S^3$.

For the reverse implication, start with a ribbon immersion $f:D^2\to S^3$. Remove narrow disjoint strip neighborhoods of all its proper preimage arcs. Choose them disjoint from every interior preimage arc; this is possible because all preimage arcs are disjoint compact sets. Cutting along a proper arc of a disk separates it into two disks, so cutting along all these strips leaves finitely many disk components. Their images are embedded and pairwise disjoint, since every original multiple point had one preimage in a removed strip. The removed strips themselves are embedded bands with pairwise disjoint images, and are disjoint from the disk boundaries except along their attaching edges: their remaining intersections with the disk components are exactly the original ribbon arcs, away from these boundaries. Rounding the cut corners gives a finite presentation by disjoint embedded disks and disjoint embedded bands. The boundaries of the disks form an unlink. Indeed each disk has a disjoint small product neighborhood, and shrinking concentric circles in its disk coordinates gives an isotopy to a small round unknot in that neighborhood; [F3] extends these disjoint isotopies. The band surgeries on this unlink recover the original boundary $K$.

The inductive invariant is a compact oriented ribbon-immersed surface with the current oriented level link as embedded boundary. Begin with the empty surface. An isotopy event acts on the whole immersion by [F3]. For a birth, its ball is disjoint from the old boundary link. The old immersed surface has empty interior in $S^3$: in each immersion chart its image is a smooth two-dimensional sheet, and finitely many such charts cover its compact domain. Its image is also closed. Hence there is a small ball inside the birth ball disjoint from the entire old image. Add an embedded disk there. Its boundary is a split unknot isotopic within the birth ball to the required newborn component, and apply [F3] to match the new boundary link. This introduces no multiple point.

For a band event, first shrink its attaching intervals in their boundary collars and slide them along the boundary, if needed, to avoid the finitely many endpoints of old ribbon arcs. This changes the banded boundary by an isotopy supported in its attaching collars. The immersion is embedded on these collars. Keep the prescribed normal framing of the band core. Perturb the core relative to these collars, as in [F4], to avoid the old double arcs and meet each regular old sheet transversely. Away from its endpoints it is compact and disjoint from the old boundary, so all resulting intersections with the old surface lie in its regular interior sheets; transversality makes their inverse image a finite discrete set. The perturbation can be arbitrarily small, so the core remains embedded, the band framing persists, and the boundary band move is unchanged up to isotopy. Shrink the framed band about that core, including its attaching intervals. This shrinking is an isotopy of the banded boundary: in the rectangle coordinates contract the width, extend the same contraction along the two attaching link intervals, and round corners in their disjoint collars. At an intersection with an old sheet the transverse core parameter is a local defining coordinate for that sheet, so the implicit function theorem expresses its intersection with a sufficiently narrow band as a single arc running across the full band width. Compactness away from these finitely many intersections allows one width small enough to exclude every other intersection. Each new double arc consequently has one proper preimage in the new band and one interior preimage in the old surface. The new band is embedded, it avoids all old double arcs, and the neighborhoods of its new intersections are disjoint, so no triple point is introduced. Glue and smooth the band at its attaching collars. The old proper preimage arcs remain proper because those collars avoided all their endpoints. The new proper arcs have endpoints on the two free band sides, hence on the new surface boundary. This proves the invariant at the saddle.

Finite induction over the movie now gives a ribbon-immersed oriented surface with boundary $K$. It is the original abstract surface: births added its zero-handles, saddles added its one-handles in the same order and with the same oriented attaching data, and boundary isotopies changed neither handle topology nor orientation. Thus its domain is a disk, not merely a surface of Euler characteristic one. Step 3.1 also shows that its only multiple points are finitely many disjoint transverse ribbon double arcs and its boundary is embedded. This proves the implication from the disk movie to a ribbon immersion.

Realize that presentation in a radial shell $S^3\times[a,1]\subset B^4$, $a>0$. At early distinct radii create a minimum disk for each unlink component, using its embedded disk to give the trace down to its cap. Between these caps and the bands keep product annuli on the unlink. At later radii attach the disjoint bands by the standard saddle traces of [F2]. Each saddle trace meets the existing surface only at its attaching collars: below that radius the surface contains only the product boundary annuli at those levels, and the band interior is disjoint from the current boundary link. The interiors of the zero-handle disks lie at earlier radii, so band intersections with their projections in $S^3$ cause no intersection in the four-ball. Distinct bands have disjoint images and disjoint attaching intervals, so they can also be placed at successive radii. Finish with a product collar up to radius one. Smooth the finitely many seams in their product charts. This is a smooth embedded disk because its abstract disks and bands reconstruct the original domain disk of step 1.2. Its radius has exactly the chosen minimum and saddle models; squared radius is their composition with an increasing smooth function having positive derivative on $[a,1]$, so it has the same nondegenerate critical points and indices. Its boundary is $K$, and the final product collar makes it proper and neat. This proves the converse and the equivalence.

current_manifest_record.title: Hecke–bracket trace dictionary and local descent
current_manifest_record.statement:
Let $A$ be an indeterminate, $R_A=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1},(A^{-4}+1)^{-1}]$,
$q=A^{-2}$, $t=q^2=A^{-4}$, $\delta=-(q+q^{-1})=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and
$z_0=-1/(t+1)$. For a nonempty regular diagram $D$, define
$\langle D\rangle$ by summing its crossing smoothings with weights $A$ and
$A^{-1}$ and the factor $\delta^{k-1}$ for a state with $k$ circles. Let
$B_n$ be the $n$-strand Artin braid group with positive geometric generators
$\sigma_i$ (label $i$ passes below the midpoint and label $i+1$ passes above),
drawn with braid parameter increasing from bottom to top; let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$. Let $H(n)$ be
the type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation
$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid relations, and distant commutation; let $\pi_n$
send $\sigma_i$ to $T_i$. Its normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$
satisfies $\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Let
$\mathrm{TL}_n$ be the noncrossing pairing algebra with loop value $\delta$,
and let $\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)=\delta^{c(D)}$ be the unnormalized trace,
where $c(D)$ is the number of circles after joining corresponding top and
bottom endpoints outside the rectangle; set
$\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$. For $\beta\in B_n$,
$n\ge1$, orient its closure in the braid direction. Under the specialization
$v\mapsto t$, $z\mapsto z_0$ of the Hecke tower, one has
$$\langle\widehat\beta\rangle =\delta^{n-1}(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\big|_{v=t,\,z=z_0}.$$
The identity gives bracket value $1$ on the one-strand identity closure. Its
positive and negative Markov stabilizations multiply the raw bracket by
$-A^3$ and $-A^{-3}$, respectively.
current_manifest_record.strategy: Identifies the bracket crossing representation with a rescaled Hecke generator, proves the normalized diagram closure trace has the specialized Markov rules, and derives uniqueness after specialization from the free tower decomposition.
