current_manifest_record.title: Singular instanton knot and sutured closure data
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume full AC for the instanton constructions. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a marked point $x$ and a preferred nonzero normal vector $v$ at $x$. Choose a small disk $D$ normal to $K$ at $x$, let $L=\partial D$, and let $\omega$ be the radius of $D$ from $x$ to a point of $L$. Then $K^\natural:=K\cup L$ is the based earring link. Choose disjoint closed tubular neighborhoods $N(K)$ and $N(L)$ of its two components, set $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(N(K)\cup N(L))$, and truncate the endpoints of $\omega$ at $\partial X$ to obtain $[\omega]\in H_1(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z/2)$.

Here $PU(2)=U(2)/U(1)\cong SO(3)$; a principal $PU(2)$ bundle $P\to X$ is equivalently an oriented real 3-plane bundle, and $w_2(P)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z/2)$ denotes its second Stiefel–Whitney class. Poincaré–Lefschetz duality for the oriented compact 3-manifold $X$ with boundary is the isomorphism $PD:H_1(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z/2)\to H^2(X;\mathbb Z/2)$. Include a bundle $P$ with $w_2(P)=PD([\omega])$ in the singular bundle data.

Such a bundle exists for every marked earring. Orient the truncated arc as a relative integral cycle and set $c=PD_{\mathbb Z}[\omega]\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$. Choose a complex line bundle $Q\to X$ with $c_1(Q)=c$, and let $P$ be the projective unitary frame bundle of $Q\oplus\underline{\mathbb C}$. On each 2-cell, a clutch of $Q$ with winding $n$ gives the projective transition whose $SU(2)$ lift ends at $(-1)^n$; its lifting obstruction is therefore $n\bmod2$. Hence $w_2(P)=c\bmod2=PD_{\mathbb F_2}[\omega]$, as required.

In a local meridional angular coordinate $\theta$, an $SU(2)$ lift of the singular connection has the standard model $A_0+\frac14\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix}d\theta$, where $A_0$ is smooth in an $O(2)$ reduction. Parallel transport (holonomy) around either meridian is conjugate in $SU(2)$ to $\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$; its image has order two in $PU(2)$. Define $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$ to be the singular instanton Floer homology $I^\omega(S^3,K^\natural;P)$ associated to these data by Analytic foundations for the singular instanton knot complex, which supplies its analytic complex and independence of auxiliary choices under full AC. This does not assert sutured closure independence or a distinguished canonical class.

For the sutured version, let $E_K$ be the compact knot exterior and put two oppositely oriented meridional sutures $\gamma$ on its boundary torus. Choose a connected oriented annulus $T$, attach $[-1,1]\times T$ along the annular sutured region, and glue the two resulting boundary surfaces by an orientation-compatible diffeomorphism fixing a chosen point from $T$. The result is a closed oriented 3-manifold $\bar Y$ with a distinguished torus $\bar R$; the fixed point determines a standard circle meeting $\bar R$ once. Choose a line bundle $w\to\bar Y$ whose first Chern class is Poincaré dual to that circle, so $\langle c_1(w),[\bar R]\rangle$ is odd. Let $I_*(\bar Y,w;\mathbb Q)$ denote the closed instanton Floer group with rational coefficients, using the admissible fixed-determinant theory in the external input below. For a homology class $z$ of dimension $0$ or $2$ in $\bar Y$, let $\mu(z)$ denote the standard instanton Floer operator associated to $z$; the point and surface operators commute and have degrees $4$ and $-2$, respectively. If $y\in\bar R$, define the closure group $KHI_{\bar Y,\bar R,w}(K;\mathbb Q)$ by
$$KHI_{\bar Y,\bar R,w}(K;\mathbb Q):=\{a\in I_*(\bar Y,w;\mathbb Q):\mu(\bar R)^N a=0\text{ for some }N\ge1,\ \mu(y)a=2a\}.$$
This uses the generalized $0$-eigenspace of the surface operator and the ordinary $+2$-eigenspace of the point operator. For this admissible torus closure it equals the simultaneous ordinary $(0,2)$ eigenspace, by the extreme-surface simplicity input stated below; no global diagonalizability of either operator is assumed. The closure group is considered up to isomorphism, with independence of these auxiliary choices supplied by the external input below and the stated well-definedness justifier; no canonical vector or preferred basis is part of this definition.

current_manifest_record.title: Presentation chains compute twisted first homology and peripheral cycles
current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $(Y,y)$ be a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected based space, and fix an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle\ \cong\ \Gamma=\pi_1(Y,y)$$
from a finite presentation. Let $P$ be its presentation $2$-complex, with its one vertex $p$. Choose based loops in $Y$ representing the specified generators. They extend, after choosing fillings of the finitely many relators, to a based map $f:P\to Y$ inducing the specified isomorphism. No CW structure on $Y$ is required. For every left $\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$-module $A$, interpreted as the base fibre of a local system with $g a=T_{\bar g}a$ in the first-loop-first convention, this map induces an isomorphism
$$H_1(P;f^*\mathcal A)\ \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\ H_1(Y;\mathcal A).$$
This assertion does not require $Y$ or its universal cover to be aspherical and does not assert that $P$ is a spine or a homotopy-equivalent model of $Y$.

There is the following explicit finite-chain form. Give universal-cover chains the right action $c\cdot g=T_{g^{-1}}c$, and choose the lifted presentation vertex $e_0$ and generator edges $e_j$ starting there. For a word $w$ in the generators and their inverses, let each positive letter $x_j$ after prefix $q$ contribute $e_j\cdot q^{-1}$, and each negative letter $x_j^{-1}$ after prefix $q$ contribute $-e_j\cdot(qx_j^{-1})^{-1}$. Denote the sum by $c_w$. Then
$$\partial c_w=e_0\cdot w^{-1}-e_0.$$
If $u\in A$ is fixed by $w$, the tensor $c_w\otimes u$ is a cycle. Under the displayed isomorphism its class is the class of the actual based loop in $Y$ represented by $w$, with initial coefficient $u$; it is independent of the word representative and the relator fillings of $f$.

In particular let $j:(T^2,*)\to(Y,y)$ be a based torus map with ordered based loops $(\lambda,\mu)$, choose words $w_\lambda,w_\mu$ for their images, and let $u$ be fixed by both. The two finite cycles $c_{w_\lambda}\otimes u,c_{w_\mu}\otimes u$ compute the images of the actual torus classes in precisely this order. If $A$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $F$, the presentation complex gives finite matrices $B:C_2\to C_1$, $C:C_1\to C_0$ and these two cycle columns $U$, with $CB=CU=0$. The actual kernel of the two peripheral classes mapping into $H_1(Y;\mathcal A)$ is exactly
$$\ker\{F^2\xrightarrow{U}\ker C/\operatorname{im}B\}.$$
Thus a one-dimensional image of those two actual peripheral classes is equivalent to $\operatorname{rank}_F(B\mid U)=\operatorname{rank}_FB+1$. All matrix entries are finite sums of matrices for generator words and their inverses. For the left coefficient action $\operatorname{Ad}\rho$ of an $SL_2$ representation they are polynomial in the representation entries and in the chosen vector $u$. For a torus restriction with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\mu))^2\ne4$, one may take $u=\rho(\mu)-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\mu))I$ in characteristic different from $2$; the two torus classes are then a basis. This applies, in particular, to an actual compact smooth knot exterior and its based peripheral torus map. No existence of a generic representation family or generic exterior rank is inferred.

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.
Every nonempty path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected space has a universal covering space.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Let $X$ be a nonempty connected CW complex with basepoint $x$, let
$p:\widetilde X\to X$ be a universal cover
([[def-universal-covering-space]], [[thm-universal-cover-existence]]), put
$\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Identify $\pi$
with the deck group by the no-reversal isomorphism of
[[thm-deck-group-of-a-universal-cover-is-the-fundamental-group]]. Write
$g c$ for the induced **left** deck action on a singular or cellular chain.

The **right group-ring action** on universal-cover chains is
$$c\cdot g:=g^{-1}c\qquad(g\in\pi),$$
extended additively and $R$-linearly to [[def-group-ring|$R[\pi]$]]. It is a
right action because
$$(c\cdot g)\cdot h=h^{-1}(g^{-1}c)=(gh)^{-1}c=c\cdot(gh),\qquad c\cdot1=c.$$
Here the multiplication $[g][h]=[gh]$ and the unit $[1]$ are those constructed
in [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]; bilinearity extends the
displayed group action uniquely to all finite formal sums in $R[\pi]$.
Every deck map is cellular for the lifted CW structure and commutes with the
singular and cellular boundaries. Hence
$$\partial(c\cdot g)=(\partial c)\cdot g,$$
and $C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)$ and
$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)$ are chain complexes of right
$R[\pi]$-modules.

Choosing one lift and one orientation of every cell of $X$ makes each cellular
chain group a free right $R[\pi]$-module on those lifted oriented cells. This
is only a basis choice, not part of the chain complex. Empty chain degrees and
the zero ring give zero modules. The inversion in the definition is forced by
the library's first-loop-first deck convention; omitting it would reverse the
balanced tensor formulas below.

For a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected base $B$, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to $\pi_1(B,b_0)$. With the library's traversal-order path product the monodromy action is a right action, and the assignment carrying a loop class to the deck transformation that moves the chosen point of the fibre to the corresponding lifted endpoint is itself an isomorphism; no path reversal is inserted.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every free module is projective. More precisely, if $F$ has basis $(e_x)_{x\in X}$, a lift of a map $F\to M$ through a surjection $E\to M$ is obtained by choosing one preimage of each basis value. For finite $X$, finite choice suffices and no form of AC is needed; for $X=\varnothing$, the lift is the unique map from $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be any unital ring, let $S$ be a left $R$-module, and let
$$C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}C_0\xrightarrow{\epsilon_C}S\longrightarrow0,\qquad D_2\xrightarrow{\delta_2}D_1\xrightarrow{\delta_1}D_0\xrightarrow{\epsilon_D}S\longrightarrow0$$
be augmented complexes of left $R$-modules, exact at $C_1,C_0,S$ and at $D_1,D_0,S$. Suppose each of the six modules $C_i,D_i$, $0\le i\le2$, is projective. No exactness at $C_2,D_2$ or further degrees is required. There are augmentation-preserving chain maps through degree $2$ between these complexes lifting $1_S$. For every right $R$-module $N$, any such comparison induces the same isomorphism of abelian groups
$$H_1(N\otimes_R C_\bullet)\ \cong\ H_1(N\otimes_R D_\bullet).$$
These isomorphisms are inverse under reversing the complexes, compose for a third such complex, and are natural in homomorphisms of right coefficient modules. In particular a supplied augmentation-preserving chain map through degree $2$ induces this isomorphism; its construction need not be the one chosen in the proof. Tensoring is not assumed exact, and $N$ need not be flat. This is a comparison of supplied algebraic complexes, not an assertion that a presentation complex is a deformation retract or a homotopy-equivalent spine of another space.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on an arbitrary space $X$. For a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, write $v_i=\sigma(e_i)$ and $\gamma_{01}^\sigma(t)=\sigma(1-t,t,0,\ldots,0)$.

The **intrinsic singular local chain group** is
$$C_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0}.$$
Write an element of the $\sigma$-summand as $m\sigma$. Its boundary is
$$\partial(m\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}(m)(\sigma\delta_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^im(\sigma\delta_i),$$
and the boundary of a zero-simplex is zero. The exceptional zeroth face transports its coefficient from the old first vertex $v_0$ to the new first vertex $v_1$; all other faces keep $v_0$.

The **intrinsic singular local cochain group** is the product
$$C^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\prod_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0},$$
so a cochain $\varphi$ assigns $\varphi(\sigma)\in\mathcal L_{v_0}$ to every simplex, with no finite-support requirement. Its positive coboundary, consistent with [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]], is
$$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(\sigma\delta_0)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\delta_i).$$
Now the exceptional face value is transported back from $v_1$ to $v_0$.

For $A\subseteq X$, restrict $\mathcal L$ along the inclusion and set
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)/C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L),\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=\ker\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)\to C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L)\bigr).$$

For a connected CW complex with chosen basepoint $x$, universal cover $\widetilde X$, $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and base fiber $M=\mathcal L_x$ carrying $g m=T_{\bar g}m$, the equivalent universal-cover models are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
The first tensor product is the balanced construction of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] using the right action of [[def-right-group-ring-action-on-the-chains-of-a-universal-cover]]. For the second, convert that right chain module to a left one by
$$g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}.$$
Thus an equivariant cochain has the correctly typed rule
$$\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c),$$
not a module-Hom between one right and one left module.

The intrinsic/tensor identification sends $\widetilde\sigma\otimes m$ to the simplex $\sigma=p\widetilde\sigma$ with coefficient obtained by transporting $m$ along the path represented by $\widetilde\sigma(e_0)$. If $\widetilde\sigma$ is replaced by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$, that path is changed by the loop $g^{-1}$ and the coefficient becomes the transport of $gm$, exactly the balanced relation. The analogous statement for cochains proves the displayed equivariance rule. These maps respect the two boundary formulas term by term.

The **cellular local chain and cochain groups** of a connected CW complex are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
For a CW pair, quotient by the lifted subcomplex before tensoring and use the corresponding relative cellular complex before applying equivariant Hom. For a disconnected CW complex, take the direct sum of chain complexes and the degreewise product of cochain complexes over its components. Universal-cover coordinates of this componentwise description require a supplied basepoint in each component; the intrinsic complexes require no simultaneous basepoint choice and remain the definition when no such family is supplied.

The next lemma proves square-zero and independence of supplied lift bases. Empty spaces and negative degrees give zero groups, the zero local system gives the zero complexes, and constant systems reduce to the ordinary formulas because every transport is the identity.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

Let $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$ be a map of pairs.

1. A coefficient morphism $\eta:\mathcal L\to f^*\mathcal K$ induces
   $$f_*:H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\longrightarrow H_n(Y,B;\mathcal K).$$
2. A coefficient morphism $\theta:f^*\mathcal K\to\mathcal L$ induces
   $$f^*:H^n(Y,B;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$

At a fixed space, both theories are covariant in coefficient morphisms. These maps preserve identities and composition. If $H:f_0\simeq f_1$ is a homotopy of pair maps, transport along $t\mapsto H(x,t)$ gives $\tau_H:f_0^*\mathcal K\to f_1^*\mathcal K$; the homology maps agree when $\eta_1=\tau_H\eta_0$, and the cohomology maps agree when $\theta_0=\theta_1\tau_H$.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic different from $2$, and let $L,M\in SL_2(F)$ commute. Write $t=\operatorname{tr}M$ and suppose $\Delta=t^2-4\ne0$. Give the torus $T^2$ an ordered pair of based oriented generating loops $(\lambda,\mu)$, and give its adjoint local system intrinsic monodromies $P=\operatorname{Ad}L$ and $Q=\operatorname{Ad}M$ on $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(F)$. Here monodromy acts on column coefficient vectors on the left. Set
$$v=M-\frac t2 I,\qquad W=\{X\in V:\operatorname{tr}(vX)=0\}.$$
Then $V=Fv\oplus W$, both summands are preserved by $P,Q$, and $P,Q$ are the identity on $Fv$. There is an explicit split chain model
$$0\longrightarrow V\xrightarrow{d_2}V\oplus V\xrightarrow{d_1}V\longrightarrow0,$$
where $d_2z=((I-Q)z,(P-I)z)$ and $d_1(x,y)=(P-I)x+(Q-I)y$, in the ordered edge coordinates $(\lambda,\mu)$. Its $W$ subcomplex is contractible, so
$$H_0(T^2;V)=F[v],\qquad H_1(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes\lambda]\oplus F[v\otimes\mu],\qquad H_2(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes[T^2]].$$
In particular the two displayed peripheral classes are an actual basis, without imposing any norm-one normalization on $v$. The splitting, contraction and classes commute with field extensions and simultaneous conjugation of $L,M$. All their matrix entries are rational expressions in the entries of $L,M$, with denominators powers of $2$ and $\Delta$. This assertion concerns boundary-torus homology only: it makes no claim about the rank of its inclusion into the homology of a knot exterior.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link (a finite disjoint union of oriented smoothly embedded circles,
[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]) with $r\ge1$ components,
and let $X_L:=S^3\setminus L$. Then $X_L$ is a connected smooth $3$-manifold
without boundary, and in particular is path-connected, locally path-connected
and semilocally simply connected; moreover $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a
finite CW complex
([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]). Consequently the
covering-space classification
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]) applies to $X_L$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$

Their overlap is an annulus, and its generator maps to the attaching word in the old complex. These are open sets also for a noninjective attaching map, as can be checked on the old complex and the disk before taking the adjunction quotient. current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $X$ be a one-dimensional irreducible component of its $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety whose peripheral image is a curve in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$. With Bénard–Florens–Rodau's variable order $A_K(L,M)$ and their slope convention, on the admissible smooth locus where the displayed derivatives are nonzero,
$$s_K(\rho)=-\frac{M}{L}\frac{\partial_M A_K}{\partial_L A_K}.$$
At an ideal point of the curve, if the associated Culler-Shalen surface has boundary slope $r$ measured by $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ with $r=b/a$, the limiting Bénard–Florens–Rodau slope is $-r$.

e0$, the rational adjoint-twisted slope is
$$s_K=- rac{M}{L} rac{\partial_M A_X}{\partial_L A_X}.$$
If $x$ is an ideal point of the smooth projective completion of this curve and the associated Culler-Shalen construction yields an essential surface of boundary slope $r$ in the fixed meridian-longitude convention, the limiting slope at $x$ is $-r$.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ have admissible adjoint local system, and let $v_\rho$ be a nonzero peripheral-adjoint-invariant vector for which $[v_\rho\otimes\lambda],[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$ form the specified ordered basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$. If a generator of the one-dimensional kernel of inclusion is $a[v_\rho\otimes\lambda]+b[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$, the **Bénard–Florens–Rodau slope** is $s_K(\rho)=-b/a\in\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$, with $a=0$ interpreted as $\infty$. Rescaling $v_\rho$ or the kernel generator does not change this projective ratio. A rational function on an irreducible character component means an element of its function field, the fraction field of its coordinate domain. A projective-valued rational function means a point of the projective line over that field; it may be identically $\infty$. The slope's rational extension has this projective meaning. Unless its generic value is $\infty$, it is an ordinary rational function, whose individual infinite values are poles. Its rational extension is not a value assigned to every singular or inadmissible character.

Assume full AC. Let $E$ be the compact exterior of a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Let $X$ be an irreducible one-dimensional component of its complex $SL_2$ character variety. Fix a one-dimensional peripheral eigenvalue-image component $Y$ arising from $X$, with coordinates $(M,L)$ ordered as (meridian,longitude), and an irreducible Laurent equation $P(M,L)=0$ for $Y$. Write $K=\mathbb C(X)$.

There is a finite extension $F/K$ with an actual generic representation $\rho:\pi_1(E)\to SL_2(F)$ and a choice of common peripheral eigenline whose eigenvalues are $M,L\in F^*$. These give the specified generic point of $Y$. Its actual intrinsic adjoint peripheral homology has a two-dimensional boundary basis ordered (longitude,meridian) and a one-dimensional inclusion kernel. With $\delta\in\{\lambda,\mu\}$ having distinct peripheral eigenvalues, set $u=\rho(\delta)-\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\delta))I/2$. In that basis its kernel is exactly
$$\ker\left\{F^2\longrightarrow\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C},\quad (a,b)\longmapsto a\,\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}+b\,\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right\}.$$
The two displayed differentials are not both zero. Thus its projective slope, with convention $s=-b/a$ for the kernel line, is
$$s=\left[\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}:\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right]=[-M P_M:L P_L]\ \in\mathbb P^1(F).$$
A ratio of one-forms here means their coordinate pair in any nonzero basis of the one-dimensional $F$-space $\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C}$. The result is independent of that basis, the finite field model, the common eigenline and simultaneous conjugation, and is defined over $K$. It includes zero when $\mathrm dL=0$ and infinity when $\mathrm dM=0$. In particular a nonconstant meridian eigenvalue is not assumed.

This is an identity of rational projective maps. It agrees with the actual specialized homology slope on a nonempty dense rank-chart open. At every point where the rational extension and the peripheral restriction are evaluated and $(P_M,P_L)\ne(0,0)$, its projective value is $[-M P_M:L P_L]$; when $P_L\ne0$ this is the ordinary value $-M P_M/(L P_L)$. For the square-free ordinary A-polynomial, replacing $P$ by the full polynomial gives the same ratio at a point where its gradient is nonzero. No assertion that all specialized exterior homology ranks are constant outside that open, nor any ideal-point tree or essential-surface construction, is part of this lemma.

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Assume also Dependent Choice for the cited minimal-prime existence theorem. Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the Nullstellensatz route. Every affine algebraic set $X$ has a finite irredundant decomposition into nonempty irreducible closed subsets, unique up to permutation. These are its maximal irreducible closed subsets. The empty set has the empty decomposition.

Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Then
$$ \dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K. $$

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with exterior $E_K$, positive meridian $\mu$, and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Define $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ to consist of all pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common invariant line on which $\rho(\mu)$ acts by $M$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ acts by $L$. The Zariski closure is the smallest Zariski-closed algebraic subset containing $\mathcal E_K$; let $V_K$ be the union of its one-dimensional irreducible components, where an irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed subset. Zero-dimensional image components are omitted. The **ordinary A-polynomial** $A_K(M,L)$ is the Laurent polynomial generating the vanishing ideal of $V_K$, chosen square-free (no repeated irreducible factors) and with primitive integer coefficients (their greatest common divisor is one). It is determined up to multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$ for $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. Its reduced curve includes the abelian component $L=1$; equivalently, its representative in $\mathbb Z[M,L]$ is divisible by $L-1$.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen compact exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$. A simple closed curve on a surface is **essential** if it is not null-homotopic there. A surface $S\subset E_K$ is properly embedded if $S\cap\partial E_K=\partial S$ and its interior lies in the interior of $E_K$. It is **incompressible** if it has no embedded disk with interior disjoint from $S$ and essential boundary in $S$; it is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no embedded disk whose boundary is the union of an arc in $S$ that does not cut off a disk and an arc in $\partial E_K$. A **boundary slope** of $K$ is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ that occurs as the boundary of a properly embedded, orientable, incompressible, boundary-incompressible surface. Using the positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$ as a homology basis, a primitive class $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ has slope $b/a\in\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}$, with $a=0$ interpreted as $\infty$. A boundary slope is **strict** if it has a realizing orientable, incompressible, boundary-incompressible surface which is not a fiber of any locally trivial fibration $E_K\to S^1$; a fiber is the inverse image of a point under that bundle projection.

derivations.claim: **The image curve is an actual A-component.** This instantiation requires excluding a larger peripheral image component. Take the actual generic matrices on an irreducible common-eigenline incidence chart of [F4], over its finitely generated function field $F$. A two-dimensional image would make $M,L$ algebraically independent and the meridian matrix nonparabolic. Over this field the trace form, cap boundary identity and pair exact sequence in [F3] give boundary dimension two and $2=\dim\ker i_*+\operatorname{rank}i_*=2\operatorname{rank}i_*$; hence its kernel is a line. Every $\mathbb C$-derivation $D$ of $F$ differentiates the actual relators to a cocycle. The explicit word/eigenbasis calculation in [F3] makes $(DL/L,DM/M)$ annihilate that SAME line. Extend $M,L$ to a finite transcendence basis and take its two coordinate derivations. Each extends through the finite algebraic extension to $F$ by $D\alpha=-(Dp)(\alpha)/p'(\alpha)$ at a minimal polynomial $p$; characteristic zero makes the denominator nonzero. Their two logarithmic pairs are independent, a contradiction. Generically reducible representations instead have $L=1$ by knot abelianization and cannot supply a two-dimensional image. Thus every peripheral-image component has dimension at most one. The closed irreducible nonconstant image curve $Y$ in the Statement is contained in their finite union, so it equals one of the one-dimensional components: a proper closed subset of an irreducible affine curve has dimension zero. Consequently [F5] supplies its defining Laurent factor $P$ in the full ordinary polynomial. No omitted two-dimensional component is presumed absent merely from the A-polynomial Definition.

**Variable order and sign.** Keep $M$ the meridian eigenvalue and $L$ the longitude eigenvalue. Writing $A_{\mathrm{BFR}}(L,M)=A_{\mathrm{library}}(M,L)$ only changes the order in which the arguments are displayed. Differentiation with respect to the NAMED variables therefore gives the same meridian derivative and the same longitude derivative, not their reciprocal. In the basis [F2], the generic kernel of $(a,b)\mapsto a\,dL/L+b\,dM/M$ has generator $(-dM/M,dL/L)$, so its slope is $(dL/L)/(dM/M)$. This fixes both the sign and the order of the quotient. A common invariant-vector rescaling changes neither coordinate ratio. Swapping the common eigenline inverts $M,L$ and changes both logarithmic differentials by minus one, preserving the projective ratio; [F3] already proves model/conjugation independence.

**Full-polynomial versus component derivatives.** Write $A=uPB$, where $u$ is a Laurent unit and $B$ is the product of the other distinct factors. At a point of $Y$ with both full derivatives nonzero, $B$ cannot vanish: if another factor vanished, every term of either product derivative would contain a vanishing factor, giving zero. On $P=0$ one has $A_M=uB P_M$ and $A_L=uB P_L$. Thus the two component derivatives are nonzero there and the common nonzero factor $uB$ cancels from their quotient. Multiplication of the whole representative by any further Laurent unit has the same effect, since its differentiated unit term is multiplied by $A=0$. This also proves that the stated derivative locus is intrinsic and avoids intersections of distinct peripheral factors. It does not exclude an extra character component with CONSTANT peripheral image at the same point.

**The complete rational instantiation.** The component formula in [F1] is $s^{\mathrm{rat}}=[-MP_M:LP_L]$. Combining steps1.2 and2.1 gives exactly $s^{\mathrm{rat}}=-M A_M/(L A_L)$ in the native BFR variable order wherever the displayed derivatives are nonzero. In particular it is finite there, and the projective extension still retains zero/infinity away from that affine locus. This instantiates the proved component theorem with the FULL square-free ordinary polynomial without changing either convention. It is so far an identity of the rational extension, not a proof about all exceptional actual kernels.

**The actual exceptional-point clause uses the external theorem.** A reducible representation has longitude eigenvalue $L=1$ because its diagonal characters factor through the knot abelianization. Since $A=(L-1)Q$, its meridian derivative is $A_M=(L-1)Q_M$ and vanishes at every such peripheral point. The stipulated nonzero-derivative locus therefore contains only irreducible characters. At every actual admissible smooth point of that locus, including points outside the local rank chart, apply the ALL-character formula of the external Theorem 4.1 in [L1], in the actual homology convention of its Definitions 3.1–3.2. Steps1.2 and2.1 identify the named variables, signs and full square-free representative. This proves the first clause at its entire original locus; the exceptional specialization is supplied externally, not by a density argument.

**Actual homology on the proved dense open.** Intersect the nonempty rank-chart open supplied by [F3] with the original smooth/derivative locus, whenever that latter locus is nonempty. The component is irreducible, so this intersection is dense and nonempty. At every point there, the finite homology specialization in [F3] identifies the rational line with the actual ordered peripheral inclusion kernel. Thus step3.1 proves the ACTUAL displayed formula on this open. This uses the direct generic/rank-chart construction, not an unverified extension of the separate rationality lemma beyond its stated dense scheme-smooth hypothesis. It does not assert that every smooth admissible point belongs to the chosen rank chart.

**The full stipulated ideal-point clause.** The curve in the preceding clause is the peripheral eigenvalue curve $Y$. Use its normalized smooth completion, exactly as in [F1], rather than replacing it by an arbitrary character ideal point with affine peripheral image. At its stipulated ideal point the actual local DVR has nonzero valuation pair $(v(L),v(M))$, and the finite representation-field valuation extends with one positive ramification factor. For a boundary circle $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ of the actual associated Culler–Shalen construction, [F1]'s inverse-image midpoint and boundary-preserving compression argument gives $a v(L)+b v(M)=0$. The logarithmic projective limit in [F1] is $[v(L):v(M)]=[-b:a]$. By [F2] this is $-b/a=-r$, including zero and infinity in the projective convention. This proves the ENTIRE conditional ideal-point clause: the construction/surface is stipulated by the original conditional, and no existence theorem for an arbitrary unrelated surface is imported or required.

Step4.2 already proves the full conditional ideal-point assertion with the stipulated associated surface; [L1]'s Theorem 5.2 independently gives the same valuation and sign convention. Together with step5.1 this establishes both original clauses without narrowing the admissible smooth locus or adding scheme-smoothness.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

citations.quote:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

Let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular diagrams of nonempty oriented links related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move, with the marked point on an unchanged exterior arc and carried to the corresponding point. The normalized integral signed Khovanov complexes have explicit bigraded chain homotopy equivalences whose maps and inverse homotopies commute with the marked actions $X_p,X_{p'}$. Consequently the quotients $C(D)/\operatorname{im}X_p$ and $C(D')/\operatorname{im}X_{p'}$, with their reduced quantum degree $j-1$, are bigraded chain homotopy equivalent. The conclusion holds over $\mathbb F_2$ by reducing these same integral formulas. It permits arbitrary other link components and arbitrary exterior connectivity. This local statement does not assert a relative movie theorem or canonical identifications between different move sequences.

Let $D$ be a finite regular diagram of an oriented link and let $p,q$ be any two points of $D$ away from crossings, possibly on different link components. Over $\mathbb F_2$, the reduced Khovanov cohomology groups defined using $p$ and $q$ are isomorphic as bigraded vector spaces. The isomorphism need not be canonical; no diagram-change invariance is asserted here.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with a marked point $p$ away from crossings, and let $C(D;\mathbb F_2)$ be its normalized Khovanov cochain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from the algebra $\mathcal A=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$ with $\deg_q(1)=1$ and $\deg_q(X)=-1$. On each resolution state, let $X_p$ multiply by $X$ on the circle containing $p$ and act as the identity on the other circle factors. Define the reduced complex by $\widetilde C(D,p)=C(D;\mathbb F_2)/\operatorname{im}X_p$, with the surviving based-circle label $1$ assigned reduced quantum degree $0$ by the shift $\widetilde j=j-1$. Its cohomology is $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p;\mathbb F_2)$. The basepoint may lie on any component; for a link, independence of the chosen component is a separate theorem.

Such an arc exists: the move models contain a continuing strand meeting the boundary of their disk, and a closed regular link diagram continues that strand outside the disk. current_manifest_record.title: Heegaard Floer plus and infinity groups and absolute grading for rational homology spheres
current_manifest_record.statement:
A rational homology sphere is a closed connected oriented three-manifold $Y$ with $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. Let $\mathfrak t$ be a Spin$^c$ structure on $Y$, meaning a principal $\mathrm{Spin}^c(3)$ lift of the oriented frame bundle. A pointed Heegaard diagram for $(Y,\mathfrak t)$ consists of a closed oriented surface $\Sigma$ of genus $g$, two systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_g)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_g)$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves which bound complete disk systems in the two genus-$g$ handlebodies of a Heegaard splitting of $Y$, with every $\alpha_i$ transverse to every $\beta_j$, and a basepoint $z\in\Sigma\setminus(\boldsymbol\alpha\cup\boldsymbol\beta)$; the diagram is restricted to the generators assigned to $\mathfrak t$. Compactness of $\Sigma$ makes the transverse intersection set finite. A periodic domain is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of attaching curves. The diagram is strongly admissible for $\mathfrak t$ when every nonzero periodic domain $P$ with $n_z(P)=0$ and $\langle c_1(\mathfrak t),[P]\rangle\ge0$ has at least one positive and one negative region coefficient.

For such a diagram, put $\mathbb T_\alpha=\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_g$ and $\mathbb T_\beta=\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_g$ in $\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)=\Sigma^g/S_g$. A generator is an intersection point $\mathbf x\in\mathbb T_\alpha\cap\mathbb T_\beta$. A Whitney disk class $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of disks in $\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)$ with boundary arcs on the two product tori and endpoints $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$; its Maslov index is $\mu(\phi)$ and its local multiplicity at $z$ is $n_z(\phi)$. For a regular almost-complex datum for which every relevant count is finite and the disk-count operator squares to zero, define $CF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)$ over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ on generators $[\mathbf x,i]$, $i\in\mathbb Z$, with differential
$$
\partial^\infty[\mathbf x,i]=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\\\mu(\phi)=1,\ n_z(\phi)\ge0}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)[\mathbf y,i-n_z(\phi)].
$$
Here $\mathbb F_2$ is the field with two elements, $U[\mathbf x,i]=[\mathbf x,i-1]$, and $\#_2$ is the finite count modulo two. The submodule generated by $[\mathbf x,i]$ with $i<0$ is $CF^-(Y,\mathfrak t)$, $CF^+(Y,\mathfrak t)=CF^\infty/CF^-$, and $HF^\infty$ and $HF^+$ denote their homology when the differential is established. Relative Maslov gradings are fixed by the Fredholm index and the shift under $U$ is $-2$.

When the standard absolute rational Maslov grading is available, normalize it so that the generator of $HF^\infty(S^3)$ has degree zero. For a smooth Spin$^c$ cobordism $(W,\mathfrak s)$ between rational homology spheres, the induced map is assigned degree shift
$$
\frac{\langle c_1(\mathfrak s)^2\rangle-2\chi(W)-3\sigma(W)}{4},
$$
where $c_1(\mathfrak s)$ is the first Chern class, $\chi(W)$ is Euler characteristic, $\sigma(W)$ is the signature, and its square is evaluated using the rational intersection form of $W$. This is a convention for a Floer package when constructed; it asserts neither existence of generic regular data nor that the disk-count differential squares to zero. Heegaard invariance, the absolute grading on general $(Y,\mathfrak t)$, and cobordism-map properties are separate claims.

derivations.claim: The minus chain complex is finite free over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, with generators $[\mathbf x,-1]$ for the finitely many intersection points in $\mathfrak t$. Its homology is finitely generated and its localization is the infinity homology, since localization is exact and the localized differentials are identical. Thus the graded image $L$ of $HF^-\to R\rho$ is nonzero. Its degrees are bounded above by the largest degree of a minus-chain generator. The set of integers $j$ with $U^j\rho\in L$ is consequently nonempty, bounded below, and closed under addition of nonnegative integers. If $a$ is its minimum, that set is exactly $\{a,a+1,\ldots\}$. Every homogeneous element of the Laurent tower is a monomial multiple of $\rho$, and the image is graded; hence $L=U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$.

The long exact sequence of the actual short exact sequence $CF^-\to CF^\infty\to CF^+$ identifies the image in plus homology, with its grading, as $R\rho/U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have exponents $j<a$, so their least degree is $\deg\rho-2(a-1)$, attained at $U^{a-1}\rho$. Sending the standard tower element $U^k$ to $U^{k+a-1}\rho$ identifies the image with $R/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ shifted by this least degree. Multiplying any individual element sufficiently many times by $U$ kills it, while decreasing exponents supplies a preimage under any power of $U$. This proves all the tower assertions.

The pointed-move maps preserve absolute grading and the minus/infinity/plus exact sequence, so they carry $L$ onto the corresponding image lattice and induce grading-preserving tower isomorphisms. Therefore the least degree is independent of the diagram and auxiliary data. Choosing $U^b\rho$ instead changes $a$ to $a-b$ and $\deg\rho$ to $\deg\rho-2b$, leaving that degree unchanged. In the genus-zero diagram of $S^3$ there is one generator $[\mathbf x_0,0]$ of degree zero, no nonconstant disks, and minus lattice $U\mathbb F_2[U][\mathbf x_0,0]$. Here $a=1$, so the least grading is zero.

citations.quote:
Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and connected rational homology sphere boundary $Y$. Choose a smoothly embedded closed four-ball $D$ in its interior and put $W=B\setminus\operatorname{int}D$. With the induced orientation,
$$\partial W=-S^3\sqcup Y.$$
The manifold $W$ is connected, $H_j(W;\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Q$ for $j=0,3$ and zero otherwise, and both inclusions $S^3\to W$, $Y\to W$ induce isomorphisms on rational homology in every degree. Its rational homological Euler characteristic is zero and its rational intersection module $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$ is zero. Consequently its signature is zero, and the square of every covector with respect to that zero intersection module is zero. These assertions hold also for the reversed cobordism $-W$ from $Y$ to $S^3$, and use no choice principle.

The last square assertion refers to the intersection-form covector convention; the lemma supplies no Floer cobordism map, absolute grading formula, or Spin-c existence theorem.

For a closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere and each Spin$^c$ structure, the pointed minus, infinity and plus Heegaard Floer complexes over $\mathbb F_2$ admit an absolute rational grading, independent of the surgery presentation, extending their relative Maslov grading, with $\deg U=-2$ and $\deg[\mathbf x_0,0]=0$ for the standard generator of $S^3$. Heegaard-move isomorphisms preserve this grading and commute with the minus/infinity/plus sequence. A smooth connected Spin$^c$ cobordism between such manifolds induces infinity and plus maps, compatible with that sequence, homogeneous of degree $(c_1(\mathfrak s)^2-2\chi(W)-3\sigma(W))/4$. These maps are obtained from the fixed-Spin$^c$ triangle counts and the one- and three-handle maps, independently of their handle presentation. Here the Chern square uses the rational relative lift of the boundary-torsion Chern class.

For every closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere $Y$ and Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, the absolutely graded infinity group $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t;\mathbb F_2)$ is a single free Laurent tower. If $W:Y_0\to Y_1$ is a smooth connected rational homology cobordism between rational homology spheres, then for each fixed Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak s$ on $W$ the infinity map is a degree-zero isomorphism. The corresponding plus map commutes with the infinity-to-plus maps. This conclusion concerns each individual extending Spin$^c$ structure, including nonprimitive handle attachments and torsion labels.

For every closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere $Y$ and Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, the standard Heegaard Floer groups $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)$ and $HF^+(Y,\mathfrak t)$ constructed from admissible pointed Heegaard diagrams are independent, up to grading-preserving isomorphism, of the diagram and regular auxiliary data. The image of $HF^\infty\to HF^+$ is a graded plus tower, isomorphic as an $\mathbb F_2[U]$-module to $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ with an absolute rational grading shift and with $U$ of degree $-2$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have a least grading, and that least grading is independent of the diagram and auxiliary data. Every tower element is $U$-torsion and is divisible by every power of $U$. In the standard normalization the least grading for $(S^3,\mathfrak t_0)$ is zero.

Put $R=\mathbb F_2[U]$, with $\deg U=-2$. For $i=1,2$ let $\Lambda_i=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ with $\deg_i U^n=a_i-2n$, $a_i\in\mathbb Q$, and let $\pi_i:\Lambda_i\to M_i$ be degree-zero $R$-linear maps to graded $R$-modules with nonzero proper kernels. Let $d_i$ be the least degree of a nonzero homogeneous element of $\operatorname{im}\pi_i$.

Suppose $F:\Lambda_1\to\Lambda_2$ is an $R$-linear isomorphism homogeneous of degree $\Delta\in\mathbb Q$, and $G:M_1\to M_2$ is an $R$-linear map of that same degree such that $G\pi_1=\pi_2F$. Then
$$d_2\ge d_1+\Delta.$$
If there are also maps in the reverse direction of degree $-\Delta$ satisfying the same hypotheses and commuting with $\pi_1,\pi_2$, then $d_2=d_1+\Delta$; those reverse maps need not be inverses of $F,G$. In particular, commuting comparisons in both directions with degree zero force equal bottom degrees. These are choice-free algebraic statements; no Floer map, Laurent-tower hypothesis or geometric degree formula is supplied by this lemma.

derivations.claim: The two boundary inclusions are rational homology isomorphisms and $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)=0$. In particular the square of the Chern class is zero, and $\chi(W)=\sigma(W)=0$. The same assertions hold for the reverse cobordism from $Y$ to $S^3$. For each of the fixed induced Spin$^c$ structures, the constructed infinity map is an isomorphism with degree $(0-2\cdot0-3\cdot0)/4=0$, and the corresponding plus map commutes with the infinity-to-plus projection. This uses the individual fixed-structure conclusion, including torsion extensions.

Apply the supplied commuting-square comparison first to $W:S^3\to Y$ and then to its reverse $Y\to S^3$. The degree-zero isomorphisms give respectively $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge d(S^3)=0$ and $d(S^3)=0\ge d(Y,\mathfrak t)$. These are exactly the two stated inequalities in both orientations.

current_manifest_record.statement:
Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and connected rational homology sphere boundary $Y$. The coefficient sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ gives an isomorphism $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. Define the cohomological linking pairing by
$$\lambda_Y(x,y)=\langle\beta^{-1}(x)\smile y,[Y]\rangle\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z.$$
Under Poincare duality $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, this pairing agrees, up to the global orientation sign, with the chain torsion linking pairing: for torsion classes represented by oriented 1-cycles $C,D$, choose $n>0$ and an integral 2-chain $F$ with $\partial F=nC$, and set $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\mathbin{\cdot}D)/n\pmod{\mathbb Z}$. The two conventions therefore have the same annihilator subgroups.
Let $M$ be the image of restriction $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and $M^\perp=\{x:\lambda_Y(m,x)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. Then the boundary Spin$^c$ structures extending over $B$ form one affine coset of $M$, the pairing is nonsingular, $M=M^\perp$, and $|M|^2=|H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)|$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For every subspace $A\subseteq X$ and abelian group $G$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{j}H^n(X;G)\xrightarrow{r}H^n(A;G)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{n+1}(X,A;G)\to\cdots.$$
Here $j$ comes from including the relative cochains, $r$ is restriction, and the connector sends a cocycle class $[a]$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, for any cochain extension $\widetilde a$ of $a$ to $X$. Negative groups are zero, so the sequence begins $0\to H^0(X,A;G)\to H^0(X;G)\to H^0(A;G)$.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice from [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let

$$
0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{q}C\longrightarrow0
$$

be a short exact sequence of abelian groups. Applying singular cochains degree
by degree gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes: injectivity on the
left follows from injectivity of $i$, and surjectivity on the right follows as
follows. A cochain is a function on the set $S_n(X)$ of singular $n$-simplices
by [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. For a $C$-valued
cochain $c$, AC is used exactly once to choose, simultaneously for every
$s\in S_n(X)$, an element of the nonempty fibre $q^{-1}(c(s))$. The resulting
function is a $B$-valued cochain $b$ with $q_*b=c$.

For a cocycle $c\in C^n(X;C)$ choose such a lift $b$. Since
$q_*(\delta b)=\delta c=0$, exactness gives a unique
$a\in C^{n+1}(X;A)$ satisfying $i_*a=\delta b$. The **Bockstein connecting
operation** is

$$
\beta\colon H^n(X;C)\longrightarrow H^{n+1}(X;A),\qquad \beta[c]=[a].
$$

This is the coefficient-sequence analogue of the cochain connector in
[[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-cohomology]]. Its independence
of $b$ and $c$ is proved in the next lemma.

For an integer $m\geq1$, two Bocksteins must be distinguished:

- the **integral Bockstein**
  $\widetilde\beta\colon H^n(X;\mathbb Z/m)\to H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z)$ comes
  from $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/m\to0$;
- the **mod-$m$ Bockstein**
  $\beta\colon H^n(X;\mathbb Z/m)\to H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z/m)$ comes from
  $0\to\mathbb Z/m\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z/m^2\to\mathbb Z/m\to0$.

In these two cyclic sequences, least nonnegative residue representatives give
the required cochain lift without AC. If $X$ is empty, or if $n<0$, the source
cochain group is zero and the lift is unique. When $m=1$ both cyclic
Bocksteins have zero source and hence are the zero operation. The mod-$m$
target is also zero, whereas the integral target $H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z)$ need
not vanish.

Assume AC and the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-bockstein-connecting-operation]]. The class $\beta[c]$ is independent
of the chosen $B$-cochain lift of $c$ and of the cocycle representing $[c]$.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume AC. Let $E\to X$ be an oriented real vector bundle over a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff compactly generated weak Hausdorff space of CW homotopy type, and suppose one numerable Spin$^c$ lift of its oriented frame bundle is given. Among numerable Spin$^c$ lifts of that same frame bundle, isomorphism classes form a torsor for $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$: tensoring a lift by a complex line bundle defines a free and transitive action, identified with $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ by the first Chern class. For a continuous map $f:X\to Z$ between bases with these hypotheses and an oriented bundle $E_Z\to Z$, the pullback action on lifts of $f^*E_Z\to X$ is equivariant for $f^*:H^2(Z;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with nonempty connected boundary $Y$, a specified Riemannian metric, and a Spin$^c(4)$ lift $P$ of its oriented tangent frame bundle. Give $Y$ the outward-normal-first orientation. The outward unit normal identifies $TM|_Y$ with $\mathbb R\oplus TY$. Restricting $P$ to $Y$ and reducing to frames with first vector that normal constructs a Spin$^c(3)$ lift $\operatorname{res}P$ of $TY$.

This construction induces a bijection between Spin$^c$ lift classes of $\mathbb R\oplus TY$ and those of $TY$, inverse to extension by $\operatorname{Spin}^c(3)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spin}^c(4)$. For every complex line bundle $L\to M$ there is a natural isomorphism
$$\operatorname{res}(P\otimes L)\cong(\operatorname{res}P)\otimes L|_Y.$$
Consequently, with the actual $H^2$ torsor actions, boundary restriction is equivariant for $H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. The determinant line of $\operatorname{res}P$ is the restriction of that of $P$; its change under a line twist is twice the line's first Chern class, while the torsor action is by the line's first Chern class itself. No Spin$^c$ existence or Floer map is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$. Then the oriented tangent frame bundle of $B$ admits a Spin$^c$ lift.

derivations.claim: Since $B$ has finite CW type by [F1] and has zero positive rational homology, each $H_i(B;\mathbb Z)$ for $i>0$ is finite. Put $a=|H_1(B;\mathbb Z)|$ and $b=|H_2(B;\mathbb Z)|$. The UCT [F3] gives $|H^2(B;\mathbb Z)|=a$ and $|H^3(B;\mathbb Z)|=b$, because the Hom terms from finite groups vanish and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb Z/m,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/m$. Poincare-Lefschetz duality [F2] gives $|H^2(B,Y;\mathbb Z)|=b$ and $|H^3(B,Y;\mathbb Z)|=a$.

In the pair sequence, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$ because $Y$ is a rational homology sphere and its first integral cohomology is $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y),\mathbb Z)$. Thus $H^2(B,Y)\to H^2(B)$ is injective. Also $H^3(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, so the map from the finite group $H^3(B;\mathbb Z)$ to $H^3(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; exactness makes $H^3(B,Y)\to H^3(B)$ surjective. It follows that the restriction image $M$ has order $a/b$, and that $H^2(Y)/M$ has order $a/b$. Hence $|H^2(Y)|=(a/b)^2$ and $|M|^2=|H^2(Y)|=|H_1(Y)|$, the last equality following from UCT and Poincare duality for the rational homology sphere.

For any $m\in M$, choose $u\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$ restricting to $m$, and let $c$ be an integral cocycle representing $u$. Since $H^2(B;\mathbb Q)=0$, the rational cocycle $c$ is $\delta q$ for a rational $1$-cochain $q$; reducing $q$ modulo $\mathbb Z$ gives a cocycle $v\in H^1(B;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with $\beta(v)=u$. It is unique because $H^1(B;\mathbb Q)=0$. Restriction of this cochain lift gives $\beta(v|_Y)=m$. For $Y$, both $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)$ and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)$ vanish, so the same coefficient sequence proves that $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism. By UCT, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$; by Poincare duality, $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. Cup evaluation is therefore the perfect character-evaluation pairing under these identifications. If $X,D$ are torsion $1$-cycles with $mX=\partial F$, the cochain represented by the rational bounding chain $F/m$, reduced modulo integral cochains, is $\beta^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}^{-1}[X])$; its evaluation against $\mathrm{PD}^{-1}[D]$ is $F\cdot D/m$ modulo $\mathbb Z$. Thus this cohomological formula agrees with the chain linking form up to the global orientation sign, which does not change annihilators.

If $x\in M$ is the restriction of $w\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$, naturality of cup product [F5] gives $\lambda_Y(m,x)=\langle v|_Y\smile w|_Y,[Y]\rangle=\langle v\smile w,i_*[Y]\rangle=0$, since $i_*[Y]=0$ in $H_3(B;\mathbb Z)$ by the homology pair sequence: $[Y]$ is the boundary of the relative fundamental class $[B,Y]$. Therefore $M\subseteq M^\perp$. For a nonsingular finite pairing on a group $G$, restriction of characters $G\to\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is onto. To see this, extend a character from a subgroup $H$ one generator $g$ at a time: if the least $n>0$ with $ng\in H$ is fixed, choose $z\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ with $nz=f(ng)$ (possible because multiplication by $n$ is onto), and set $f'(h+kg)=f(h)+kz$; the relation $ng\in H$ makes $f'$ well defined. Since $G$ is finite this process terminates. Hence $|M^\perp|=|G|/|M|$. Apply this with $G=H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $|M^\perp|=|M|$. Thus $M=M^\perp$.

By [F7], choose a Spin$^c$ structure on $B$. Then [F6] makes the Spin$^c$ structures on $B$ an affine $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$-space. Restriction is equivariant, so the image of this nonempty affine space is one affine coset of the image subgroup $M$. This proves the extension-set assertion. If $M=0$, the same sequence gives $|H^2(Y)|=1$, so the trivial subgroup is its own annihilator; the empty-boundary case is excluded by the connected-boundary hypothesis.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

Assume AC. If $D\subset B^4$ is a smooth proper embedded disk, the connected double cover $W\to B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented smooth $4$-manifold with $H_i(W;\mathbb F_2)=0$ for $i>0$, hence $H_i(W;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $i>0$. Its boundary is the double cover of $S^3$ branched over $\partial D$.

Here a proper embedded disk means a smooth embedding of the closed disk $D^2$ whose interior lies in the interior of $B^4$ and whose boundary circle lies in $S^3=\partial B^4$; the embedding is taken neat, so it meets $S^3$ transversely along $\partial D$ and carries a boundary collar. All homology below is singular homology.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the connected branched double cover $W_D$ has the rational homology of a point; smoothness and properness of the disk are exactly the hypotheses of that supplier.

The restriction of the covering map to $\partial B^4=S^3$ is the connected double cover branched along $\partial D=K$. Its monodromy sends a positive meridian of $K$ to the nontrivial element of $\mathbb Z/2$, because a meridian disk normal to $D$ has local branched model $z\mapsto z^2$. Therefore its oriented boundary is precisely $\Sigma_2(K)$ under [F1]. The supplier was used only for smooth disks, so no topological-disk conclusion follows.

Removing an open four-ball from the interior gives a Spin$^c$ cobordism $W$ with boundary $-S^3\sqcup Y$, and each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism on rational homology. In both orientations, the induced Heegaard Floer infinity map is an isomorphism of degree zero and the corresponding plus-map inequality gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge0$ and $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le0$.

derivations.claim: The forward punctured-cobordism map gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge0$ by [F1].

citations.quote:
Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$ be a typed nonempty unoriented regular
link diagram with finite crossing set $C(D)$. At each crossing use the chart
with the over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins the left endpoints and the
right endpoints with weight $A$, while B joins the top endpoints and bottom
endpoints with weight $A^{-1}$. The Kauffman bracket state-sum algorithm
terminates after exactly $2^{|C(D)|}$ state visits and returns
$$\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1},$$
where $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count the two smoothing types and $|S|$ counts the
circles in the smoothed diagram. The algorithm takes a mathematical diagram
as input and makes no claim about parsing strings or rejecting malformed
encodings.

Input a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings,
fixed finite orderings of its arcs and crossings, and an odd prime $p$. The algorithm returns the full set
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$ of assignments of residues in $\mathbb F_p$ to the
arcs satisfying the Fox crossing equations, together with
$|\operatorname{Col}_p(D)|$.

1. Create one variable $x_j$ for each arc in the supplied order, and process
   crossings in the supplied order.
2. At each crossing with overarc $o$ and the two underarcs $i$ and $j$, append
   the homogeneous linear equation $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.
   At a crossing, add the coefficients of any repeated arc in that row.
3. Set the next pivot-row index to $r=1$ and process columns from left to
   right. If $r>c$, mark this and every remaining column free and stop. If
   $r\le c$, search rows $r,\ldots,c$ in order for the first nonzero entry in
   the current column. If none exists, mark this column free and continue
   without changing $r$. Otherwise swap the selected row into row $r$, divide
   row $r$ by its nonzero entry in this column, and add multiples of row $r$
   to every other row to clear this column. Record this column as a pivot
   column with pivot row $r$, then increase $r$ by one. After the scan, every
   column not recorded as a pivot column is free.
4. List the free columns in increasing order and enumerate every tuple in
   $\mathbb F_p^f$ in lexicographic order using the residue representatives
   $0,\ldots,p-1$, where $f$ is the number of free columns. If $f=0$, process
   the empty tuple once. For each tuple, assign its coordinates to the free
   variables. For each pivot row, set its pivot variable equal to the negative
   of the sum of the row's free-column coefficients times those assigned free
   variables. Append the resulting assignment in the supplied arc order.
   Return all appended assignments and their number.

For every odd prime $p$ and every finite regular oriented link diagram $D$,
the algorithm in the Definition terminates and returns exactly
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$. If its reduced system has $f$ free variables, it
returns $p^f$ colorings. For a diagram with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings it uses
at most $\min(a,c)$ pivots, at most $ac$ pivot-search entry tests, at most $ac$
row additions to clear pivot columns, at most $a^2c$ coefficient updates in
those row additions, and at most $a^2$ divisions to normalize pivot rows.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. A Fox $p$-coloring of a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ assigns an element of $\mathbb F_p$ to each arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing, where $x_o$ is the overarc color and $x_i,x_j$ are the two underarc colors. If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move of type R1, R2, or R3, restriction outside the move disk gives a bijection from the Fox $p$-colorings of $D$ to those of $D'$. Consequently the number of Fox $p$-colorings is unchanged along every finite sequence of such moves. The local bijections use no choice principle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The stated incidences and [F3] give the equations $2x_1-x_2-x_3=0$, $2x_2-x_3-x_1=0$, and $2x_3-x_1-x_2=0$. In $\mathbb F_3$, $-1=2$, so all three rows are $(2,2,2)$. Row reduction leaves one nonzero row and two zero rows, hence one pivot and two free variables. By [F4], the algorithm returns $3^2=9$ trefoil colorings.
The crossingless unknot has one arc and no crossing equations, so its matrix has one column and zero rows, rank zero, and one free variable. By [F4], it has $3^1=3$ colorings.

The crossing equation $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ is symmetric in the two underarc colors and independent of strand arrows, so reversing a component orientation does not change its Fox coloring set. If the trefoil and unknot were ambient-isotopic as unoriented knots, choose their orientations so the equivalence preserves orientation. By [A1] and [F6] the oriented diagrams would then be joined by a finite Reidemeister sequence, and [F5] would force equal coloring counts. The computed values $9$ and $3$ contradict this, so the underlying knot types are distinct.

current_manifest_record.title: Haken–Jaco–Tollefson normal-surface unknot search
current_manifest_record.statement:
**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or oriented planar-diagram code in the code conventions of the planar-code definition, and a mode, either **Haken** or **JT**.

**Output:** The first validation error with its witness; **not-a-knot** for a valid code with more than one component; **disk-certificate** with a normal-coordinate vector and its finite witness data; or **no-candidate** after the selected search is exhausted.

**Procedure:**

1. Run the planar-code validation procedure. Return its first invalid result if validation fails. If the validated code represents more than one component, return **not-a-knot**.
2. Let $n$ be its crossing count. Construct the good triangulated exterior $E$ with $t\le C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and the marked original meridian path.
3. In Haken mode, enumerate all vectors $v\in\mathbb Z^{7t}$ with $0\le v_i\le t2^{7t+2}$ in lexicographic order. Discard a vector unless it is nonzero and satisfies all matching equations and quadrilateral restrictions. To test whether the remaining vector is fundamental, enumerate all integer vectors $u$ with $0\le u_i\le v_i$ in lexicographic order. Mark $v$ decomposable if some $u$ and $v-u$ are both nonzero and both satisfy all matching equations and quadrilateral restrictions; otherwise mark $v$ fundamental. Discard every decomposable vector. Fundamentalness supplies connectedness. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first vector passing these tests; return **no-candidate** after the finite box is exhausted.
4. In JT mode, let $A$ be the integer matching matrix and put $m=7t$. Enumerate all subsets $Z\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in lexicographic order. For each $Z$, append the equations $v_i=0$ for $i\in Z$ to $Av=0$. If the combined matrix has rank $m-1$ and its one-dimensional kernel contains a nonzero nonnegative vector, compute the unique relatively prime nonnegative integer generator $v$ of that ray. Require that its positive-coordinate support be exactly the complement of $Z$; this visits each ray once, at its exact zero-coordinate support. Discard vectors that violate the quadrilateral restriction. A primitive generator on an extreme ray is fundamental, so its surface is connected. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first passing vector; return **no-candidate** after all subsets have been processed.

The candidate tests use the boundary arcs and Euler-characteristic data computed from the compressed normal coordinates. No correctness or complexity assertion is part of this algorithm definition.

current_manifest_record.title: Connected-diagram bracket span bound and alternating equality
current_manifest_record.statement: For a connected regular link diagram $D$ with $c$ crossings, the Laurent-polynomial span of its Kauffman bracket is at most $4c$. If $D$ is reduced and alternating, then changing any one crossing from the all-$A$ state or the all-$B$ state merges two distinct state circles, both extreme coefficients are nonzero, and the bracket span is exactly $4c$. The span of a nonzero Laurent polynomial is its largest exponent minus its smallest exponent.
current_manifest_record.strategy: Bound state degrees by the all-A and all-B states, use the connected saddle surface to show the two extreme circle counts sum to at most c+2, then use checkerboard faces and reducedness to obtain equality and noncancelling extreme terms.
