citations.quote: A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

Let $P\subset S^2$ be the finite connected 4-valent graph underlying a regular link projection. Its complementary regions have exactly two colorings with two colors such that regions sharing an edge have different colors.

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.

If a connected plane graph has vertex, edge and face sets $V,E,F$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]), then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=2.$$

Deletion is as in [[def-graph-deletion-contraction-minor-and-subdivision]], the tree boundary case uses [[prop-plane-forest-has-one-face]], and the finite induction is [[thm-induction-principle]].
For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

derivations.claim:
Let $\mu$ be the number of components represented by $D$. By [F8],
$$(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle\big|_{A=1}=(-2)^{\mu-1}\ne0.$$
The writhe-normalizing factor is a Laurent monomial and hence a unit, so $\langle D\rangle$ is nonzero and its span is defined. Now let $s_A$ and $s_B$ be the numbers of circles in the all-$A$ and all-$B$ states. If a state has $j$ $B$-smoothings, then its weight factor is $A^{c-2j}$. A single smoothing change is a band surgery and changes the circle count by exactly $1$ or $-1$, so a state with $k$ circles has $k\le s_A+j$. Since the highest degree of $\delta^{k-1}$ is $2(k-1)$, every state term has degree at most $c-2j+2(k-1)\le c+2(s_A-1)$. Reversing $A$ and $B$ gives minimum degree at least $-c-2(s_B-1)$. Hence $\operatorname{span}_A\langle D\rangle\le2c+2(s_A+s_B-2)$.

If $c>0$, the connected projection has finite disk faces. To see this, thicken a spanning tree to a disk, then add the remaining edge strips one at a time. The core of each added edge lies in one complementary disk and is a properly embedded arc there. Its strip cuts that disk along the arc; after rounding corners, the two new boundary curves are smooth Jordan curves, and [F7] makes their closed sides disks. At each stage the new edge lies in one old region and splits it into exactly the two regions adjacent to the new edge, so these disk complements correspond one-to-one to the projection regions. Thus each complementary region has a disk core disjoint from the graph. Now suppose $D$ is reduced and alternating. Color its regions by [F3]. At one crossing choose the color name so the $A$-smoothing follows the two black sectors. Moving along a projection arc to the next crossing, alternation switches which branch is over; the chart definition of the $A$-smoothing therefore continues to follow the same color. Connectedness propagates this choice to every crossing. Thus the all-$A$ state circles trace the black disk cores and the all-$B$ circles trace the white disk cores. Embed the black Tait graph by placing vertices in black cores and drawing each crossing edge through its crossing disk; its complementary faces are precisely the white disk cores. Hence it is connected by [F6], has $c$ edges, $s_A$ vertices, and $s_B$ faces by [F4]. Euler's formula [F5] gives $s_A-c+s_B=2$.

Suppose $c>0$. Put the all-$A$ state on the lower level $S^2\times\{0\}$ and the all-$B$ state on the upper level $S^2\times\{1\}$. Outside the crossing disks, join corresponding state arcs by product rectangles; inside each crossing disk, join the two local smoothings by one saddle cobordism. The resulting compact surface $\Sigma$ has boundary the $s_A+s_B$ state circles and exactly $c$ index-one saddles, hence $\chi(\Sigma)=-c$. Form a bipartite incidence graph with one vertex for each state circle and one for each saddle, joining a saddle to every state circle containing one of its attaching arcs. It is connected: each projection edge lies on one all-A and one all-B state circle, both incident to the saddles at its endpoints, and the projection is connected. Every state circle contains a projection edge, so it is incident to a saddle. Thus $\Sigma$ is connected. Cap each boundary circle by a disk, obtaining a connected closed surface $\widehat\Sigma$ with $\chi(\widehat\Sigma)=s_A+s_B-c$. Give it a finite cellulation and take cellular chains $C_i$ over $\mathbb F_2$, with boundary maps $\partial_i$. If $r_i=\operatorname{rank}\partial_i$ and $h_i=\dim H_i$, then rank-nullity gives $\dim C_i=h_i+r_i+r_{i+1}$; alternating the sum over $i=0,1,2$ cancels the $r_i$ terms and yields $\chi(\widehat\Sigma)=h_0-h_1+h_2$. Connectedness gives $h_0=1$. A 2-cycle has equal coefficients on the two faces adjacent to every edge; the dual graph of a connected closed surface is connected, so all face coefficients agree and $h_2=1$. Therefore $\chi(\widehat\Sigma)=2-h_1\le2$, and $s_A+s_B-c\le2$. For $c=0$, a connected projection is one circle and $s_A=s_B=1$, giving the same inequality. Combining this bound with step 1.1 proves $\operatorname{span}_A\langle D\rangle\le4c$.

At any crossing, reducedness in [F2] says the two black sectors belong to distinct black regions and the two white sectors belong to distinct white regions. The all-$A$ smoothing circles trace the black regions, so changing one crossing from all-$A$ joins two distinct state circles by a band and merges them; the all-$B$ change similarly merges two distinct white state circles. If a state changes $j\ge1$ crossings from all-$A$, the first change lowers the circle count to $s_A-1$, and each later change can increase it by at most one; hence its circle count is at most $s_A+j-2$. Its term's degree is therefore at most $c-2j+2(s_A+j-3)=c+2(s_A-3)$, four below the all-$A$ term's top degree $c+2(s_A-1)$. The all-$A$ term has top coefficient $(-1)^{s_A-1}\ne0$, so it cannot cancel. The same argument at all-$B$ proves a nonzero bottom coefficient. When $c=0$, the single state has bracket $1$, and the same conclusions hold vacuously.

Using $s_A+s_B=c+2$ from step 1.2, the highest degree minus the lowest degree is $\bigl(c+2(s_A-1)\bigr)-\bigl(-c-2(s_B-1)\bigr)=2c+2(s_A+s_B-2)=4c$. The extreme coefficients are nonzero by step 2.2, so this is the actual bracket span. The $c=0$ case has span $0=4c$.

citations.quote:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

derivations.claim: Use source coordinates $(u,v)$ with their standard positive orientation and positive projection coordinates $(t,x)$ on the braid box. For $h>0$, the map $(t,x)=(v,-2hu)$ has determinant $2h>0$. It sends the source over direction $(1,1)$ to $(1,-2h)$ and the source under direction $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is $4h>0$. The source left/right pairs have constant $u$, hence constant braid position $x$ and give the through pairing $I$; the source top/bottom pairs have constant $v$, hence constant braid time $t$ and give the cup-cap $e_i$. The displayed page coordinates $(x,t)$ reverse the positive projection orientation; their visual quarter-turn is not the orientation comparison.
